一句话：给光栅化的 3DGS 管线加一个稀疏可见性预言机，补上缺失的遮挡信息，实现材质与光照分解。

要点：

  • 标准 3DGS 光栅化没有真实可见性，逆渲染分解质量受限
  • 用基于点的射线追踪构建稀疏可见性预言机
  • 按采样光照方向估计高斯基元的透射率加权遮挡

为什么值得看：3DGS 从「能看」走向「能重光照、能编辑」的关键一环，直接影响引擎里的动态光照方案。

中文摘要：作者研究基于 3D 高斯泼溅（3DGS）的逆渲染，重点是为重光照以及材质、光照分解引入显式可见性建模。方法在标准光栅化 3DGS 管线上增加一个稀疏可见性预言机，从采样光照方向估计高斯基元的透射率加权遮挡。该预言机用基于点的射线追踪实现，在不放弃实时光栅化性能的前提下补上遮挡信息，提升重光照与材质分解质量。

来源：arXiv·cs.GR 最新（English） 相关度：13.1 正文：41300 字 / 16 图

作者：Sven Kluge、Oliver Staadt

分类：cs.CV / cs.GR

接收/备注：10 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Published at WSCG 2026 ｜ WSCG 2026, Computer Science Research Notes (CSRN) Vol. 3601, pp. 131-140 ｜ DOI 10.24132/CSRN.2026-E17

PDF：https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.19847v1

命中：gaussian splatting、gaussian、splatting、lighting、occlusion、relight

We address inverse rendering with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by introducing explicit visibility modeling for relighting as well as material and light decomposition. Our approach augments the standard rasterized 3DGS pipeline with a sparse visibility oracle that estimates transmittance-weighted occlusion for Gaussian primitives from sampled lighting directions. This oracle is implemented using a

VisibilitySplat: Ray-Traced Occlusion for Relighting with 3D Gaussian Splatting

Sven KlugeUniversity of RostockAlbert-Einstein-Straße 2218059 Rostock, Germanysven.kluge@uni-rostock.deOliver StaadtUniversity of RostockAlbert-Einstein-Straße 2218059 Rostock, Germanyoliver.staadt@uni-rostock.de

ABSTRACT

We address inverse rendering with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by introducing explicit visibility modeling for relighting as well as material and light decomposition. Our approach augments the standard rasterized 3DGS pipeline with a sparse visibility oracle that estimates transmittance-weighted occlusion for Gaussian primitives from sampled lighting directions. This oracle is implemented using a point-based ray tracer accelerated by a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) and queried sparsely within the inverse-rendering objectives, while the original 3DGS loop is retained for training efficiency, interactive visualization, and tooling compatibility. Shading follows a physically based rendering (PBR) formulation with a principled microfacet bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) and low-resolution high-dynamic-range (HDR) environment maps. We evaluate our method on the TensoIR synthetic dataset against baselines based on neural radiance fields (NeRFs), tensor representations, and 3DGS. The results show competitive performance and improvements over several earlier baselines for novel-view synthesis (NVS), albedo reconstruction, and relighting. Ablations indicate that explicit visibility modeling is an important contributor to relighting and material-illumination disentanglement, while pure PBR supervision can favor appearance fitting in NVS. Overall, the findings suggest that sparse, point-based visibility queries effectively complement rasterized splatting for inverse rendering while preserving the practical advantages of the 3DGS ecosystem.

Keywords

inverse rendering; 3D Gaussian splatting; relighting; visibility; physically based rendering

1

Inverse rendering (IR) seeks to recover geometry, reflectance, and illumination from images by inverting the image formation process. Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) enable high-fidelity novel-view synthesis (NVS) and have been extended toward relightable decompositions under unknown illumination (e.g., NeRFactor and TensoIR ), but their implicit volumetric formulation is costly to train and render. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) instead optimizes explicit point primitives via differentiable rasterization, enabling real-time rendering and practical tooling, and has recently been adopted for IR (e.g., 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering (GS-IR) and Gaussian Inverse Rendering (GIR) ). A key challenge is visibility: screen-space alpha compositing provides limited information about cast shadows and mutual occlusion, which are crucial for stabilizing material-light disentanglement under unknown illumination. While 3DGS-based IR pipelines benefit from fast forward rendering, visibility signals derived from the rasterizer alone can be too weak or too view-dependent to constrain shadows robustly. Recent work, including Inter-Reflective Gaussian Splatting (IRGS), therefore augments splatting with ray-based visibility estimation . We take a pragmatic step along this trajectory by adding a sparse visibility oracle that estimates transmittance-weighted occlusion from sampled lighting directions, while retaining the original 3DGS rasterization loop for training efficiency and interactive visualization. This lightweight division of labor injects physically meaningful visibility constraints without replacing the splatting renderer (Fig. ). Rather than proposing a highly specialized approximation or learned visibility model, we deliberately study a direct formulation based on explicit visibility queries. This provides a reference baseline for assessing how much transmittance-weighted visibility contributes to IR and relighting with 3DGS. Our contributions are as follows: (i) a sparse visibility oracle for 3DGS that estimates how much light reaches each Gaussian from sampled environment directions, implemented with a point-based ray tracer accelerated by a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH); (ii) a reference baseline on the TensoIR synthetic benchmark, including comparisons to NeRF-based, tensor-based, and 3DGS-based IR methods and ablations that isolate the effect of explicit visibility.[]25[]41[]18[]19[]22[]30[, ]14151

2

2.1

The original NeRF method introduced neural volumetric representations for NVS, with subsequent work improving anti-aliasing and efficiency via scale-aware integration and more explicit encodings . 3DGS further shifts computation to explicit anisotropic Gaussian primitives rendered by a custom rasterizer, enabling real-time performance. Geometry-oriented variants and BVH-based Gaussian ray tracing broaden the representation toward editing and secondary-ray effects.[]25[, , , , , , ]2342713127[]19[, ]1637[]26

2.2

IR aims to recover geometry, materials, and illumination from images and is intrinsically ill-posed. Early NeRF-based methods reduced ambiguity with simplifying assumptions: PhySG represents bidirectional reflectance distribution functions (BRDFs) and lighting using spherical Gaussians (SGs) but omits complex visibility and indirect transport. NeRFactor factorizes shape and reflectance under unknown lighting. InvRender derives spatially varying indirect illumination directly from the learned radiance field to improve albedo recovery. Ref-NeRF improves specular handling via a reflected-radiance parameterization that also yields better normals. To raise physical fidelity without losing efficiency, TensoIR builds on tensor-factorized fields to support on-the-fly visibility queries and second-bounce effects during reconstruction. Complementary surface-aligned fields stabilize geometry and normals for IR pipelines . More recent work targets illumination modeling itself: ENVIDR learns a neural environment for shiny scenes. NeRF-as-Emitter replaces the distant-light assumption with a near-field light NeRF, improving accuracy under spatially varying illumination, and NeILF++ jointly learns incident-light and outgoing-radiance fields with inter-reflections to better disentangle material and lighting.Neural fields for inverse rendering:[]39[]41[]42[]31[]18[, ]3532[]21[]23[]38

Adopting 3DGS for IR leverages real-time forward rendering but introduces new challenges: splats lack native surface normals, and forward splatting does not natively model occlusion or multi-bounce light. GS-IR addresses these by regularizing per-Gaussian normals and baking visibility for secondary effects while recovering geometry, spatially varying bidirectional reflectance distribution functions (SVBRDFs), and environment lighting under unknown illumination. Subsequent work deepens physical correctness: GaussianShader estimates robust normals and per-splat shading for reflective scenes. DeferredGS decouples geometry from lighting and performs deferred shading for editable relighting and Ref-Gaussian targets glossy reflections with a specialized deferred pipeline. Beyond perfect mirrors, SSS-GS introduces subsurface scattering to a 3DGS framework using an explicit surface plus an implicit scattering component. To improve general relighting, RNG conditions radiance on view and light directions with shadow cues and depth refinement, while BiGS unifies surface and volumetric materials via bidirectional spherical harmonics (SH), supporting near- and distant-light setups. Finally, GI-GS explicitly decomposes direct/indirect components and uses lightweight path tracing on a G-buffer for multi-bounce global illumination, bringing 3DGS-based IR closer to physically faithful relighting at interactive rates. These efforts are complementary to geometry-focused 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) and surface extraction with Gaussian Opacity Fields (GOF) , as well as to BVH-accelerated Gaussian ray tracing for secondary-ray phenomena .Gaussian splatting for inverse rendering:[]22[]17[]33[]34[]10[]11[]24[]8[]16[]37[]26

3

3.1

3DGS  is a method for rendering 3D scenes in real time, offering high visual quality and fast training. A scene is represented as a cloud of anisotropic 3D Gaussians:[]19

$g_{i}(x)=e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu_{i})^{T}\Sigma^{-1}_{i}(x-\mu_{i})}$ (1)

with mean $\mu_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and covariance $\Sigma_{i}$ .

The complete parameter set for each Gaussian is defined as $G_{i}=(\mu_{i},\Sigma_{i},\alpha_{i},c_{i})$ , where the mean $\mu_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ specifies the position, the full covariance $\Sigma_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}$ encodes the ellipsoidal footprint, $\alpha_{i}$ denotes the opacity, and $c_{i}$ is the color, stored as a set of SH coefficients. The covariance matrix $\Sigma_{i}$ can be decomposed into a scaling matrix $\mathbf{S}_{i}=\mathrm{diag}(s_{x},s_{y},s_{z})$ and a rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}_{i}$ constructed from a unit quaternion $\mathbf{q}$ , which results in $\Sigma_{i}=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{S}^{T}\mathbf{R}^{T}$ .

With the extrinsic camera matrix $\mathbf{T}$ and intrinsic camera matrix $\mathbf{K}$ , the screen-space mean $\mu^{\prime}_{i}$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma^{\prime}$ are defined as

$\mu^{\prime}_{i}=\mathbf{KT}[\mu_{i},1]^{T},\quad\Sigma^{\prime}=\mathbf{JT}\Sigma\mathbf{T}^{T}\mathbf{J}^{T}$ (2)

where $\mathbf{J}$ is the Jacobian matrix of the affine approximation of the perspective projection .[]43

The final color at pixel $u$ is obtained by depth-sorting Gaussians and accumulating color in a front-to-back manner:

$\hat{C}=\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}T_{i}g_{i}\alpha_{i}c_{i},\quad T_{i}=\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}(1-g_{j}\alpha_{j})$ (3)

where $T_{i}$ denotes the accumulated transmittance, and for readability we use the shorthand $g_{i}\equiv g_{i}(u\mid\mu^{\prime}_{i},\Sigma^{\prime}_{i})$ .

3.2

We follow a physically based rendering (PBR) formulation similar to recent IR systems such as TensoIR , NeRFactor , and GS-IR . Image formation is expressed by the surface rendering equation with geometric visibility and an energy-conserving microfacet BRDF, while geometry, reflectance, and illumination are represented by differentiable fields and optimized from multi-view images. Formally,[]18[]41[]22

$L_{o}(\mathbf{x},\omega_{o})=\int_{\Omega}f_{r}(\mathbf{x},\omega_{i},\omega_{o})L_{i}(\mathbf{x},\omega_{i})V(\mathbf{x},\omega_{i})(\mathbf{n}\cdot\omega_{i})d\omega_{i}.$ (4)

Here, $\mathbf{x}$ is the shaded surface point, $\omega_{o}$ is the outgoing view direction, and $\omega_{i}$ is an incident lighting direction integrated over the hemisphere $\Omega$ around the surface normal $\mathbf{n}$ . $L_{o}$ and $L_{i}$ denote outgoing and incident radiance, $f_{r}$ is the BRDF, $V\in[0,1]$ is the visibility or transmittance term, and $(\mathbf{n}\cdot\omega_{i})$ is the cosine foreshortening factor.

For reflectance, we adopt a reduced principled microfacet model in the Disney family and remove the metallic degree of freedom to keep the inverse problem better constrained. We use a fixed dielectric base reflectance $F_{0}=0.04$ , and write[]6

$\displaystyle f_{r}$ $\displaystyle=f_{diff}+f_{spec},$ (5) $\displaystyle f_{spec}$ $\displaystyle=\frac{D(\mathbf{h})G(\omega_{i},\omega_{o})F(\omega_{o}\cdot\mathbf{h};F_{0}=0.04)}{4(\mathbf{n}\cdot\omega_{i})(\mathbf{n}\cdot\omega_{o})}$

where $D$ is the normal-distribution function, $G$ is the masking-shadowing term, and $F$ is the Fresnel term (typically Schlick) evaluated with fixed $F_{0}$ . Roughness controls the lobe width. Fixing $F_{0}$ and removing metallicity reduces the number of learnable appearance parameters, which improves stability in this under-constrained setting while retaining a physically plausible BRDF.

In practice, illumination is computed by evaluating the integral over scene lights and/or an environment map together with the visibility term $V$ . Many IR systems employ this same BRDF formulation but differ in how geometry, visibility, and indirect effects are estimated. For example, TensoIR introduces efficient online visibility and secondary shading, NeRFactor learns a visibility field, and GS-IR attaches BRDF parameters to Gaussians with an occlusion approximation.

3.3

Accurate recovery of incident illumination is essential for robust IR. We model distant lighting as a high-dynamic-range (HDR) spherical environment map parameterized in equirectangular coordinates . Unlike SGs or mixtures of SGs, this image-based representation preserves high-frequency angular detail and thus supports sharp cast shadows without requiring many analytic lobes.[]9

Each HDR environment-map texel stores radiance $L$ , and we optimize these values directly during training with solid-angle compensation to account for the non-uniform texel area of equirectangular maps.

Because reflectance acts as an angular low-pass filter, the recoverable illumination bandwidth is limited by the object’s BRDF lobes . Accordingly, we use a compact environment-map parameterization, with concrete settings summarized in the implementation details paragraph.[]29

3.4

Reconstructing scene geometry, in particular surface normals, is essential for IR and PBR.

We estimate depth with the expected depth $z_{E}$ of the Gaussian mixture along each ray, obtained by linearly accumulating depth samples $z_{i}$ and normalizing by the accumulated weight:Depth estimation:

$z_{E}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}w_{i}z_{i}}{W},\;W=\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}w_{i},\;w_{i}=T_{i}g_{i}\alpha_{i}.$ (6)

We evaluate alternative depth formulations, including inverse-depth variants, and find that expected depth provides the best overall reconstruction quality and the most stable downstream supervision in our setting. We therefore use $z_{E}$ as the geometric signal for pseudo-normal supervision in optimization and for computing surface positions that initialize ray-tracing queries.

Purely gradient-based normals derived from rendered depth are sensitive to noise and often lack multi-view consistency when applied to 3D Gaussian surfaces. We therefore assign each Gaussian $i$ a learnable unit normal $n_{i}$ and compute per-pixel predictions using splatting weights $w_{i}=T_{i}g_{i}\alpha_{i}$ :Normal estimation:

$\tilde{n}=\frac{\sum^{N}_{i=1}w_{i}n_{i}}{\sum^{N}_{i=1}w_{i}+\epsilon_{n}},\quad\hat{n}=\frac{\tilde{n}}{\|\tilde{n}\|_{2}+\epsilon_{n}},$ (7)

where $\epsilon_{n}$ is a small constant for numerical stability. As a geometry-anchored target, we derive pseudo-normals from expected depth $z_{E}$ . World-space normals $\hat{n}_{\nabla}$ are obtained from image-space gradients $\nabla z_{E}=(\partial_{x}z_{E},\partial_{y}z_{E})$ , and predictions are aligned to this estimate with

$\mathcal{L}_{n-p}=||\hat{n}-\hat{n}_{\nabla}||.$ (8)

To further smooth predictions, we follow GS-IR  and add a total variation (TV) loss $TV_{normal}$ .[]22

The overall normal objective is

$\mathcal{L}_{n}=\mathcal{L}_{n-p}+\lambda_{n-TV}TV_{normal},$ (9)

and is optimized jointly with the photometric loss $\mathcal{L}_{c}$ of the splatting model.

3.5

In our pipeline, the ray tracer is not used as a replacement renderer. It serves as a sparse visibility oracle for evaluating transmittance along sampled light directions.

The 3DGS rasterizer is a highly optimized, tile-based renderer: for each screen-space tile it collects all projected splats overlapping the tile, sorts them in front-to-back order, and evaluates color and opacity via elliptical weighted average (EWA) splatting in that order. This design delivers excellent throughput for primary views but is tied to camera projection and ordered blending per tile.[]43

A point-based ray tracer allows us to evaluate Gaussian splatting from any point in space in any direction. The 3D starting points for our rays are computed from the expected-depth map $z_{E}$ . Following 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing (3DGRT) , each 3D Gaussian is enclosed by an anisotropically stretched regular icosahedron and the triangles of this proxy mesh are inserted into a BVH for fast ray-triangle traversal. The proxy is scaled so that it tightly bounds the region where the particle’s response exceeds a small minimum $\epsilon$ . The scale explicitly incorporates the particle’s opacity $\alpha$ so that nearly transparent splats receive proportionally tighter bounds (”adaptive clamping”), which reduces false-positive hits during traversal. Rays then query the BVH to gather the next batch of intersections, evaluate contributions in sorted order, and early-terminate once the accumulated transmittance reaches a preset threshold.[]26

For occlusion-only queries, we use the fact that transmittance along a ray can be accumulated multiplicatively $T\leftarrow T\cdot(1-\Delta_{a_{i}})$ where $\Delta_{a_{i}}$ is the per-hit attenuation computed from the Gaussian’s line integral along the ray segment covered by the proxy. Because multiplication commutes, the hits need not be depth-sorted for this visibility pass. They can be processed in arbitrary order while maintaining correctness for $T$ . We early-terminate when $T\leq T_{stop}$ . In practice, $T_{stop}$ should match the early-out used by the rasterizer to keep consistency between visibility estimated by ray tracing and the screen-space renderer. To make the ray tracer a drop-in companion to standard 3DGS (so we can reuse pretrained point clouds and the existing rasterizer), we evaluate Gaussians on a ray with the same EWA-splatting formulation as the rasterizer. For a ray $r(t)=o+td$ , we instantiate a one-pixel virtual camera at $o$ whose optical axis is $d$ (i.e., a local camera frame aligned with the ray). We then reuse the unmodified rasterizer to splat exactly the Gaussians reported by the BVH for that ray into the center pixel of this virtual camera. This yields consistent blending with the original tile-based renderer while allowing us to drive the evaluation from rays rather than from a full image plane.

Alternative ray-based renderers make different evaluation choices that deviate from EWA splatting: 3DGRT evaluates each Gaussian at the maximum response along the ray and processes batches of intersections in sorted order using a k-buffer scheme. IRGS collapses 3D Gaussians to planar 2D Gaussian disks to obtain a closed-form ray-splat intersection. These choices are effective but generally require training with their respective renderer to avoid a mismatch with classic 3DGS splatting.[]26[]15[]16

3.6

Our optimization method consists of a two-stage strategy, as shown in Fig. .2

The first step in our optimization pipeline is pretraining a standard Gaussian model with the extension that we jointly train the normal $\hat{n}$ . During this stage, we observe partially transparent regions where background color can leak through the object silhouette. To address this, we add an opacity-mask lossInitial stage.

$\mathcal{L}_{mask}=||\hat{\alpha}-M||_{1},$ (10)

where $\hat{\alpha}$ is the rendered opacity and $M$ is the binary foreground mask. By measuring the deviation of Gaussian splats from the expected surface, we find that this term reduces that deviation and pulls splats closer to the surface, yielding a better-defined geometry proxy for our ray-tracing pass.

We use the color reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{c}$ from standard Gaussian splatting, the normal loss $\mathcal{L}_{n}$ , and the opacity-mask loss $\mathcal{L}_{mask}$ . The full loss function for our initial stage is:

$\mathcal{L}_{init}=\mathcal{L}_{c}+\mathcal{L}_{n}+\lambda_{mask}\mathcal{L}_{mask}.$ (11)

After pretraining the 3D Gaussian model, we freeze geometric Gaussian attributes (positions, covariance, opacity, and normals) and optimize BRDF material parameters jointly with the HDR environment map. We use an L1 photometric loss $\mathcal{L}^{pbr}_{1}$ with unit weight in this stage. For reproducibility, Tab.  enumerates trainable/frozen variables and active losses for both stages.Second stage.1

Implementation-specific optimization and runtime settings are summarized in the implementation details paragraph below.

The visibility ray tracer is implemented with NVIDIA OptiX, and our Gaussian-splatting training and relighting pipeline is built on top of the Gaussian-splatting Python framework . We pretrain for 30,000 iterations in stage 1 and 400 iterations in stage 2. On an NVIDIA RTX A6000 graphics processing unit (GPU), stage 1 takes around 15 minutes and stage 2 around 10 minutes. We observe that longer second-stage training degrades relighting quality because the albedo begins to absorb illumination information. We use a compact $16\times 32$ environment map and normal-based hemisphere sampling, which halves the number of rays per pixel compared with full-sphere sampling. With a $16\times 32$ environment map, there are 512 candidate directions, after hemisphere culling and empty-space removal, the OptiX visibility pass takes approximately 436 ms at the evaluation resolution, corresponding to about 127 MRays/s. This measures only transmittance-weighted visibility queries. A full second-stage optimization iteration takes approximately 1.25 s/it, while final PBR relighting renders at about 0.83 s/image. Forward relighting spends about 55% of its time on visibility queries and 44% on BRDF/environment-map integration.Implementation details.GSplat[]36

4

We compare our method against previous state-of-the-art methods and also present an ablation study to isolate the contribution of each design component. Baselines are selected based on popularity and code availability.

Our evaluation focuses on masked single-object scenes. This choice narrows the range of real-world inverse-rendering ambiguities (e.g., clutter, contact shadows, interreflections, and segmentation errors), but it is technically motivated by our lighting model: we sample illumination from a distant environment map, and without modeling secondary bounces the incident radiance can vanish when the environment is occluded by surrounding structures. Isolated objects therefore provide a well-defined direct-lighting signal and allow us to isolate the effect of explicit visibility queries.

4.1

We report experimental results on the synthetic TensoIR dataset for IR of single objects. It contains four objects, each with reference images rendered under ten different lighting conditions, along with albedo and normal maps. We evaluate normal-estimation quality using mean angular error (MAE). For relighting, NVS, and albedo reconstruction, we report peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index (SSIM), and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) . Some results of our method for each model can be seen in Fig. .[]18[]405

Following prior work, we compensate for the inherent albedo-shading scale ambiguity by scaling each predicted albedo with a single global RGB factor that minimizes MSE to the ground truth . We do not apply color correction , all reported and visualized synthetic albedo results therefore use this scale normalization unless stated otherwise. To visualize the HDR environment maps, we follow TensoIR  and apply gamma tonemapping to convert HDR radiance to low-dynamic-range (LDR) values for display. NVS results are rendered using PBR with the estimated material parameters and environment lighting.[, , , , , , ]2014118223014[]5[]18

4.2

We compare our method with previous inverse rendering methods, NeRFactor , InvRender , NVDiffrec , GS-IR , TensoIR and IRGS on the TensoIR synthetic dataset. All comparisons are performed using multi-view images captured under unknown lighting conditions. Tab. summarizes the quantitative comparison and Fig. shows a visual comparison.[]41[]42[]28[]22[]18[]1523

Our method is competitive with prior 3DGS-based IR approaches and improves over several earlier baselines across NVS, albedo reconstruction, and relighting. However, IRGS achieves the best overall results on this benchmark. These results position VisibilitySplat as a direct explicit-visibility baseline that remains competitive with specialized 3DGS-based IR methods while retaining the standard rasterized 3DGS pipeline for training and visualization. We attribute our performance gains over earlier baselines primarily to the explicit visibility term: on masked, single-object scenes the dominant ambiguity is often cast-shadow visibility and mutual occlusion under direct environment lighting, while multi-bounce transport is comparatively weak. In this regime, sparse but physically grounded transmittance queries already provide a large part of the benefit for disentangling albedo and lighting. Compared to IRGS, our lightweight separation between rasterized splatting for efficient training/preview and sparse ray-based visibility queries offers a favorable practicality-accuracy trade-off, but still leaves room for improvement in terms of absolute reconstruction quality.[]15

Our main source of error is imperfect surface reconstruction rather than instability of the occlusion ray tracer. In particular, inaccurate normals lead to visibly curved shadow boundaries and local relighting artifacts (see Fig. ). This interpretation is consistent with our higher mean angular error compared to competing methods. Despite these geometric limitations, our relighting quality in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS remains competitive with state-of-the-art approaches.4(b)

At the measured $800\times 800$ evaluation resolution on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU, final PBR relighting takes about 0.83 s/image, so the current implementation is not real-time. Forward relighting time is dominated by explicit visibility queries (about 55%) and discrete BRDF/environment-map integration (about 44%), the remaining time is spent on standard 3D Gaussian splatting and minor overhead. Thus, real-time deployment would require optimizing both the visibility pass and the PBR integration.

4.3

We conduct an ablation study on the components of our method to validate their effectiveness. We report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS for NVS, albedo reconstruction, and relighting on the Lego model from the TensoIR Synthetic dataset (Tab. ), including a PBR-only baseline without visibility and without opacity-mask loss, as well as single-component removals.3

We disable both the visibility ray tracer and the opacity-mask loss and optimize with PBR supervision alone. Interestingly, this baseline yields the highest NVS PSNR (and lowest LPIPS), though not the highest SSIM. We attribute this behavior to stronger appearance fitting, where albedo absorbs more illumination information and therefore reproduces the training lighting more easily. However, this entanglement hurts decomposition: albedo reconstruction and relighting quality both degrade compared to the full model.PBR-only baseline.

To isolate the visibility term, we compare the variant (with opacity-mask loss retained) against the full model. Reintroducing explicit visibility improves relighting metrics and yields cleaner shadow behavior, indicating better separation of material and illumination.Visibility.without visibility

As described in the optimization section, this term mainly acts through improved geometric support for ray-based visibility queries. Comparing with the full model shows lower relighting quality. Removing the opacity-mask loss also decreases albedo PSNR, while albedo SSIM and LPIPS remain nearly unchanged. This suggests that coarse albedo structure is preserved but radiometric consistency degrades. Better-defined occluding geometry from opacity regularization allows visibility rays to produce cleaner shadow estimates, which in turn stabilizes relighting.Opacity mask loss.without opacity loss

5

We present VisibilitySplat, an IR approach that augments 3DGS with a sparse visibility oracle for transmittance-weighted occlusion. Implemented using BVH-accelerated point-based ray tracing, the oracle complements the standard rasterized 3DGS training and visualization loop while injecting explicit visibility cues for material-illumination disentanglement. On a synthetic benchmark, we improve over several baselines in PSNR for NVS, albedo reconstruction, and relighting, while remaining competitive in SSIM and LPIPS. Ablations suggest that explicit visibility queries primarily improve relighting and decomposition quality, even when a PBR-only variant can score higher on NVS appearance metrics.

Our evaluation targets single, masked, static objects, behavior in cluttered or dynamic scenes, or under imperfect segmentation, is not assessed. The illumination model accounts for direct lighting only. Indirect transport (interreflection, subsurface, participating media) and very high-frequency environment lighting are not modeled. Finally, experiments are restricted to synthetic data, robustness to real captures, complex materials (e.g., glass, hair, translucency), and sensor noise remains untested.Limitations.

Future extensions include multi-object and full-scene evaluation, incorporation of indirect lighting, tighter coupling between splatting and visibility (e.g., differentiable or cached variants), improved geometric robustness, and investigations toward real-time deployment and comprehensive testing on real datasets.Future work.

We will release the full implementation and supporting resources upon publication of this paper.Code availability.

item.title: AgentGarten：同时做到「忠实」与「逼真」的智能体训练世界 ｜ AgentGarten: Code Worlds for Evolving Agents
item.description:
一句话：把模拟器的状态一致性与视觉真实感解耦再组合，让智能体能在更多世界里训练。

要点：

  • 智能体能学到什么，受限于它训练时所在的环境
  • 好环境要同时满足：状态规则一致（faithful）与观察分布真实（realistic）
  • 框架把仿真与渲染解耦组合，跨世界复用组件

为什么值得看：如果做「AI 原生引擎」——用引擎批量生成训练环境——这篇给了环境设计的工程范式。

中文摘要：交互式虚拟世界让智能体通过探索与交互学习，但能学到什么受限于训练环境。理想环境必须既忠实（状态、规则、动力学一致）又真实（观察分布接近真实世界），而在多样世界上同时做到这两点一直是瓶颈。作者提出 AgentGarten 框架，把仿真与渲染解耦并组合，从而在不同世界间复用组件、批量产出可训练环境。

作者：Jiawei Chi、Shangchen Miao、Zhiyuan Shi 等 15 人

分类：cs.CV

接收/备注：Project page: https://mirros-lab.github.io/agent-garten

PDF：https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.12374v2

命中：renderer

[Extension=.otf,ItalicFont=lmromandemi10-oblique]lmromandemi10-regular MirroS Technical Report [Blog][Code][Project Page][Code worlds for evolving agents. : Diverse environments spanning distinct geometries, visual appearances, and interactive tasks. : Agents continuously evolve through environmental interactions, developing increasingly sophisticated strategies such as shelter-building and ramp-crossing.]\pdfauthor\metadatahttps://mirros.ai/blog/worlds-for-evolving-agents\metadatahttps://github.com/MirroS-Lab/AgentGarten\metadatahttps://mirros-lab.github.io/agent-garten\teaserfigure\captionleadfontTopBottom

AgentGarten: Code Worlds for Evolving Agents

MirroS Technical Report October 8, 2026

Abstract

Interactive virtual worlds allow agents to learn through exploration and interaction. What agents can learn is bounded by the environments they practice in, which must be , with consistent state, rules, and dynamics, and , with observations that follow the real-world visual distributions. Achieving both across diverse worlds remains a bottleneck. We introduce , a framework that couples simulators and game engines with a shared to build real-time interactive environments. Its simulation backends maintain persistent world state and execute program-defined interaction rules, while the renderer generates visual observations from structured conditions exported through a common interface. To build the neural renderer, we adapt a pretrained video model to geometry conditions, distill it with our proposed , and optimize inference for real-time interaction. Adversarial Forcing makes history prefilling differentiable through exact replay, so that losses on later predictions update how the renderer encodes prior observations, and adds real-data adversarial supervision to improve its visual quality. In AgentGarten, agents perceive the world through visual observations, interact with it in real time, and improve by distilling each round of experience into playbooks that subsequent agents inherit and refine. Our empirical study demonstrates a substantial gain in learning efficiency, with agents learning from just 4 rounds compared with millions for a conventional reinforcement learning counterpart. As new worlds can be written as code and rendered through the same interface, environments can scale in both number and difficulty alongside their agents, a step toward agents that keep evolving through interactive experience.faithfulrealisticAgentGartenneural rendererAdversarial Forcing

world models, code worlds, executable environments, neural rendering, autoregressive video generation, distribution matching distillation, agents

keywords

1

Agents learn from trajectories of actions and observations. Developing scalable, generalizable agent capabilities requires environments that not only faithfully preserve the consequences of past actions over extended interactions, but also support flexible variation in layouts, objects, and task rules. Across navigation, manipulation, and multi-agent interaction, scaling these environments therefore requires both controllable, inspectable dynamics and diverse visual observations.

However, existing approaches face a fundamental trade-off. Simulators and game engines support agent learning through explicit state and programmable interaction rules . Yet expanding their visual diversity entails substantial 3D asset creation and complex rendering pipelines, making new environments costly to build and customize. Conversely, video world models synthesize rich, interactive visual observations from data . In these models, however, task-relevant state and physical transition rules remain implicit within generated histories and learned representations, precluding direct inspection, editing, and testing of the environment’s behavior.[, , ]123[, , , ]4567

We introduce , a framework for building that combines programmable dynamics with a shared, real-time neural renderer (Figure ). In AgentGarten, each scene program runs in a simulator or game engine that maintains persistent state and executes explicit interaction rules. A shared neural renderer synthesizes the agent’s visual observations from structured conditions exported by the engine through a unified interface. This separation preserves rigorous control over state and rules while allowing compatible engines to share a single renderer. New environments can thus be authored by coding agents from text or image inputs, then edited and extended entirely in code without creating bespoke visual assets for every scene.AgentGartencode worlds1

Operating a video model as an interactive neural renderer requires it to strictly follow updated engine conditions, maintain visual consistency across extended rollouts, and synthesize observations in fine-grained, short blocks so that agents receive immediate feedback after brief actions. We adapt a pretrained bidirectional video model to structured conditions, convert it to block-causal generation, and distill it into a real-time renderer on a single GPU with , which trains the renderer on its own rollouts via distribution matching and introduces two key advances. First, to allow later losses to update the history-encoding computation without the memory cost of a fully differentiable rollout, we adopt two-pass training and introduce : a block-by-block execution schedule that eliminates numerical divergence between sampling and recomputation and achieves bitwise-identical recomputation of the rollout trajectory. Second, to prevent the visual degradation that score distillation alone exhibits over long rollouts, we incorporate a real-data adversarial objective and derive an exact R1/R2 regularization scheme for a discriminator with a frozen backbone, entirely avoiding double-backward passes through fused attention kernels.Adversarial Forcing[, , ]8910[]11exact replay[, ]1012

Code worlds provide rich environments for agents to practice and evolve. We evaluate pretrained foundation-model agents across rounds of interaction, where they perceive the world strictly through rendered observations, diagnose failures, and distill key insights into written inherited by subsequent rounds. In hide-and-seek , agents rapidly grounded abstract spatial knowledge into closed-loop physical execution, with ramp use and shelter construction emerging within a handful of games. The same reflective loop improved performance across rounds in several additional, diverse environments (Section ).playbooks[]135

Our contributions are: {contributions}

A framework for code worlds that couples persistent, editable environment state to a shared real-time neural renderer through structured conditions, enabling programmable interaction and diverse visual observations across compatible engines without per-scene visual asset authoring.

, a distillation method for a few-step, block-causal neural renderer. It combines distribution matching on self-rollouts with exact bitwise replay for history gradients, alongside a real-data adversarial objective whose exact R1/R2 regularization avoids double-backward through fused attention.Adversarial Forcing

An empirical study of evolving agents. Pretrained agents observing exclusively through neural rendering rapidly ground semantic tool knowledge and improve outcomes across rounds through written playbooks in hide-and-seek and several further distinct worlds.

2

2.1

A code world combines a scene program $p$ , an engine that executes it, and a neural renderer $R_{\theta}$ . The program specifies the scene and interaction rules. Let $s_{t}$ denote the scene state, including object poses, articulations, and task variables; $\pi_{t}$ the observing camera pose; and $a_{t}$ the actions of one or more agents. The engine updates the state and captures a structured condition $c_{t}$ from the camera:

$(s_{t+1},\pi_{t+1})=f_{p}(s_{t},\pi_{t},a_{t}),\qquad c_{t}=h_{p}(s_{t},\pi_{t}),$ (1)

where $f_{p}$ implements the state transition and $h_{p}$ renders the visible geometry. Given an appearance reference $x_{0}$ and a text description $y$ , the neural renderer generates subsequent observations from visual history $x_{ $x_{t}=R_{\theta}\!\left(x_{(2)

The agent receives $x_{t}$ and selects $a_{t}$ , which determines the next state and condition through Eq. ().1

Unlike a video world model, whose state resides in generated history, the transition $f_{p}$ takes no rendered observation as input: the renderer influences the state only through the actions that agents select, so rendering errors cannot accumulate in the state. A recorded state trajectory can consequently be rendered again under a different appearance reference or camera without altering the underlying events. Conversely, the renderer observes the state only through $c_{\leq t}$ ; attributes that the conditions leave undetermined, such as color and material, are specified by $x_{0}$ and $y$ and carried by the visual history. The renderer consumes conditions and visual history in blocks, as described in Section .3

2.2

We use colorized depth or surface normals as structured conditions. Both can be estimated from video or rendered by an engine, and their three-channel representation allows us to reuse the pretrained video encoder and Transformer. For real videos, we obtain depth with ViPE , using Depth Anything 3  as its depth backend, and normals with NormalCrafter . Simulated scenes supply these maps directly from geometry, without requiring detailed materials or textures. During training, each sample uses one randomly chosen modality (Section ).[]14[]15[]163.2

We encode depth with the Vision Banana mapping  and camera-space unit normals as $(n+1)/2$ , using consistent coordinate and orientation conventions across estimated and rendered maps (Appendix ).[]17A.2

2.3

A coding agent constructs a code world from either a single image or a text description, producing an executable scene program along with an appearance reference $x_{0}$ . Because appearance is delegated to the neural renderer, the scene program does not require detailed materials or leaf-level assets; it only needs coarse geometry that faithfully conveys layout, silhouettes, occlusion, and motion dynamics.

From an image.

The input image serves simultaneously as $x_{0}$ and the reference layout (Figure ). Perception and generation models lift the visible content into instance masks , monocular depth and camera intrinsics , 3D bounding boxes , and extracted object meshes . A coding agent fits these assets to the estimated geometry, completes unobserved regions as plausible spatial extensions, and binds physical properties and interaction rules.2[]18[]15[]19[]20

From text and agentic refinement.

When building from text, the agent writes the scene program directly using geometric primitives and engine assets. An initial render is transformed into $x_{0}$ via an image editing model while preserving scene layout. In both modalities, the agent refines the scene through an interactive feedback loop: it evaluates test rollouts from multiple probe cameras, inspects engine verification queries (contact, collision clearance, and occlusion), and iteratively repairs faulty poses, unsupported structures, or ambiguous motions before deployment.

3

We train a geometry-conditioned autoregressive video model to implement the renderer in Section . Starting from a pretrained bidirectional backbone, training proceeds through geometry conditioning, teacher-forcing adaptation, and . The final stage combines distribution matching on the model’s own rollouts with exact history-gradient replay and real-data adversarial training. A bounded key–value cache and streaming decoding support continuous inference within the interaction loop in Figure .2.1Adversarial Forcing1

3.1

We initialize from Cosmos 3-Nano and separate its understanding (UND) and generation (GEN) towers. The frozen UND tower encodes the caption $y$ into per-layer keys and values consumed by GEN. This separation allows independent compilation and distributed execution of the two towers; during distillation, the student, teacher, and fake-score networks share one UND tower and reuse its outputs for the same caption.[]21

A frozen Wan video autoencoder maps RGB and geometry videos to latents. The appearance reference $x_{0}$ uses the backbone’s native clean-frame representation: it receives no diffusion timestep and is never denoised. Architecture sizes and training configurations are given in Appendix .[]22A.1

3.2

Condition tokens.

Depth and normals use the three-channel encodings of Section . Spatial average pooling reduces the condition encoder’s input size and the number of tokens processed during training and inference. For an encoded condition frame indexed by $t$ , we form2.2

$G_{t}=W_{\mathrm{in}}\,\mathcal{P}\!\big([E(S(c))]_{t}\big)+e_{\mathrm{geo}},$ (3)

where $S$ pools the condition video spatially, $E$ is the frozen video encoder, and $\mathcal{P}$ groups latent patches. We reuse the pretrained RGB input projection $W_{\mathrm{in}}$ and add a zero-initialized modality embedding $e_{\mathrm{geo}}$ . Condition tokens receive no diffusion timestep.

Joint attention.

We concatenate geometry and RGB tokens along the sequence dimension and process them with the same Transformer layers. We use neither channel concatenation nor control branches , to avoid imposing a pixel-aligned inductive bias. Writing $R_{t}$ for RGB latent tokens, the visual sequence is[]23[, ]2425

$[\,G_{0},G_{1},\dots\,]\;[\,R_{0},R_{1},\dots\,],$ (4)

with $R_{0}$ encoding $x_{0}$ and text keys and values integrated via cross-attention. Geometry and RGB share temporal rotary coordinates; spatial coordinates map both grids to the same image extent. This preserves geometric alignment while allowing cross-token interactions. Only noisy RGB tokens produce velocity predictions.

Robust conditions.

Geometry estimated from natural video differs from engine-rendered geometry in texture leakage, alignment, and missing observations. To reduce dependence on estimator-specific cues, we randomly retain depth or normals, with occasional dropout of both modalities; dropped inputs are black. We suppress fine texture by down- and upsampling, perturb alignment with a smooth spatial warp anchored to the first frame, and add noise to condition latents. Preprocessing and augmentation settings appear in Appendix .A.2

3.3

Stage 2 adapts the geometry-conditioned model to blockwise autoregressive generation. We partition the latents after the reference into fixed-length blocks. Each block is generated from its aligned geometry and previously completed blocks, without access to future blocks.

Parallel teacher forcing.

Training uses two copies of each block inside one Transformer: a clean copy $P_{j}$ that represents history and a noisy copy $Q_{j}$ that is denoised. Each copy carries its own aligned condition tokens. With $A_{0}$ the reference, the attention mask permits

$P_{j}\longrightarrow A_{0}\cup P_{\leq j},\qquad Q_{j}\longrightarrow A_{0}\cup P_{(5)

where an arrow points from a query to the tokens it may read; text is visible to both (Figure ). The noisy copy of a block therefore sees clean earlier blocks and attends bidirectionally within itself, but never its own clean target. This lets all target blocks be trained in parallel with independently sampled flow times. With $z_{j}$ the clean latent block and $\mathcal{C}=(x_{0},y,c)$ the reference, text, and conditions,3

$\displaystyle z_{j,t_{j}}$ $\displaystyle=(1-t_{j})\,z_{j}+t_{j}\,\epsilon_{j},\qquad\epsilon_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I),$ (6) $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TF}}$ $\displaystyle=\mathop{\mathbf{E}}\nolimits\!\left[\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\big\|v_{\theta}(z_{j,t_{j}},t_{j}\mid z_{

where $M$ is the number of target blocks and conditioning on $z_{

3.4

Stage 3, , distills the teacher-forced model into a few-step renderer that is trained on its own rollouts. It has three components: distribution matching against the bidirectional teacher, exact replay of each rollout so that gradients reach the history it wrote, and a real-data adversarial objective with exact R1/R2 regularization.Adversarial Forcing

3.4.1

We match autoregressive student rollouts to the bidirectional teacher through distribution matching distillation (DMD) in the manner of Self Forcing . The student starts from stage 2 and generates each block in a few denoising steps, conditioning on its own preceding outputs. The frozen stage-1 teacher scores the resulting clip jointly. An auxiliary model, initialized from the teacher, learns the student’s distribution.[, , ]8910fake-score

For a student prediction $\widetilde{z}_{\theta}$ corrupted to $y_{\tau}=(1-\tau)\widetilde{z}_{\theta}+\tau\epsilon$ , let $f_{\mathrm{T}}$ and $f_{\psi}$ denote clean estimates from the teacher and fake-score model. The student objective is

$\displaystyle g$ $\displaystyle=\frac{f_{\psi}(y_{\tau},\tau\mid\mathcal{C})-f_{\mathrm{T}}(y_{\tau},\tau\mid\mathcal{C})}{a},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DMD}}=\mathop{\mathbf{E}}\nolimits\!\left[\frac{1}{2N}\big\|\widetilde{z}_{\theta}-\operatorname{sg}(\widetilde{z}_{\theta}-g)\big\|_{2}^{2}\right],$ (7)

where $a$ is a per-video normalization, $N$ the number of latent elements, and $\operatorname{sg}$ stops gradients. The fake-score model is trained by flow matching on detached student samples. Sampling schedules, guidance, and update ratios are specified in Appendix .A.4

The other two components extend this objective: replay restores gradients through history encoding, and an adversarial loss supplies supervision from real videos.

3.4.2

In standard Self Forcing, completed blocks are encoded into a detached KV cache. Subsequent losses therefore supervise prediction from that cache, but not the history-prefill computation that produced its keys and values. Keeping this computation differentiable in a single serial rollout would retain the recursively connected cache-formation graphs across blocks, with substantial memory cost.

Similar to Self Gradient Forcing (SGF) , we decouple rollout and gradient propagation using two passes. A no-gradient rollout records each block’s input $U$ at the final denoising time $t^{*}$ and its clean output $Z$ . A differentiable replay then recomputes both history and predictions with the visibility pattern of Eq. (). For block $j$ ,[]115

$\widetilde{z}_{\theta,j}=\operatorname{sg}(U_{j})-t^{*}\,v_{\theta}\!\left(\operatorname{sg}(U_{j}),t^{*}\mid\operatorname{sg}(Z_{(8)

The recorded latents stay detached, but their history encodings are recomputed inside the graph. Later losses thus update the parameters that write history into the cache, without differentiating through the sampling trajectory. Both DMD and generator adversarial losses use this replayed prediction.

SGF implements its second pass with full-sequence FlexAttention . Although the attention mask matches cached generation, the kernel, tensor shapes, and reduction order differ; in finite precision, replay can consequently diverge from the sampled trajectory. We preserve the rollout’s execution structure: attention runs block by block with scaled dot-product attention (SDPA), using the same key–value order and call shapes. Projections and feed-forward layers use the same block grouping as well. The history keys and values are recomputed and assembled differentiably, so the matching execution retains the history-gradient path (Figure ). Section  evaluates numerical agreement and cost.[]2644.2

3.4.3

Distribution matching uses teacher and fake-score estimates on generated samples, without directly contrasting them with real videos. Following DMD2 , we add an adversarial objective. A trainable head $h_{\phi}$ aggregates intermediate features from the frozen teacher backbone $B$ into a discriminator logit. Conditioning the backbone on geometry and the reference lets the discriminator assess appearance together with geometric consistency. Section  compares the resulting renderer with one trained by Self Forcing alone.[]104.1

Relativistic objective.

We use the relativistic pairing of R3GAN . With $r$ and $f$ the logits of a real clip and of the student’s prediction, corrupted with the same noise and timestep under the same conditions,[]12

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{G}}=\mathop{\mathbf{E}}\nolimits\!\left[\operatorname{softplus}(\operatorname{sg}(r)-f)\right],\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}}=\mathop{\mathbf{E}}\nolimits\!\left[\operatorname{softplus}(f-r)\right],$ (9)

and the student minimizes $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DMD}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{G}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{G}}$ . The generator-side gradient is injected into the second-pass graph through a linear surrogate, so both objectives act on Eq. ().8

Exact R1/R2 without double backward.

R3GAN regularizes the discriminator with R1 and R2, the squared input-gradient norms on real and generated samples:

$D_{\phi}(x)=h_{\phi}(B(x)),\qquad R_{1}=\mathop{\mathbf{E}}\nolimits_{x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}\|\nabla_{x}D_{\phi}(x)\|_{2}^{2},\qquad R_{2}=\mathop{\mathbf{E}}\nolimits_{x\sim p_{\theta}}\|\nabla_{x}D_{\phi}(x)\|_{2}^{2}.$ (10)

Their parameter gradients normally require differentiating through a backward pass. The fused attention kernels in our backbone, such as FlashAttention , do not support this double backward. APT sidesteps the problem with a random-perturbation approximation of R1. We compute the exact penalty and its exact head-parameter gradient instead, using the fact that the backbone is frozen.[]27[]28

Consider one sample and write $z=B(x)$ , $A=J_{B}(x)$ and $u=\nabla_{z}h_{\phi}(z)$ . Then

$g=A^{\top}u,\qquad R=g^{\top}g,\qquad v=Ag,$ (11)

where $g$ is obtained by one vector–Jacobian product (a backward pass through the head, with its parameters frozen, and then through the backbone) and $v$ by one Jacobian–vector product that carries $g$ forward through the frozen backbone without a gradient graph. Neither step materializes $A$ . Because $z$ and $A$ do not depend on $\phi$ ,

$\nabla_{\phi}R=2\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial\phi}\right)^{\!\top}v=\nabla_{\phi}\!\left[\,2\,J_{z}h_{\phi}(z)\,\operatorname{sg}(v)\,\right].$ (12)

The right-hand side is the gradient of a directional derivative of the head alone, which we compute by writing the head’s Jacobian–vector product with ordinary differentiable operations (Appendix ). With $s=2J_{z}h_{\phi}(z)\,\operatorname{sg}(v)$ , the surrogateB

$\widetilde{R}=\operatorname{sg}\!\left(\|g\|_{2}^{2}\right)+s-\operatorname{sg}(s)$ (13)

has the value of the true penalty and its exact first derivative with respect to $\phi$ . The discriminator then minimizes $\lambda_{\mathrm{D}}\big(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}}+\tfrac{\gamma}{2}(\widetilde{R}_{1}+\widetilde{R}_{2})\big)$ with weights $\lambda_{\mathrm{D}}$ and $\gamma$ . A single head forward on the detached features $z$ and directions $v$ of the real and generated samples produces both the relativistic logits and the directional terms, and one ordinary backward pass updates the head (Figure ). No step differentiates through a backward kernel, and no finite difference or random direction is involved.5

3.5

The renderer prefills the reference and text, denoises incoming blocks, and commits clean predictions into a bounded KV cache. The cache maintains a permanent prefix (including $x_{0}$ ) and a sliding window of recent history (Figure ). For rollouts exceeding the training horizon, we apply top-aligned rotary position remapping: the active block is clamped at the horizon boundary while recent history is shifted to precede it and re-rotated, preserving relative temporal distances while geometry tracks the true simulation timeline (Appendix ).sink6C

Low-latency execution and deployment.

Transformer execution over short blocks is primarily bounded by memory bandwidth and kernel launch overhead. Rather than relying on , which incurs minutes-long cold-start compilation delays, we implement custom Triton kernels to fuse elementwise operations around attention (RMSNorm, RoPE rotation, and gated activations) without intermediate memory round-trips. CUDA graph capture and replay further eliminate host-side launch overhead for fixed-shape blocks. To bypass the heavy latent decoding bottleneck during real-time serving, we optionally replace the standard VAE decoder with a distilled tiny decoder , which reconstructs pixel frames in under 10 ms (Table ). In interactive deployments, the engine pushes conditions to a GPU worker, and decoded frames are streamed to the agent or browser over WebRTC with bounded queuing latency (Section ).torch.compile[]29[]30[]3124.3

5

Code worlds give agents many places to act, and a world that answers every action is also a place to practice. This section presents environments built on the shared renderer, revisits hide-and-seek with agents that perceive the world only through rendered observations, describes the round-by-round procedure through which they improve, and applies it to four further worlds.

5.1

Different scene programs and compatible engines form code worlds with a shared renderer (Figure ). The examples include navigation, manipulation, tool use, and multi-agent interaction. Our interactive deployment adds browser games whose rules live entirely in code, including bowling, a penalty shootout, and a crate-vault puzzle; a player’s keyboard, mouse, or gamepad input advances the code world, and the rendered stream is the only view of it. Because state evolution is explicit, it can also be replayed and rendered again: a recorded rollout can be re-shot in a different visual style, or from a different camera, without changing what happened.8

5.2

In OpenAI’s hide-and-seek study , agents trained with self-play and reinforcement learning developed strategies such as building shelters, using ramps, and defending against those tools. The study reports shelter construction after roughly 25 million episodes, followed by seeker ramp use after another 75 million; the environment made a sequence of increasingly sophisticated strategies possible through repeated competition. Those agents observed object state. We revisit the setting with a pretrained agent  that can reason about what happened and revise how it acts, and that perceives the world only through our renderer.[]13[]32

Setting.

We use a sequential one-hider, one-seeker variant of the physics environment. The hider prepares the scene and then hands control to the seeker. Each agent receives first-person observations generated by the neural renderer from the environment’s structured conditions. It acts by submitting short Python programs for movement and object interaction, and then observes the resulting changes through the renderer. It never receives object coordinates, hidden world state, or the opponent’s private observations.

Each role keeps its own , organized as a library of short , Markdown notes that may contain code, with one lesson per file. The recorded run begins with empty playbooks and contains several rounds of five games each, over sampled layouts and seeds. After each round, each role reviews its own action programs and the visual evidence it was permitted to see, identifies failures, and adds skill files to its playbook. In the next round, the agents receive the accumulated skills, interpret the current scene, and determine which prior experience is relevant. Both successful and unsuccessful attempts contribute to subsequent revisions.playbookskill files

Emergent behaviors.

Figure  highlights three characteristic behaviors that emerged during the interaction: a hider builds cover by moving a barrier panel to block an entrance; a seeker transports a ramp to an inner wall and climbs over it; and, after an initial leap falls short, a seeker repositions the ramp closer to the wall and tries again. These maneuvers demonstrate the agents’ ability to acquire and refine multi-step physical tool-use strategies purely from neural-rendered first-person observations.9

These emergent strategies mirror the hallmark milestones of the 2019 study, providing a reference point for physical tool use and counter-strategies in this domain (Table ). There, shelter construction and ramp usage emerged after roughly 25 million and 100 million training episodes of self-play reinforcement learning, respectively. In our setting, the hiders used panels to build a shelter by round 4, and the seekers used a ramp to cross walls by round 10.3

Crucially, these numbers reflect two fundamentally different learning paradigms rather than a direct sample-efficiency ratio. The 2019 agents learned physical dynamics and competitive coordination from scratch with random weights, operating directly on ground-truth coordinate state. In contrast, foundation model agents already possess abstract knowledge of objects, tools, and geometry from web-scale pretraining. Their primary challenge is not discovering concepts from nothing, but grounding abstract knowledge into closed-loop sensorimotor action, diagnosing spatial execution failures purely from synthesized visual observations without state access, and refining tactical execution across rounds. This comparison illustrates how combining a rich neural renderer with reflective playbooks enables agents with general priors to bypass tabula rasa exploration and rapidly converge on effective tool-use strategies in physical environments.

5.3

Hide-and-seek is one instance of a general procedure (Figure ). Practice runs in rounds. A round begins with a that states the goal, the available actions, and the limits, but no solution. One or more agents then play in parallel, each within a fixed budget of steps or simulated time. They see the world only through camera frames synthesized by the neural renderer: no coordinates, no map, and no score until the episode ends. Afterwards each agent writes a playbook that records what it tried, what it observed, what it still doubts, and what to test next. Playbooks are archived, and the next round’s agents, started in fresh conversations, receive the task file and the playbooks of earlier rounds.10task file

5.4

We ran the same procedure in four more worlds (Figure ); only the world and its task file change. In the world an agent has a 60-second session to keep a dog willingly engaged by offering a hand, petting, and playing with a ball. On the , two cars, each driven by its own agent from a windshield view, must swap ends of a bridge that fits one car, as quickly as possible. In , two dogs seeing only from their own eye height guide four sheep into a pen and hold them there for five seconds. In the , a wheel loader must push two rocks onto staging pads, deliver one to a bunker behind a wall, and park, within 360 seconds. Each world has its own actions, time limit, and score, described to the agent only in its task file (Appendix ), and each ran for four rounds. In all four worlds, the agents act directly on first-person observations synthesized in real time by the neural renderer, without access to internal simulation state or raw engine geometry buffers. Figure  shows representative frames from the recorded runs.11companion-dogone-lane bridgeherdingquarryD11

Table  lists the outcome of every round. In the companion-dog world, the engagement score rose from 13 to 19. On the bridge, both cars arrived in every round, and the time they needed fell from 71 to 41 seconds. The herding pair timed out in round 1 with three of four sheep penned, and penned all four in every later round. The loader cleared the rocks in round 1 and got no further, scored nothing in round 2, and in round 4 cleared the rocks, delivered one, and parked, in 329 of its 360 seconds.4

6

Executable environments and code worlds.

Simulated environments have long been the substrate of embodied learning. Habitat 2.0 supports household rearrangement by simulated robots, while ManiSkill2 provides a benchmark for diverse manipulation skills . ProcTHOR generates interactive houses procedurally at scale , and the hide-and-seek study of shows how a simple physics environment with movable objects can support a sequence of increasingly sophisticated strategies. Language models now automate environment construction: Holodeck translates language into assets and spatial constraints, SceneCraft synthesizes scene code with visual feedback, and LLMR generates and revises interactive Unity experiences . Code2Worlds and SimWorld Studio extend this to dynamic scenes and to environments with standard interfaces for embodied learning . A related line uses code to recover dynamics rather than author them: WorldCoder infers transition and reward functions from interaction, code world models translate the rules and trajectories of a game into a program that a planner can search, and Code as Worlds constructs and tests executable hypotheses from multimodal observations . All of these share an explicit representation that can be executed, inspected, and revised; their observations, however, are rendered by conventional graphics pipelines and inherit the fidelity of the available assets.[, ]12[]3[]13[, , ]333435[, ]3637[, , ]383940

Explicit state behind a video model.

Recent work also keeps the state of the world outside the video model and uses the model to render it. The state may be learned jointly with the frames , advanced by an engine , or written as code by an agent . These systems and ours share the separation of world evolution from appearance. Our interface is depth or surface normals, which any simulator with a 3D scene exports and which can be estimated from real videos; our renderer is causal and runs in short blocks in real time, so new actions enter throughout a rollout; and the state is a complete executable environment in which pretrained agents act and improve over repeated rounds.[, , ]414243[, , , ]23444546[, , , ]40474849

Rendering from coarse or intermediate representations also relates to neural and generative rendering: from graphics buffers and from coarse 3D simulations of crowds .[, , ]505152[]53

Interactive video world models.

Video generation offers a learned route to interactive environments. Genie learns latent actions from unlabeled video, and GameNGen simulates DOOM from action–observation trajectories . Later systems address control and memory over longer interactions: Matrix-Game 2.0 generates in real time from mouse and keyboard inputs, WorldPlay combines action and camera conditioning with retrieved spatial context, Matrix-Game 3.0 adds error-aware rollout training and camera-aware retrieval, and SolarWM and Astronex-World scale data and training for long-horizon, real-time interaction . Genie 3 adds world events triggered by text, Wonder improves camera control and memory for real-time exploration, and ActWorld keeps the frames in which an interaction happened so that changed objects stay changed . LingBot-World places pilot and director agents around a video world model to steer actions and events . In these systems the world is represented by generated history and learned memory. In ours, actions first advance an executable environment, and the renderer is responsible only for appearance; visual continuity is still learned, and generated frames need not perfectly realize the supplied state.[, ]454[, , , , ]55565657[, , ]585960[]7

Autoregressive video generation and distillation.

CausVid adapts a bidirectional video diffusion model into a causal student with asymmetric distribution matching . Self Forcing trains an autoregressive student on its own rollouts rather than on ground-truth prefixes , and LongLive extends this to long sequences . Causal Forcing, Causal-rCM, and Mask Forcing refine the initialization and rollout of self-forcing distillation . These methods train the student with score distillation ; DMD2 adds a GAN loss on real data . Self Gradient Forcing similarly introduces a second pass to differentiate history; our formulation introduces exact replay, eliminating numerical divergence and matching the rollout bitwise. Adversarial post-training is also a route to few-step generation in its own right ; its approximate R1 regularizer motivates our exact alternative. With few sampling steps, decoding becomes a large share of the remaining cost; tiny autoencoders distilled from a video VAE reduce it .[]61[]8[]62[, , ]636465[]9[]10[]11[, ]2866[]31

Agents that learn from written experience.

Pretrained language models can improve at a task by keeping what they learn in text. Reflexion has an agent reflect in words on a failed attempt and carry the reflection into the next one ; ExpeL extracts reusable insights from a pool of past trajectories ; and Voyager grows a library of executable skills while exploring Minecraft through a text interface to the game’s state . Our playbooks belong to this family. What differs is the setting: the agents perceive the world through camera frames, in hide-and-seek through the neural renderer alone, the task file gives no solution, and playbooks pass between independent agents in fresh conversations, so each lesson has to be stated well enough for another reader to check it. Emergent strategy in hide-and-seek was first shown with self-play reinforcement learning from random initialization ; we ask what the same environment yields when the players start from a pretrained model and a handful of games.[]67[]68[]69[]13

Gradient penalties and higher-order derivatives.

R1 and R2 penalize the discriminator’s input-gradient norm on real and generated samples ; R3GAN combines them with a relativistic loss into a stable modern baseline . Computing their parameter gradients requires differentiating an input gradient, which fused attention kernels such as FlashAttention do not support . Forward-over-reverse products and fused attention JVP kernels provide the ingredients we combine for an exact penalty with a frozen discriminator backbone.[]70[, ]7112[]27[]72[]73

7

More compact and complete conditions.

Depth and surface normals provide a practical conditioning interface, but dense geometry videos are redundant: once an object’s shape is known, its rigid motion is described by a few pose parameters, while a condition video repeats the resulting surfaces across many pixels and frames. Spatial downsampling reduces this cost but can remove thin structures, narrow gaps, and small contact changes needed for precise control. Geometry alone also leaves some of the world’s state unspecified. A rotationally symmetric object can spin without changing its depth or normals even as a painted marking rotates, and material, color, and object identity are not determined by geometry. Visual history can preserve these attributes, but may lose them after long occlusions or revisits beyond the memory window. Future conditioning interfaces could use more abstract and compact representations of the state the code world already maintains, such as structured text describing object attributes and interaction states, or high-dimensional latent features. Structured text could, for example, specify the orientation and angular velocity of a bullet spinning about its long axis even when its depth and normal maps do not change. Aligning such representations with the code world’s state, and adapting pretrained video models to use them, remain open problems.

Scaling environments.

The interface also decides which worlds can be shown at all. A renderer that receives only geometry cannot tell a spinning wheel from a still one, so tasks that depend on such state are out of reach today. A richer interface widens the range of possible worlds, but someone still has to write them. We built the worlds in this report one at a time. Since a world is a program, the next step is to let coding agents write and revise worlds , with the shared renderer supplying appearance. Generating a world is the easy part. The harder question is whether it deserves an agent’s time: whether the task can be solved from what the agent sees, whether a careless strategy fails, and whether there is something to learn that carries into the next round. We want these checks to run automatically, before any agent practices in a new world.[, ]4047

Scaling experience.

More worlds change how experience has to be kept. Here each playbook belongs to one world and is short enough to read in full. Across many worlds, agents must decide which lessons to keep, merge, or drop, and find the few that apply to the scene in front of them. Code worlds help: a world can be reset and replayed exactly, so a lesson can be tested before it is passed on. Lessons that hold in several worlds, such as how to confirm that a grasp held or which visual cues mislead, become general knowledge about acting in physical scenes, and unseen worlds can measure it. The two grow together: where agents fail tells us which worlds to write next, and each new world tests what they wrote down before.

8

What an agent can learn is bounded by the environment it practices in. AgentGarten builds environments that are both faithful and realistic by dividing the work: a simulator or game engine maintains persistent state and executes the rules of each world, and a shared neural renderer, trained with Adversarial Forcing, turns the geometry it exports into observations in real time. An agent can therefore act, see the consequence, and act again, in a world whose state it can rely on. In these environments, pretrained agents improve from their own experience: they play, review each round, and write playbooks that later agents inherit and build upon. In hide-and-seek, seen only through rendered observations, shelters appeared by round 4 and ramp crossings by round 10, and the same procedure improved outcomes in four further worlds. Because a new world is written as code and rendered through the same interface, environments can grow in number and difficulty alongside the agents that practice in them. We expect agents that keep evolving through interaction to come from that loop.
