item.title: MeshSuite：三角面与网格神经渲染的首个统一基准 ｜ MeshSuite: A Unified Benchmark for Triangle- and Mesh-Based Neural Rendering
item.description:
一句话：此前各家方法评测口径不一，这个基准第一次在同一设置下比较，并把「在引擎里部署」作为评测维度。

要点：

  • 三角面基元的神经渲染是连接神经表示与图形引擎的桥梁
  • 现有方法开发与评测设置不一致，几乎没有直接对比
  • 首次系统性评估引擎部署与非欧几里得网格场景

为什么值得看：想评估「神经渲染能不能进产线引擎」，这个基准给出了统一口径与工程侧指标。

中文摘要：基于三角面与网格的神经渲染试图用与标准光栅化兼容的三角基元，把神经表示与图形引擎连接起来。但现有方法是在不一致的设置下开发与评估的，很少有直接比较，也几乎没人在图形引擎里评估。作者推出 MeshSuite，这是第一个系统性评估引擎部署与非欧几里得网格场景的基准，为后续方法提供统一比较口径。

来源：arXiv·神经渲染（English） 相关度：11.7 正文：75558 字 / 2 图

作者：Kaixuan Zhang、Minxian Li、Mingwu Ren 等 4 人

分类：cs.GR / cs.CV

PDF：https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.01306v4

命中：neural rendering、rendering、mesh、splatting、rasterization

Triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering seeks to bridge neural representations and graphics engines through triangle primitives compatible with standard rasterization. Yet existing methods were developed and evaluated under inconsistent settings, with few direct comparisons and little evaluation in graphics engines. We introduce MeshSuite, the first benchmark for systematic evaluation of engine

License: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 arXiv:2609.01306v4 [cs.GR] 16 Oct 2026

MeshSuite: A Unified Benchmark for Triangle- and Mesh-Based Neural Rendering

Kaixuan Zhang Nanjing University of Science and Technology Affiliation: Minxian Li †Corresponding author.†thanks: Nanjing University of Science and Technology Affiliation: Mingwu Ren Nanjing University of Science and Technology Affiliation: Xiatian Zhu University of Surrey Affiliation: 

Abstract

Triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering aims to bridge neural scene representations and existing graphics engines (, Unity, Blender) by leveraging primitives compatible with standard rasterization hardware. There have been several such methods driven by parallel efforts, developed and evaluated under inconsistent settings, with little or no comparison with each other; critically, most even have never used graphics engines for evaluation nor considered deployability in practice – significantly undermining the objective and motivation. To address these issues, we introduce , the first benchmark of its kind to enable systematic evaluation of graphics-engine deployment and the reference Source Renderer for triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering methods. Importantly, our deployment protocol includes two engine deployment settings: (1) – a conventional opaque mesh pipeline with vertex colors and hardware Z-buffering; (2) – adding method-specific engine implementations supporting the retained appearance and compositing features (, alpha blending), so that the characteristics of each specific model can be taken into account. For mesh splatting, we further propose a structural audit of exported surfaces, diagnosing topological and geometric integrity toward downstream graphics assets. We highlight several results: (1) Graphics engine deployment would incur image-quality degradation under both deployment options. Among the triangle- and mesh-based NVS methods studied, MeshSplatting degrades the least under Standard Mesh Deployment. (2) The deployment setting matters – Custom Engine Deployment can retain the majority of fidelity at a roughly 5 $\sim$ 33 $\times$ slowdown relative to Standard Mesh Deployment across the two deployment datasets. (3) About mesh splatting, the current approaches to explicit connectivity and shared indexing are still limited: shared vertex indexing alone does not ensure manifoldness or global connectivity. From this benchmark, we validate that , and highlight the significance of assessing the graphics engine deployment process (, the degree of engine compatibility). The project page is accessible at .e.g.triangleMeshSuiteStandard Mesh DeploymentCustom Engine Deploymente.g.rasterizability is merely part of graphics readinesse.g.https://surrey-up-lab.github.io/MeshSuite

1

Reconstructing a scene from multi-view images allows users to explore it from arbitrary viewpoints beyond those originally captured, supporting a wide range of vision and graphics applications, including AR/VR , gaming , and robotic perception . Recent advances in neural rendering, particularly Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) , have enabled increasingly realistic novel-view synthesis (NVS). Specifically, NeRFs use multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) to encode scene density and view-dependent color, synthesizing novel views through volume rendering . However, their practical use is constrained by high computational costs and the lack of an explicit geometric representation. In contrast, 3DGS represents scenes explicitly with 3D Gaussian primitives and uses efficient differentiable splatting to substantially reduce rendering costs .()Broxton et al., 2020()Lachambre et al., 2017()Zhu et al., 2022()Mildenhall et al., 2020()Kerbl et al., 2023()Mildenhall et al., 2020()Kerbl et al., 2023

Despite these advances, neither representation is directly compatible with the standard rendering pipelines of established computer graphics (CG) engines, such as Blender and Unity . These engines have benefited from decades of development and optimization, providing efficient rendering pipelines and integrated tools for lighting and shadows, material editing, and animation. Their mature ecosystems also offer extensive collections of reusable assets and plugins , facilitating the integration of reconstructed scenes into practical applications.()Blender Foundation, 2026()Unity Technologies, 2026(; )Unity Technologies, 2026Blender Foundation, 2026

To better take advantage of these engines, researchers have increasingly explored triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering methods, which optimize triangle primitives already supported by standard graphics hardware . These methods have demonstrated impressive NVS performance comparable to that of NeRFs and 3DGS, while offering a promising path toward integration with existing CG engines . However, existing triangle- and mesh-based works follow separate evaluation protocols, with differences in data preprocessing, image formats, evaluation metrics, and metric implementations, and none evaluates the methods in a graphics engine. Using triangles alone also does not ensure complete engine compatibility. Existing methods use triangles with substantially different features (Tab. ), including continuous or discrete opacity , coverage defined inside or outside a triangle , varying color representations (, view-dependent spherical harmonics (SHs) or neural networks ), and the presence or absence of neural texture decoders . These variations pose challenges for engine rendering and may require method-specific shaders, buffers, sorting strategies, and runtime state. Furthermore, existing mesh splatting methods evaluate exported mesh quality solely through vertex sharing, lacking a comprehensive analysis of critical structural and topological properties such as manifoldness and global connectivity.(; )Held et al., 2026bHeld et al., 2026a(; ; )Held et al., 2026bSheng et al., 2025Held et al., 2026a1(; )Held et al., 2026bHeld et al., 2026a(; )Sheng et al., 2025Held et al., 2026be.g.()Held et al., 2026a()Tojo et al., 2026(; )Tojo et al., 2026Held et al., 2026b()Held et al., 2026a

To address these questions, we introduce , a unified benchmark for evaluating triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering (see Fig. ). This benchmark enables: (a) integration of existing triangle- and mesh-based splatting methods; (b) fair and consistent comparison of different methods in a unified setting; (c) extensive evaluation of both triangle- and mesh-based models during training and inference; (d) Source Renderer evaluation and two engine deployment settings: - converting a trained model to a standard opaque vertex-colored mesh before rendering in a graphics engine; - adding a customized layer to implement method-specific designs, such as specialized appearance representations and alpha compositing.MeshSuite1Standard Mesh DeploymentCustom Engine Deployment

We note three key findings. , engine deployment reduces visual quality relative to the Source Renderer, with MeshSplatting losing the least quality under Standard Mesh Deployment among the studied methods (Tab. ). Second, Custom Engine Deployment produces more visually appealing renderings than Standard Mesh Deployment, at the cost of a roughly 5 $\sim$ 33 $\times$ slowdown (Tab. ). Third, existing mesh splatting methods’ exported meshes exhibit non-manifold structures and substantial fragmentation (Tab. ). These results show that ; appearance preservation, efficiency, and mesh structure must be evaluated together.First()Held et al., 2026a446using triangles alone does not ensure graphics readiness

Our are as follows: () the first unified benchmark, , for evaluating triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering methods; () Custom Engine Deployment of existing methods in a graphics engine (, Unity), retaining their specific designs during engine rendering; and () an extensive evaluation of existing models in terms of novel-view synthesis, training/inference cost, and mesh structure.contributionsIMeshSuiteIIi.e.III

2

Novel-view synthesis (NVS) aims to synthesize images of a scene from viewpoints beyond those observed in the input images. A central component of this task is a scene representation that captures both geometry and appearance. NeRF represents a scene as a continuous function and synthesize views through volumetric integration . Later methods improve reconstruction quality and anti-aliasing or accelerate rendering through explicit, factorized, and hashed structures . 3DGS replaces repeated network queries with optimized anisotropic Gaussian primitives and a dedicated splatting rasterizer . Follow-up works refine Gaussian optimization or encourages surface-aligned geometry . These methods establish strong NVS baselines, but their representations are not natively supported by conventional graphics engines (, Unity and Blender). Integration with existing CG engines therefore requires specialized rendering implementations or conversion to mesh-based assets.Dominant neural representations.()Mildenhall et al., 2020(; ; )Barron et al., 2021Barron et al., 2022Barron et al., 2023(; ; ; ; )Reiser et al., 2024Yu et al., 2021Fridovich-Keil et al., 2022Chen et al., 2022Müller et al., 2022()Kerbl et al., 2023(; ; )Kheradmand et al., 2024Huang et al., 2024Guédon and Lepetit, 2024e.g.

To facilitate integration with conventional graphics engines, methods such as MobileNeRF and BakedSDF convert learned radiance fields into mesh-based representations. For explicit splats, SuGaR and GaMeS extract mesh surfaces from 3D Gaussian primitives or bind Gaussian primitives to deformable mesh faces. Although these conversion pipelines produce standard mesh assets, they often rely on lossy post-processing (, Marching Cubes, Poisson surface reconstruction, or heuristic simplification) that decouples the optimization target from the final rendering objective.()Chen et al., 2023()Yariv et al., 2023()Guédon and Lepetit, 2024()Waczyńska et al., 2024e.g.

Established CG engines, such as Blender and Unity , provide optimized rendering pipelines and integrated tools for scene editing, lighting, and animation, together with mature ecosystems of reusable assets and plugins. Triangle meshes are widely supported by these pipelines, making them a natural choice for bringing learned scene representations into existing graphics workflows.Triangle- and mesh-based neural representations.()Blender Foundation, 2026()Unity Technologies, 2026

To exploit this support, triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering methods optimize geometry directly represented by triangle primitives . These approaches use either with independent faces or with shared vertices and explicit connectivity. 2DTS and Triangle-Splatting optimize independent triangles with soft coverage and alpha blending, DiffSoup uses neural texture features and a color decoder, and MeshSplatting introduces shared-vertex connectivity. Tab.  summarizes and contrasts the key design features across these representations alongside reference Gaussian baselines. These works demonstrate the potential of triangle- and mesh-based representations for high-quality NVS and offer promising routes toward graphics-engine integration.(; ; ; )Held et al., 2026bSheng et al., 2025Held et al., 2026aTojo et al., 2026triangle soupsindexed meshes()Sheng et al., 2025()Held et al., 2026b()Tojo et al., 2026()Held et al., 2026a1

However, using triangle primitives alone does ensure complete engine compatibility, as method-specific appearance and transparency models may still require additional adaptation. These methods are also developed and reported under different evaluation pipelines, making direct cross-method comparison difficult. Their original evaluations primarily use research-oriented source renderers rather than assess the learned representations after deployment in a graphics engine. MeshSuite addresses both gaps through unified evaluation and explicit graphics-engine deployment.not

Existing frameworks have sought to improve the reproducibility and comparability of NVS. Nerfstudio and GauStudio provide modular research frameworks for NeRF and Gaussian Splatting, while gsplat offers an efficient Gaussian rasterization library with extensive performance evaluations. More directly, NerfBaselines standardizes datasets, evaluation protocols, and metrics across NeRF and 3DGS methods while preserving their original implementations. Splatwizard further provides a specialized benchmark for 3DGS compression, evaluating rendering fidelity, computational efficiency, and geometric accuracy. The nvs-bench project facilitates reproducible NVS comparisons across different representations, including Triangle Splatting . Complementary studies investigate perceptual rendering quality and robustness under corrupted observations .Neural rendering benchmarks.()Tancik et al., 2023()Ye et al., 2024()Ye et al., 2025()Kulhanek and Sattler, 2025()Liu et al., 2026()nvs-bench contributors, 2026()Held et al., 2026b()Liang et al., 2024()Wang et al., 2024

Despite these efforts, existing benchmarks primarily focus on reconstruction quality and rendering efficiency within research-oriented source renderers, leaving graphics-engine deployment largely unexplored. MeshSuite addresses this gap by extending the evaluation of triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering to graphics-engine deployment, alongside a structural assessment of reconstructed meshes.

3

MeshSuite provides an end-to-end benchmark spanning evaluation with official Source Renderers and deployment in graphics engines. As illustrated in Fig. , it evaluates each trained representation under matched camera views, backgrounds, and evaluation metrics across three settings: Source Renderer, Standard Mesh Deployment, and Custom Engine Deployment. Comparisons across these settings reveal how graphics-engine deployment affects visual fidelity and rendering efficiency. For exported indexed meshes, we also assess structural usability, including local/global connectivity and manifoldness. Fig.  provides a more detailed overview of MeshSuite’s software architecture.16

3.1

Fair cross-method comparisons require consistent data and evaluation settings . MeshSuite standardizes three aspects:(; )Kulhanek and Sattler, 2025Liu et al., 2026

For a held-out camera set $\mathcal{C}$ , the benchmark standardizes camera coordinate frames, optical axes, field of view, and projection matrices.Camera and viewpoint alignment:

Prior works adopt inconsistent backgrounds: for example, on DTU , Triangle-Splatting uses an unmasked black background, whereas 2DTS uses object masks and a white background. We standardize all methods to the white-background protocol for masked objects. Using the RGBA alpha channel as an opacity matte, both ground-truth target images and novel-view renderings are composited asBackground compositing policy:()Jensen et al., 2014()Held et al., 2026b

$\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{white}}=\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{RGB}}\odot\bm{\alpha}+(1-\bm{\alpha})\cdot\mathbf{1}.$ (1)

Here, $\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{RGB}}$ and $\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{white}}$ denote the input RGB and composited images, respectively; $\bm{\alpha}$ is the per-pixel opacity matte with values in [0, 1]; $\odot$ denotes element-wise multiplication, with $\bm{\alpha}$ applied to all RGB channels; and $\mathbf{1}$ is an all-ones image. The renderer background is also set to white, giving all methods the same evaluation background.

We use the same implementations of PSNR , SSIM , and LPIPS for all methods. LPIPS uses a VGG backbone with images normalized to [-1, 1].Metric standardization:()Hore and Ziou, 2010()Wang et al., 2004()Zhang et al., 2018()Simonyan and Zisserman, 2015

3.2

Existing triangle- and mesh-based methods encode geometry, appearance, and opacity in method-specific ways (Tab. ). For example, 2DTS and Triangle-Splatting use independent triangles with learned opacity, MeshSplatting uses shared vertices with view-dependent appearance, and DiffSoup represents appearance through learned features and a neural decoder. Engine deployment therefore requires method-specific interpretation of the trained model’s parameters.1()Sheng et al., 2025()Held et al., 2026b()Held et al., 2026a()Tojo et al., 2026

To support deployment through a common interface, MeshSuite introduces a implemented by an adapter $\mathcal{E}_{m}$ for method $m$ . For each trained model $\mathcal{S}_{m}$ , the adapter maps its parameters to an engine asset $\mathcal{A}_{m}$ that follows the unified interface:translation layer

$\mathcal{S}_{m}\xrightarrow{\mathcal{E}_{m}}\mathcal{A}_{m}.$ (2)

The asset covers geometry, appearance, and opacity for different mesh structures. Translation decodes the trained model before deployment, allowing the engine to consume the exported asset independently of the training framework. The asset supplies the geometry and appearance data used by Standard Mesh Deployment and Custom Engine Deployment (see Appendix Fig. ).6

3.3

As illustrated in Fig. , MeshSuite organizes rendering into three evaluation settings: Standard Mesh Deployment, Custom Engine Deployment, and the reference Source Renderer. The Source Renderer serves as the baseline for the two engine-deployment settings.1

We render representations as conventional opaque meshes with static vertex colors and hardware Z-buffering. This setting omits method-specific shaders, neural decoders, and alpha blending. DiffSoup is unavailable in this setting.Standard Mesh Deployment ( $\mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{std}}_{m}$ ):

We implement method-specific Unity renderers under the same evaluation protocol that retain each method’s appearance and compositing features (Tab. ). Comparing them with the Source Renderer and Standard Mesh Deployment reveals how much quality these features preserve and their runtime cost (Tab. ).Custom Engine Deployment ( $\mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{cust}}_{m}$ ):24

We render each trained checkpoint $\mathcal{S}_{m}$ with its official Source Renderer $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{src}}_{m}$ : $\mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{src}}_{m}(c)=\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{src}}_{m}(\mathcal{S}_{m},c),\forall c\in\mathcal{C}$ , where $c$ denotes a camera in the held-out set $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{src}}_{m}(c)$ is the corresponding rendered image. This establishes baseline image quality before engine deployment.Source Renderer ( $\mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{src}}_{m}$ ):

Although Custom Engine Deployment retains the same appearance and compositing functions, the graphics engine and Source Renderers can differ in primitive ordering, coverage, and attribute evaluation. These differences affect transparency and view-dependent appearance, particularly for large or oblique primitives, and contribute to the adaptation gap.Differences from Source Renderer.

3.4

MeshSuite groups evaluation metrics into three categories: NVS quality, mesh quality, and computational cost.

3.4.1

Following Sec. , we report PSNR , SSIM , and LPIPS (VGG backbone, normalized images). For an image-quality metric $q$ (, PSNR, SSIM, or LPIPS), we compute the mean score $Q_{m}^{r}$ over the held-out camera set $\mathcal{C}$ :Visual fidelity and deployment gaps:3.1()Hore and Ziou, 2010()Wang et al., 2004()Zhang et al., 2018e.g.

$Q^{r}_{m}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}q(\mathbf{I}_{m}^{r}(c),\mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{gt}}(c)),\qquad r\in\{\mathrm{src},\mathrm{std},\mathrm{cust}\},$ (3)

where $m$ indexes methods, $c$ denotes a held-out camera, and $|\mathcal{C}|$ is the number of evaluated cameras. The images $\mathbf{I}_{m}^{r}(c)$ and $\mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{gt}}(c)$ are the rendering of method $m$ under setting $r$ and the corresponding ground truth, respectively. The setting labels $\mathrm{src}$ , $\mathrm{std}$ , and $\mathrm{cust}$ denote Source Renderer, Standard Mesh Deployment, and Custom Engine Deployment, respectively.

Then we define three pairwise gaps:

$\Delta Q^{\mathrm{adapt}}_{m}=\left|Q^{\mathrm{src}}_{m}-Q^{\mathrm{cust}}_{m}\right|,\quad\Delta Q^{\mathrm{port}}_{m}=\left|Q^{\mathrm{cust}}_{m}-Q^{\mathrm{std}}_{m}\right|,\quad\Delta Q^{\mathrm{deploy}}_{m}=\left|Q^{\mathrm{src}}_{m}-Q^{\mathrm{std}}_{m}\right|.$ (4)

The measures the change from the Source Renderer to Custom Engine Deployment; the measures the additional change under Standard Mesh Deployment; and the measures the overall change from the Source Renderer to Standard Mesh Deployment. The gaps report absolute differences; the metric values indicate whether quality improves or declines.adaptation gap $\Delta Q^{\mathrm{adapt}}_{m}$ portability gap $\Delta Q^{\mathrm{port}}_{m}$ deployment gap $\Delta Q^{\mathrm{deploy}}_{m}$

3.4.2

We evaluate Chamfer Distance (CD) on DTU, which adopts standard pipelines to isolate the object surface, complementing the white-background image protocol in Sec. .Surface geometry:3.1

Rendering as triangles does not guarantee a valid geometric surface. Let $\mathbf{V}$ , $\mathbf{E}$ , and $\mathbf{F}$ denote the sets of unique vertices, undirected edges, and triangular faces in an exported mesh, with $|\cdot|$ denoting set cardinality. We audit three complementary aspects:Mesh structural integrity:

  • •

    The ratio $|\mathbf{V}|/|\mathbf{F}|$ (abbreviated as V/F in tables) measures unique vertices per face, and average valence $2|\mathbf{E}|/|\mathbf{V}|$ summarizes local adjacency density. With a common export convention, lower $|\mathbf{V}|/|\mathbf{F}|$ indicates greater vertex sharing.Local reuse.

  • •

    The boundary-edge and non-manifold-edge ratios are $|\mathbf{E}_{1}|/|\mathbf{E}|$ and $|\mathbf{E}_{>2}|/|\mathbf{E}|$ , where $\mathbf{E}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{E}_{>2}$ contain edges incident to one and more than two faces, respectively. The non-manifold-vertex ratio is $|\mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{nm}}|/|\mathbf{V}|$ , where $\mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{nm}}$ is the set of vertices whose incident faces fail to form a single valid fan. Valid fans may be closed around an interior vertex or open at a boundary while disconnected fans are non-manifold. (see Fig.  for illustration).Local structure.2

  • •

    Two faces are considered adjacent if they share an edge. LCC faces and LCC area report the fractions of faces and surface area in the largest connected component (LCC), while Components counts the edge-connected components. We read component counts together with LCC fractions and visual inspection to account for differences in scene size and resolution. These three groups distinguish vertex sharing, local manifoldness, and fragmentation. Appendix Sec.  gives the audit details.Global connectivity.C

    • 3.4.3

    We audit computational overhead across training and inference. During training, we track peak VRAM (MiB) and optimization time (min). During engine deployment, we report GPU frame latency, wall-clock throughput (FPS), and renderer graphics allocations (MiB) separately. We additionally report serialized asset size (MiB) to characterize storage requirements.

    4

    4.1

    We evaluate four representative triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering methods, covering different designs in geometry connectivity, opacity, and appearance (Tabs.  and ):Methods.12

  • •

    replaces Gaussian primitives with independent planar triangle facelets and renders them through differentiable alpha blending. Its opacity function is defined using barycentric coordinates, with a compactness parameter controlling the transition from diffuse splats toward sharper triangle surfaces.2DTS()Sheng et al., 2025

  • •

    directly optimizes independent triangles using a differentiable window function confined to each projected triangle.     Before comparing methods, we check our reproductions against published results and public codebases. Across all 27 Mip-NeRF 360 method–scene pairs with published per-scene results, the mean absolute PSNR difference is only 0.075 dB and the maximum relative deviation is below 0.8%.     Tab.  reports the standardized Source Renderer results across all four datasets. On Mip-NeRF 360 , NeRF-Synthetic , and DTU , 2DTS achieves the highest PSNR (28.16 dB, 33.65 dB, and 29.66 dB), while using the least peak training memory on NeRF-Synthetic and DTU (3172 MiB and 2470 MiB).     Tab.  compares quality and throughput across the three settings on Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples; Appendix Fig.  summarizes the PSNR trajectories of the four triangle- and mesh-based methods.     The evaluated triangle- and mesh-based methods rely on specialized appearance models or compositing operations that limit their direct compatibility with conventional opaque mesh pipelines. Our Standard Mesh Deployment tests this compatibility using static vertex colors and hardware Z-buffering. Methods that depend on rendering operations beyond this pipeline can lose substantial image quality when adapted to it.Deployment quality.

    On Mip-NeRF 360, adapting 2DTS, Triangle-Splatting, and MeshSplatting to Standard Mesh Deployment lowers mean PSNR by 15.64 dB, 12.36 dB, and 4.89 dB, respectively, relative to the Source Renderer (Tab. ). MeshSplatting has the smallest overall deployment gap ( $\Delta Q_{m}^{\mathrm{deploy}}$ ) among these three methods. They still fall short of the Source Renderer: the remaining adaptation losses ( $\Delta Q_{m}^{\mathrm{adapt}}$ ) are 4.88 dB for 2DTS, 4.17 dB for Triangle-Splatting, and 2.20 dB for MeshSplatting.     4.4

    We audit MeshSplatting’s exported indexed meshes across all four datasets using the three metric groups defined in Sec. . Tab.  reports the mean of each metric over all scenes in each dataset. We consider the large, unbounded scenes of Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples separately from the smaller, object-centric scenes of DTU and NeRF-Synthetic. Appendix Sec.  provides per-scene results and audit details. We highlight the following results:3.46C

  • •

    Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples exhibit similar vertex sharing, with mean $|\mathbf{V}|/|\mathbf{F}|$ ratios of 0.523 and 0.516 and mean valence of 6.49 on both datasets. The object-centric datasets show greater reuse: DTU and NeRF-Synthetic have lower $|\mathbf{V}|/|\mathbf{F}|$ ratios of 0.428 and 0.339, with higher valence of 7.36 and 8.59, respectively. Vertex sharing is evident in both scene groups, but its extent differs.Local reuse.

  • •

    Vertex sharing does not ensure manifoldness. On Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples, approximately 18% of edges and 65 $\sim$ 66% of vertices are non-manifold. On DTU and NeRF-Synthetic, the non-manifold-edge ratios rise to 22% and 28%, and the non-manifold-vertex ratios to 73% and 87%, respectively. Thus, greater reuse on the object-centric datasets coexists with more non-manifold neighborhoods. Boundary edges account for 37 $\sim$ 46% of edges across the four datasets, indicating open surfaces while such boundaries can be expected in partially observed scenes. Non-manifold edges and vertices, in contrast, violate local manifold connectivity, and lower ratios indicate better local structural integrity.Local structure.

  • •

    On the large-scene datasets, the largest connected component (LCC) contains approximately 70% of faces, with 69% of surface area on Mip-NeRF 360 and 67% on Tanks and Temples. On DTU and NeRF-Synthetic, the LCC contains 77% and 80% of faces and 78% and 80% of area, respectively. Despite these dominant components, approximately 20 $\sim$ 30% of faces and 20 $\sim$ 33% of area remain distributed across other components. Together with mean component counts in the tens to hundreds of thousands, these fractions reveal substantial fragmentation in both scene groups. Absolute component counts depend on mesh size and do not provide a structural-quality ranking across datasets. On the two deployment datasets, MeshSplatting’s leading Standard Mesh Deployment image quality among the four studied methods (Tab. ) coexists with these structural defects, showing that visual fidelity does not ensure structural integrity.Global connectivity.4

    • 5

    We introduced MeshSuite, a unified benchmark for triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering that connects evaluation with official Source Renderers to graphics-engine deployment. MeshSuite combines standardized evaluation protocols, a unified asset interface, and method-specific Unity renderers to compare the Source Renderer, Standard Mesh Deployment, and Custom Engine Deployment. It evaluates visual fidelity and computational cost alongside surface accuracy and mesh structural integrity. Our experiments show that visual quality and method rankings depend on the deployment setting. Custom Engine Deployment better preserves appearance but incurs higher runtime costs than Standard Mesh Deployment. Among the four studied methods, mesh splatting methods achieve the highest image quality under Standard Mesh Deployment on Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples, yet their exported meshes exhibit non-manifold structures and substantial fragmentation across both large, unbounded and object-centric scenes. These findings show that triangle rasterization and shared-vertex connectivity alone do not ensure practical graphics usability. Evaluation must jointly consider appearance preservation, rendering efficiency, and the structural requirements of downstream tasks. Future work can extend the benchmark to additional graphics engines and directly assess exported meshes in tasks such as editing, remeshing, and collision handling.

    • Appendix A

    Fig.  details the modular software architecture of , expanding the conceptual overview in Fig. . The infrastructure is built with decoupling and modularity as first principles, ensuring that model training, format translation, graphics-engine deployment, and multi-dimensional evaluation operate independently through clearly specified interfaces.6MeshSuite1

    MeshSuite is organized into five cohesive subsystems: (1) : Standardizes canonical camera frames, optical axes, field-of-view definitions, and resolution downsampling across datasets. For masked object captures (, DTU), this layer automatically computes object alpha mattes and applies the white-background compositing convention specified in Eq. . (2) : Provides standardized training harnesses wrapping the official implementations of 2DTS , Triangle-Splatting , MeshSplatting , and DiffSoup . It follows each method’s original training pipeline while applying shared data and evaluation protocols under a common single-GPU hardware environment. (3) : The central translation bridge implementing method-specific adapters $\mathcal{E}_{m}$ . It parses trained model parameters and extracts explicit geometry, opacity fields, and appearance representations into standardized intermediate assets $\mathcal{A}_{m}$ . (4) : In-engine renderers implemented in Unity using C# Scriptable Render Pipelines and custom HLSL shaders. This layer provides both Standard Mesh Deployment and Custom Engine Deployment. (5) : Automated evaluation scripts computing standard 2D image fidelity metrics (, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS), hardware timing profiles (GPU P50/P95 latency percentiles and memory allocations), and geometric mesh topology audits.Modular Component Design.Dataset Managemente.g.1Algorithm Pool and Training()Sheng et al., 2025()Held et al., 2026b()Held et al., 2026a()Tojo et al., 2026Universal Translation LayerGraphics Engine DeploymentEvaluation and Audit Suitee.g.

    Under the Universal Translation Layer, trained models are converted into portable asset files prior to engine execution. Independent triangle soup models (2DTS, Triangle-Splatting, DiffSoup) are serialized into flat vertex arrays and attribute textures, whereas indexed meshes (MeshSplatting) are serialized with shared vertex coordinate tables, triangle face indices, and per-vertex SH coefficients. Crucially, the resulting asset bundles are completely self-contained and ingested directly by the graphics engine, decoupling real-time deployment from PyTorch, CUDA extension compilers, and Python runtime overhead. This architectural separation allows new neural rendering representations to be benchmarked by implementing a single translation adapter, and enables future deployment to other graphics engines (, Unreal Engine, Blender) without modifying upstream training pipelines.Asset Serialization and Decoupled Execution.e.g.

    Appendix B

    Tab.  complements the per-scene PSNR reproduction differences illustrated in Fig.  with comprehensive dataset-level evaluations comparing our reproduced metrics against published paper numbers and official public repositories. Sec.  outlines the primary experimental setup.734.1

    For 2DTS, Triangle-Splatting, and MeshSplatting, MeshSuite closely matches published dataset-level PSNR on Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples. On Mip-NeRF 360, the mean absolute PSNR difference across their 27 scene-method pairs is only 0.075 dB, and the maximum relative deviation across these pairs is below 0.8%. Specifically, 2DTS reproduces at 28.16 dB PSNR (vs. 28.18 dB in the paper and 28.51 dB in the public repository), Triangle-Splatting achieves 27.13 dB (vs. 27.17 dB reported and 27.20 dB in public code), and MeshSplatting achieves 24.72 dB (vs. 24.78 dB in both paper and code). For DiffSoup, where per-scene Mip-NeRF 360 results were not reported in the original paper, MeshSuite is closer to the public codebase in dataset-level PSNR (23.54 dB vs. 23.69 dB) than to the paper (24.76 dB); on Tanks and Temples, it achieves 18.90 dB vs. 18.38 dB in public code. LPIPS differences are larger for several methods, so close PSNR agreement does not imply equal agreement across all image metrics.Quantitative Reproduction Fidelity.1 DiffSoup is omitted since it does not report per-scene metrics in its original paper.11

    Differences between published figures, public repositories, and MeshSuite may reflect preprocessing, camera conventions, background compositing, metric implementations, and numerical variation. We do not isolate their individual contributions: (1) : Image interpolation filters can affect reconstructed image values; MeshSuite applies shared data preparation while retaining the downsampling requirements of each method (Sec. ). (2) : Differences in principal point handling and coordinate conventions can affect alignment; MeshSuite enforces standardized projection matrices aligned with graphics conventions. (3) : On masked datasets such as DTU, prior works alternated between evaluating against unmasked black backgrounds and masked white backgrounds; MeshSuite standardizes all evaluations to the alpha matte white-background protocol (Eq. ). (4) : MeshSuite uses a common metric implementation, including VGG-based LPIPS (Sec. ), while parallel floating-point accumulation can also introduce numerical variation. The comparisons document agreement and remaining differences rather than establishing a single cause for them.Sources of Discrepancies and Impact of Standardization.Image Downsampling Kernels4.1Camera Intrinsics and Principal PointsBackground Compositing Conventions1Metric Implementations and Numerical Variation3.1

    Sec.  defines the structural metrics. For connected-component analysis, we exclude faces with repeated vertex indices from the face-adjacency graph and apply no component-size threshold. Tabs.  and  report per-scene results for all four datasets. Each mean row is the arithmetic average of scene-level metrics. The main-text summary is in Tab. .     Appendix D

    The following sections, figures, and tables provide the complete deployment-gap visualization, dataset-level runtime summaries, and scene-level measurements supporting Sec. . The primary deployment comparison and four-dataset Source Renderer benchmark are reported in main-text Tabs.  and ; reproduction comparisons are documented in Appendix Sec. .4.343B

    D.1

    Fig.  visualizes the PSNR trajectories of the four studied triangle- and mesh-based NVS representations across the Source Renderer, Standard Mesh Deployment, and Custom Engine Deployment on Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples. Tab.  summarizes the corresponding GPU latency percentiles (P50 and P95) and active graphics memory allocations, providing an extensive dataset-level view that expands the compact summary in main-text Tab. .7105

    Across both deployment benchmarks, the visual quality trajectories reveal a consistent two-tier pattern: (1) : Unconstrained triangle soup methods (2DTS and Triangle-Splatting) rely heavily on soft blending kernels and continuous opacity to represent fine structures and semi-transparent boundaries. When forced into Standard Mesh Deployment—where triangles are treated as fully opaque surfaces with hardware Z-buffering—these methods suffer dataset-mean PSNR drops of 11.02 $\sim$ 15.64 dB relative to the Source Renderer. In scenes with complex foliage or fine geometric thinness (, or ), overlapping transparent triangles collapse into severe opaque, jagged polygon shards (see Fig. ). (2) : In contrast, MeshSplatting exhibits far greater resilience under Standard Mesh Deployment, dropping by only 4.89 dB on Mip-NeRF 360 (19.83 dB vs. 24.72 dB) and 6.15 dB on Tanks and Temples (14.38 dB vs. 20.53 dB). Because its geometry is constrained to an indexed mesh surface, disabling alpha compositing causes significantly fewer occluding artifacts, allowing it to lead the four triangle- and mesh-based methods under Standard Mesh Deployment despite lower initial Source Renderer fidelity.Cross-Setting Trajectory Analysis.Severe Deployment Degradation for Triangle Soupse.g.treehillbonsai4Surface-Constrained Resilience in MeshSplatting

    As reported in Tab. , Custom Engine Deployment preserves image quality at the expense of substantial computational and memory overhead. On Mip-NeRF 360, Custom Engine Deployment increases GPU P50 latency by approximately 5.8 $\sim$ 7.6 $\times$ compared to Standard Mesh Deployment, based on the displayed dataset means (2.1 $\sim$ 6.4 ms vs. 0.3 $\sim$ 1.1 ms), while mean renderer graphics allocations for these three methods increase from 54 MiB to 927 $\sim$ 1559 MiB. DiffSoup represents a distinct operating point: utilizing neural texture decoding rather than millions of independent Gaussian-like primitives, it achieves sub-millisecond GPU latency (0.4 $\sim$ 0.5 ms) and mean renderer graphics allocations of 276 $\sim$ 288 MiB, though at the cost of lower overall image fidelity (17.02 $\sim$ 23.15 dB).Runtime Resource Trade-Offs.10

    Tab.  provides detailed per-scene measurements of GPU frame time percentiles (median P50 and 95th-percentile P95) and active renderer graphics allocations across all nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes under both Custom Engine Deployment and Standard Mesh Deployment settings. Sec.  discusses the primary deployment trade-offs.114.3

    The per-scene breakdown highlights a stark contrast in resource demands between scene categories: (1) : For indoor scenes (, , , ), graphics allocations remain moderately bounded, averaging 571 MiB for 2DTS, 1023 MiB for Triangle-Splatting, and 855 MiB for MeshSplatting. In contrast, outdoor scenes (, , , , ) require dramatic scaling, averaging 1595 MiB for 2DTS (peaking at 1602 MiB on ) and 1988 MiB for Triangle-Splatting (peaking at 2136 MiB on ). DiffSoup, by contrast, maintains an almost invariant footprint of 280 $\sim$ 298 MiB across both indoor and outdoor environments. (2) : Under Standard Mesh Deployment, renderer graphics allocations collapse to an almost identical 51 $\sim$ 57 MiB (mean 54 MiB) across all nine scenes and all three supported methods. This uniformity suggests a substantial fixed overhead in the measured renderer graphics resources at the evaluated viewport resolution; it does not establish the total engine memory footprint.Indoor vs. Outdoor Memory Scaling.Custom Engine Deployment AllocationsbonsaicounterkitchenroombicycleflowersgardenstumptreehillgardenflowersStandard Mesh Deployment Overhead

    GPU latency percentiles show limited spread on the evaluated scenes. Under Custom Engine Deployment, DiffSoup’s displayed P95 exceeds P50 by at most 0.1 ms on every scene, while 2DTS has differences of 0.2 ms on and and at most 0.1 ms elsewhere. Triangle-Splatting and MeshSplatting have maximum differences of 0.5 ms and 0.3 ms, respectively (, Triangle-Splatting on : 3.2 ms P50 vs. 3.7 ms P95). These measurements describe GPU latency variability; they do not establish deterministic end-to-end frame pacing.Latency Stability and Tail Profiling.counterkitchene.g.counter

    The methods differ in geometry and appearance evaluation, but the reported timings do not isolate costs by rendering stage: (1) : 2DTS and Triangle-Splatting use independent triangles, whereas MeshSplatting uses shared vertex indices. These designs imply different geometry-processing requirements; the aggregate GPU latency measurements do not establish which stage dominates. (2) : MeshSplatting combines SH evaluation with alpha compositing. DiffSoup decodes appearance from neural texture features without per-primitive alpha compositing or depth sorting (Tab. ) and achieves sub-millisecond mean GPU latency. The measurements do not isolate the contribution of each feature to this runtime difference.Representation Features and Runtime Differences.Geometry OrganizationAppearance and Compositing2

    Tab.  reports per-scene image fidelity, throughput, GPU latency, and resource metrics for and .12traintruck

    Triangle-Splatting achieves the highest Custom Engine Deployment quality on (20.63 dB PSNR, 0.733 SSIM, 0.215 LPIPS), whereas 2DTS leads in PSNR on (18.79 dB), while Triangle-Splatting has the highest SSIM (0.705) and lowest LPIPS (0.301). Under Standard Mesh Deployment, Triangle-Splatting degrades severely on (dropping 9.18 dB from Custom Engine Deployment to 9.26 dB), while MeshSplatting retains 13.88 dB on and 14.88 dB on , leading the four triangle- and mesh-based methods (14.38 dB mean). DiffSoup provides extreme throughput exceeding 2300 FPS (2345 $\sim$ 2431 FPS) at 0.4 ms GPU latency, albeit with lower visual fidelity (17.02 dB mean).Per-Scene Fidelity and Robustness.trucktraintraintraintruck

    Comparing active renderer memory against serialized asset size reveals key trade-offs: (1) Under Standard Mesh Deployment, measured renderer graphics allocations are 48 MiB while serialized assets range from 234 $\sim$ 556 MiB. These allocations do not measure total GPU memory. (2) Custom Engine Deployment reports renderer graphics allocations of 276 MiB for DiffSoup and 518 $\sim$ 1103 MiB for the other three methods (, 1103 MiB for a 469 MiB asset in 2DTS on ). Practical edge deployment must account for renderer allocations, total GPU memory, and storage constraints separately.Serialized Asset Footprint vs. Active Graphics Allocation.e.g.truck

    (1) : MeshSplatting offers higher Standard Mesh Deployment image quality than the two splatting soup methods on the evaluated datasets, with mean renderer graphics allocations of 48 $\sim$ 54 MiB. (2) : DiffSoup reaches 2388 FPS on Tanks and Temples and 1995 FPS on Mip-NeRF 360 without primitive sorting overhead; these benchmark measurements do not directly establish XR performance. (3) : Incorporating geometric priors during training is vital to penalize non-manifold edges and fragmentation for downstream physics.Engine Deployment Recommendations.Standard PipelinesHigh-Framerate XRTopological Regularization

    Appendix E

    Fig.  illustrates the qualitative rendering behavior of 2DGS on the scene across the evaluated deployment protocols, serving as a supplement to the triangle- and mesh-based methods in Fig. .8()Huang et al., 2024counter4

    In Sec. , 2DGS and DiffSoup illustrate opposing extremes of graphics-engine compatibility. DiffSoup couples explicit triangle geometry with neural feature textures: while its neural color decoder prevents native execution under the fixed-function Standard Mesh Deployment protocol, our custom engine shader successfully preserves its appearance under Custom Engine Deployment (reaching 23.15 dB on Mip-NeRF 360 and 18.90 dB on Tanks and Temples). In contrast, 2DGS operates as a collection of 2D oriented planar Gaussian splats rendered with a specialized tile-based splatting rasterizer. To extract polygonal geometry, 2DGS integrates truncated signed distance field (TSDF) fusion across depth maps predicted by the splats, exporting an explicit indexed triangle mesh with per-vertex colors. However, this meshing process completely discards the underlying 2D Gaussian covariances, normal vectors, and view-dependent opacity blending models. Consequently, 2DGS is fundamentally incompatible with our Custom Engine Deployment pipeline (marked in Fig.  and Tab. ), as the exported asset retains no splatting primitives for in-engine custom rasterization.Asymmetry with Neural Feature Decoding.4.3N/A84

    While the reconstructed TSDF mesh can be natively imported and rasterized via standard graphics pipelines at high frame rates (exceeding 4000 FPS on Tanks and Temples and 2700 FPS on Mip-NeRF 360), relying strictly on an opaque triangle surface with static vertex coloring induces drastic perceptual fidelity degradation: (1) : On the metallic mixing bowl shown in Fig. , the official Source Renderer accurately captures sharp, specular reflections and metallic sheen (27.02 dB dataset-mean PSNR). Under Standard Mesh Deployment, the shiny surface collapses into diffuse, cloudy shading, completely erasing the specular highlight in the highlighted red inset. (2) : As shown in the cyan inset (cutting board and background plastic containers), fine object boundaries and high-frequency textural details are blurred out during TSDF voxel discretization and marching cubes extraction. The lack of alpha transparency around thin structures causes occluded background elements to either disappear or merge unnaturally with foreground objects. (3) : Across Mip-NeRF 360, this geometric transition causes a 14.65 dB drop in dataset-mean PSNR (from 26.79 dB to 12.70 dB) and increases LPIPS from 0.252 to 0.594 (Tab. ). These qualitative artifacts confirm that standard triangle mesh conversion cannot faithfully preserve the appearance of 2D Gaussian primitives without specialized real-time engine shaders.Visual Degradation under Standard Mesh Deployment.Loss of View-Dependent Reflection8Geometric Oversmoothing and Boundary ArtifactsQuantitative Contrast4

一句话：此前各家方法评测口径不一，这个基准第一次在同一设置下比较，并把「在引擎里部署」作为评测维度。

要点：

  • 三角面基元的神经渲染是连接神经表示与图形引擎的桥梁
  • 现有方法开发与评测设置不一致，几乎没有直接对比
  • 首次系统性评估引擎部署与非欧几里得网格场景

为什么值得看：想评估「神经渲染能不能进产线引擎」，这个基准给出了统一口径与工程侧指标。

中文摘要：基于三角面与网格的神经渲染试图用与标准光栅化兼容的三角基元，把神经表示与图形引擎连接起来。但现有方法是在不一致的设置下开发与评估的，很少有直接比较，也几乎没人在图形引擎里评估。作者推出 MeshSuite，这是第一个系统性评估引擎部署与非欧几里得网格场景的基准，为后续方法提供统一比较口径。

来源：arXiv·神经渲染（English） 相关度：11.7 正文：75558 字 / 2 图

作者：Kaixuan Zhang、Minxian Li、Mingwu Ren 等 4 人

分类：cs.GR / cs.CV

PDF：https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.01306v4

命中：neural rendering、rendering、mesh、splatting、rasterization

Triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering seeks to bridge neural representations and graphics engines through triangle primitives compatible with standard rasterization. Yet existing methods were developed and evaluated under inconsistent settings, with few direct comparisons and little evaluation in graphics engines. We introduce MeshSuite, the first benchmark for systematic evaluation of engine

License: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 arXiv:2609.01306v4 [cs.GR] 16 Oct 2026

MeshSuite: A Unified Benchmark for Triangle- and Mesh-Based Neural Rendering

Kaixuan Zhang Nanjing University of Science and Technology Affiliation: Minxian Li †Corresponding author.†thanks: Nanjing University of Science and Technology Affiliation: Mingwu Ren Nanjing University of Science and Technology Affiliation: Xiatian Zhu University of Surrey Affiliation: 

Abstract

Triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering aims to bridge neural scene representations and existing graphics engines (, Unity, Blender) by leveraging primitives compatible with standard rasterization hardware. There have been several such methods driven by parallel efforts, developed and evaluated under inconsistent settings, with little or no comparison with each other; critically, most even have never used graphics engines for evaluation nor considered deployability in practice – significantly undermining the objective and motivation. To address these issues, we introduce , the first benchmark of its kind to enable systematic evaluation of graphics-engine deployment and the reference Source Renderer for triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering methods. Importantly, our deployment protocol includes two engine deployment settings: (1) – a conventional opaque mesh pipeline with vertex colors and hardware Z-buffering; (2) – adding method-specific engine implementations supporting the retained appearance and compositing features (, alpha blending), so that the characteristics of each specific model can be taken into account. For mesh splatting, we further propose a structural audit of exported surfaces, diagnosing topological and geometric integrity toward downstream graphics assets. We highlight several results: (1) Graphics engine deployment would incur image-quality degradation under both deployment options. Among the triangle- and mesh-based NVS methods studied, MeshSplatting degrades the least under Standard Mesh Deployment. (2) The deployment setting matters – Custom Engine Deployment can retain the majority of fidelity at a roughly 5 $\sim$ 33 $\times$ slowdown relative to Standard Mesh Deployment across the two deployment datasets. (3) About mesh splatting, the current approaches to explicit connectivity and shared indexing are still limited: shared vertex indexing alone does not ensure manifoldness or global connectivity. From this benchmark, we validate that , and highlight the significance of assessing the graphics engine deployment process (, the degree of engine compatibility). The project page is accessible at .e.g.triangleMeshSuiteStandard Mesh DeploymentCustom Engine Deploymente.g.rasterizability is merely part of graphics readinesse.g.https://surrey-up-lab.github.io/MeshSuite

1

Reconstructing a scene from multi-view images allows users to explore it from arbitrary viewpoints beyond those originally captured, supporting a wide range of vision and graphics applications, including AR/VR , gaming , and robotic perception . Recent advances in neural rendering, particularly Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) , have enabled increasingly realistic novel-view synthesis (NVS). Specifically, NeRFs use multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) to encode scene density and view-dependent color, synthesizing novel views through volume rendering . However, their practical use is constrained by high computational costs and the lack of an explicit geometric representation. In contrast, 3DGS represents scenes explicitly with 3D Gaussian primitives and uses efficient differentiable splatting to substantially reduce rendering costs .()Broxton et al., 2020()Lachambre et al., 2017()Zhu et al., 2022()Mildenhall et al., 2020()Kerbl et al., 2023()Mildenhall et al., 2020()Kerbl et al., 2023

Despite these advances, neither representation is directly compatible with the standard rendering pipelines of established computer graphics (CG) engines, such as Blender and Unity . These engines have benefited from decades of development and optimization, providing efficient rendering pipelines and integrated tools for lighting and shadows, material editing, and animation. Their mature ecosystems also offer extensive collections of reusable assets and plugins , facilitating the integration of reconstructed scenes into practical applications.()Blender Foundation, 2026()Unity Technologies, 2026(; )Unity Technologies, 2026Blender Foundation, 2026

To better take advantage of these engines, researchers have increasingly explored triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering methods, which optimize triangle primitives already supported by standard graphics hardware . These methods have demonstrated impressive NVS performance comparable to that of NeRFs and 3DGS, while offering a promising path toward integration with existing CG engines . However, existing triangle- and mesh-based works follow separate evaluation protocols, with differences in data preprocessing, image formats, evaluation metrics, and metric implementations, and none evaluates the methods in a graphics engine. Using triangles alone also does not ensure complete engine compatibility. Existing methods use triangles with substantially different features (Tab. ), including continuous or discrete opacity , coverage defined inside or outside a triangle , varying color representations (, view-dependent spherical harmonics (SHs) or neural networks ), and the presence or absence of neural texture decoders . These variations pose challenges for engine rendering and may require method-specific shaders, buffers, sorting strategies, and runtime state. Furthermore, existing mesh splatting methods evaluate exported mesh quality solely through vertex sharing, lacking a comprehensive analysis of critical structural and topological properties such as manifoldness and global connectivity.(; )Held et al., 2026bHeld et al., 2026a(; ; )Held et al., 2026bSheng et al., 2025Held et al., 2026a1(; )Held et al., 2026bHeld et al., 2026a(; )Sheng et al., 2025Held et al., 2026be.g.()Held et al., 2026a()Tojo et al., 2026(; )Tojo et al., 2026Held et al., 2026b()Held et al., 2026a

To address these questions, we introduce , a unified benchmark for evaluating triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering (see Fig. ). This benchmark enables: (a) integration of existing triangle- and mesh-based splatting methods; (b) fair and consistent comparison of different methods in a unified setting; (c) extensive evaluation of both triangle- and mesh-based models during training and inference; (d) Source Renderer evaluation and two engine deployment settings: - converting a trained model to a standard opaque vertex-colored mesh before rendering in a graphics engine; - adding a customized layer to implement method-specific designs, such as specialized appearance representations and alpha compositing.MeshSuite1Standard Mesh DeploymentCustom Engine Deployment

We note three key findings. , engine deployment reduces visual quality relative to the Source Renderer, with MeshSplatting losing the least quality under Standard Mesh Deployment among the studied methods (Tab. ). Second, Custom Engine Deployment produces more visually appealing renderings than Standard Mesh Deployment, at the cost of a roughly 5 $\sim$ 33 $\times$ slowdown (Tab. ). Third, existing mesh splatting methods’ exported meshes exhibit non-manifold structures and substantial fragmentation (Tab. ). These results show that ; appearance preservation, efficiency, and mesh structure must be evaluated together.First()Held et al., 2026a446using triangles alone does not ensure graphics readiness

Our are as follows: () the first unified benchmark, , for evaluating triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering methods; () Custom Engine Deployment of existing methods in a graphics engine (, Unity), retaining their specific designs during engine rendering; and () an extensive evaluation of existing models in terms of novel-view synthesis, training/inference cost, and mesh structure.contributionsIMeshSuiteIIi.e.III

2

Novel-view synthesis (NVS) aims to synthesize images of a scene from viewpoints beyond those observed in the input images. A central component of this task is a scene representation that captures both geometry and appearance. NeRF represents a scene as a continuous function and synthesize views through volumetric integration . Later methods improve reconstruction quality and anti-aliasing or accelerate rendering through explicit, factorized, and hashed structures . 3DGS replaces repeated network queries with optimized anisotropic Gaussian primitives and a dedicated splatting rasterizer . Follow-up works refine Gaussian optimization or encourages surface-aligned geometry . These methods establish strong NVS baselines, but their representations are not natively supported by conventional graphics engines (, Unity and Blender). Integration with existing CG engines therefore requires specialized rendering implementations or conversion to mesh-based assets.Dominant neural representations.()Mildenhall et al., 2020(; ; )Barron et al., 2021Barron et al., 2022Barron et al., 2023(; ; ; ; )Reiser et al., 2024Yu et al., 2021Fridovich-Keil et al., 2022Chen et al., 2022Müller et al., 2022()Kerbl et al., 2023(; ; )Kheradmand et al., 2024Huang et al., 2024Guédon and Lepetit, 2024e.g.

To facilitate integration with conventional graphics engines, methods such as MobileNeRF and BakedSDF convert learned radiance fields into mesh-based representations. For explicit splats, SuGaR and GaMeS extract mesh surfaces from 3D Gaussian primitives or bind Gaussian primitives to deformable mesh faces. Although these conversion pipelines produce standard mesh assets, they often rely on lossy post-processing (, Marching Cubes, Poisson surface reconstruction, or heuristic simplification) that decouples the optimization target from the final rendering objective.()Chen et al., 2023()Yariv et al., 2023()Guédon and Lepetit, 2024()Waczyńska et al., 2024e.g.

Established CG engines, such as Blender and Unity , provide optimized rendering pipelines and integrated tools for scene editing, lighting, and animation, together with mature ecosystems of reusable assets and plugins. Triangle meshes are widely supported by these pipelines, making them a natural choice for bringing learned scene representations into existing graphics workflows.Triangle- and mesh-based neural representations.()Blender Foundation, 2026()Unity Technologies, 2026

To exploit this support, triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering methods optimize geometry directly represented by triangle primitives . These approaches use either with independent faces or with shared vertices and explicit connectivity. 2DTS and Triangle-Splatting optimize independent triangles with soft coverage and alpha blending, DiffSoup uses neural texture features and a color decoder, and MeshSplatting introduces shared-vertex connectivity. Tab.  summarizes and contrasts the key design features across these representations alongside reference Gaussian baselines. These works demonstrate the potential of triangle- and mesh-based representations for high-quality NVS and offer promising routes toward graphics-engine integration.(; ; ; )Held et al., 2026bSheng et al., 2025Held et al., 2026aTojo et al., 2026triangle soupsindexed meshes()Sheng et al., 2025()Held et al., 2026b()Tojo et al., 2026()Held et al., 2026a1

However, using triangle primitives alone does ensure complete engine compatibility, as method-specific appearance and transparency models may still require additional adaptation. These methods are also developed and reported under different evaluation pipelines, making direct cross-method comparison difficult. Their original evaluations primarily use research-oriented source renderers rather than assess the learned representations after deployment in a graphics engine. MeshSuite addresses both gaps through unified evaluation and explicit graphics-engine deployment.not

Existing frameworks have sought to improve the reproducibility and comparability of NVS. Nerfstudio and GauStudio provide modular research frameworks for NeRF and Gaussian Splatting, while gsplat offers an efficient Gaussian rasterization library with extensive performance evaluations. More directly, NerfBaselines standardizes datasets, evaluation protocols, and metrics across NeRF and 3DGS methods while preserving their original implementations. Splatwizard further provides a specialized benchmark for 3DGS compression, evaluating rendering fidelity, computational efficiency, and geometric accuracy. The nvs-bench project facilitates reproducible NVS comparisons across different representations, including Triangle Splatting . Complementary studies investigate perceptual rendering quality and robustness under corrupted observations .Neural rendering benchmarks.()Tancik et al., 2023()Ye et al., 2024()Ye et al., 2025()Kulhanek and Sattler, 2025()Liu et al., 2026()nvs-bench contributors, 2026()Held et al., 2026b()Liang et al., 2024()Wang et al., 2024

Despite these efforts, existing benchmarks primarily focus on reconstruction quality and rendering efficiency within research-oriented source renderers, leaving graphics-engine deployment largely unexplored. MeshSuite addresses this gap by extending the evaluation of triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering to graphics-engine deployment, alongside a structural assessment of reconstructed meshes.

3

MeshSuite provides an end-to-end benchmark spanning evaluation with official Source Renderers and deployment in graphics engines. As illustrated in Fig. , it evaluates each trained representation under matched camera views, backgrounds, and evaluation metrics across three settings: Source Renderer, Standard Mesh Deployment, and Custom Engine Deployment. Comparisons across these settings reveal how graphics-engine deployment affects visual fidelity and rendering efficiency. For exported indexed meshes, we also assess structural usability, including local/global connectivity and manifoldness. Fig.  provides a more detailed overview of MeshSuite’s software architecture.16

3.1

Fair cross-method comparisons require consistent data and evaluation settings . MeshSuite standardizes three aspects:(; )Kulhanek and Sattler, 2025Liu et al., 2026

For a held-out camera set $\mathcal{C}$ , the benchmark standardizes camera coordinate frames, optical axes, field of view, and projection matrices.Camera and viewpoint alignment:

Prior works adopt inconsistent backgrounds: for example, on DTU , Triangle-Splatting uses an unmasked black background, whereas 2DTS uses object masks and a white background. We standardize all methods to the white-background protocol for masked objects. Using the RGBA alpha channel as an opacity matte, both ground-truth target images and novel-view renderings are composited asBackground compositing policy:()Jensen et al., 2014()Held et al., 2026b

$\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{white}}=\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{RGB}}\odot\bm{\alpha}+(1-\bm{\alpha})\cdot\mathbf{1}.$ (1)

Here, $\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{RGB}}$ and $\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{white}}$ denote the input RGB and composited images, respectively; $\bm{\alpha}$ is the per-pixel opacity matte with values in [0, 1]; $\odot$ denotes element-wise multiplication, with $\bm{\alpha}$ applied to all RGB channels; and $\mathbf{1}$ is an all-ones image. The renderer background is also set to white, giving all methods the same evaluation background.

We use the same implementations of PSNR , SSIM , and LPIPS for all methods. LPIPS uses a VGG backbone with images normalized to [-1, 1].Metric standardization:()Hore and Ziou, 2010()Wang et al., 2004()Zhang et al., 2018()Simonyan and Zisserman, 2015

3.2

Existing triangle- and mesh-based methods encode geometry, appearance, and opacity in method-specific ways (Tab. ). For example, 2DTS and Triangle-Splatting use independent triangles with learned opacity, MeshSplatting uses shared vertices with view-dependent appearance, and DiffSoup represents appearance through learned features and a neural decoder. Engine deployment therefore requires method-specific interpretation of the trained model’s parameters.1()Sheng et al., 2025()Held et al., 2026b()Held et al., 2026a()Tojo et al., 2026

To support deployment through a common interface, MeshSuite introduces a implemented by an adapter $\mathcal{E}_{m}$ for method $m$ . For each trained model $\mathcal{S}_{m}$ , the adapter maps its parameters to an engine asset $\mathcal{A}_{m}$ that follows the unified interface:translation layer

$\mathcal{S}_{m}\xrightarrow{\mathcal{E}_{m}}\mathcal{A}_{m}.$ (2)

The asset covers geometry, appearance, and opacity for different mesh structures. Translation decodes the trained model before deployment, allowing the engine to consume the exported asset independently of the training framework. The asset supplies the geometry and appearance data used by Standard Mesh Deployment and Custom Engine Deployment (see Appendix Fig. ).6

3.3

As illustrated in Fig. , MeshSuite organizes rendering into three evaluation settings: Standard Mesh Deployment, Custom Engine Deployment, and the reference Source Renderer. The Source Renderer serves as the baseline for the two engine-deployment settings.1

We render representations as conventional opaque meshes with static vertex colors and hardware Z-buffering. This setting omits method-specific shaders, neural decoders, and alpha blending. DiffSoup is unavailable in this setting.Standard Mesh Deployment ( $\mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{std}}_{m}$ ):

We implement method-specific Unity renderers under the same evaluation protocol that retain each method’s appearance and compositing features (Tab. ). Comparing them with the Source Renderer and Standard Mesh Deployment reveals how much quality these features preserve and their runtime cost (Tab. ).Custom Engine Deployment ( $\mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{cust}}_{m}$ ):24

We render each trained checkpoint $\mathcal{S}_{m}$ with its official Source Renderer $\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{src}}_{m}$ : $\mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{src}}_{m}(c)=\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{src}}_{m}(\mathcal{S}_{m},c),\forall c\in\mathcal{C}$ , where $c$ denotes a camera in the held-out set $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{src}}_{m}(c)$ is the corresponding rendered image. This establishes baseline image quality before engine deployment.Source Renderer ( $\mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{src}}_{m}$ ):

Although Custom Engine Deployment retains the same appearance and compositing functions, the graphics engine and Source Renderers can differ in primitive ordering, coverage, and attribute evaluation. These differences affect transparency and view-dependent appearance, particularly for large or oblique primitives, and contribute to the adaptation gap.Differences from Source Renderer.

3.4

MeshSuite groups evaluation metrics into three categories: NVS quality, mesh quality, and computational cost.

3.4.1

Following Sec. , we report PSNR , SSIM , and LPIPS (VGG backbone, normalized images). For an image-quality metric $q$ (, PSNR, SSIM, or LPIPS), we compute the mean score $Q_{m}^{r}$ over the held-out camera set $\mathcal{C}$ :Visual fidelity and deployment gaps:3.1()Hore and Ziou, 2010()Wang et al., 2004()Zhang et al., 2018e.g.

$Q^{r}_{m}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}q(\mathbf{I}_{m}^{r}(c),\mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{gt}}(c)),\qquad r\in\{\mathrm{src},\mathrm{std},\mathrm{cust}\},$ (3)

where $m$ indexes methods, $c$ denotes a held-out camera, and $|\mathcal{C}|$ is the number of evaluated cameras. The images $\mathbf{I}_{m}^{r}(c)$ and $\mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{gt}}(c)$ are the rendering of method $m$ under setting $r$ and the corresponding ground truth, respectively. The setting labels $\mathrm{src}$ , $\mathrm{std}$ , and $\mathrm{cust}$ denote Source Renderer, Standard Mesh Deployment, and Custom Engine Deployment, respectively.

Then we define three pairwise gaps:

$\Delta Q^{\mathrm{adapt}}_{m}=\left|Q^{\mathrm{src}}_{m}-Q^{\mathrm{cust}}_{m}\right|,\quad\Delta Q^{\mathrm{port}}_{m}=\left|Q^{\mathrm{cust}}_{m}-Q^{\mathrm{std}}_{m}\right|,\quad\Delta Q^{\mathrm{deploy}}_{m}=\left|Q^{\mathrm{src}}_{m}-Q^{\mathrm{std}}_{m}\right|.$ (4)

The measures the change from the Source Renderer to Custom Engine Deployment; the measures the additional change under Standard Mesh Deployment; and the measures the overall change from the Source Renderer to Standard Mesh Deployment. The gaps report absolute differences; the metric values indicate whether quality improves or declines.adaptation gap $\Delta Q^{\mathrm{adapt}}_{m}$ portability gap $\Delta Q^{\mathrm{port}}_{m}$ deployment gap $\Delta Q^{\mathrm{deploy}}_{m}$

3.4.2

We evaluate Chamfer Distance (CD) on DTU, which adopts standard pipelines to isolate the object surface, complementing the white-background image protocol in Sec. .Surface geometry:3.1

Rendering as triangles does not guarantee a valid geometric surface. Let $\mathbf{V}$ , $\mathbf{E}$ , and $\mathbf{F}$ denote the sets of unique vertices, undirected edges, and triangular faces in an exported mesh, with $|\cdot|$ denoting set cardinality. We audit three complementary aspects:Mesh structural integrity:

  • •

    The ratio $|\mathbf{V}|/|\mathbf{F}|$ (abbreviated as V/F in tables) measures unique vertices per face, and average valence $2|\mathbf{E}|/|\mathbf{V}|$ summarizes local adjacency density. With a common export convention, lower $|\mathbf{V}|/|\mathbf{F}|$ indicates greater vertex sharing.Local reuse.

  • •

    The boundary-edge and non-manifold-edge ratios are $|\mathbf{E}_{1}|/|\mathbf{E}|$ and $|\mathbf{E}_{>2}|/|\mathbf{E}|$ , where $\mathbf{E}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{E}_{>2}$ contain edges incident to one and more than two faces, respectively. The non-manifold-vertex ratio is $|\mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{nm}}|/|\mathbf{V}|$ , where $\mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{nm}}$ is the set of vertices whose incident faces fail to form a single valid fan. Valid fans may be closed around an interior vertex or open at a boundary while disconnected fans are non-manifold. (see Fig.  for illustration).Local structure.2

  • •

    Two faces are considered adjacent if they share an edge. LCC faces and LCC area report the fractions of faces and surface area in the largest connected component (LCC), while Components counts the edge-connected components. We read component counts together with LCC fractions and visual inspection to account for differences in scene size and resolution. These three groups distinguish vertex sharing, local manifoldness, and fragmentation. Appendix Sec.  gives the audit details.Global connectivity.C

    • 3.4.3

    We audit computational overhead across training and inference. During training, we track peak VRAM (MiB) and optimization time (min). During engine deployment, we report GPU frame latency, wall-clock throughput (FPS), and renderer graphics allocations (MiB) separately. We additionally report serialized asset size (MiB) to characterize storage requirements.

    4

    4.1

    We evaluate four representative triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering methods, covering different designs in geometry connectivity, opacity, and appearance (Tabs.  and ):Methods.12

  • •

    replaces Gaussian primitives with independent planar triangle facelets and renders them through differentiable alpha blending. Its opacity function is defined using barycentric coordinates, with a compactness parameter controlling the transition from diffuse splats toward sharper triangle surfaces.2DTS()Sheng et al., 2025

  • •

    directly optimizes independent triangles using a differentiable window function confined to each projected triangle. Learned opacity, view-dependent color, and depth-ordered alpha blending support image-based optimization, while adaptive densification and pruning refine the allocation of triangles.Triangle-Splatting()Held et al., 2026b

  • •

    represents scenes with a compact triangle soup carrying neural texture features and binary opacity. Stochastic opacity masking makes binary opacity trainable within a depth-tested rasterization pipeline, while a neural color decoder maps texture features to rendered colors.DiffSoup()Tojo et al., 2026

  • •

    constructs a shared-vertex mesh through restricted Delaunay triangulation and jointly refines geometry and per-vertex spherical-harmonic appearance. Opacity and window parameter schedules progressively guide optimization toward opaque triangles.MeshSplatting()Held et al., 2026a

    • The first three methods produce without explicit shared-vertex connectivity, whereas MeshSplatting produces an . We audit the structure of its exported mesh in Sec. . We additionally include 3DGS and 2DGS as Gaussian-based reference baselines.triangle soupsindexed mesh4.4()Kerbl et al., 2023()Huang et al., 2024

    We evaluate on four complementary datasets spanning real-world environments and object-centric captures:Datasets.

  • •

    comprises nine real scenes, with surrounding camera trajectories, cluttered geometry, and large depth variations that challenge reconstruction of both foreground and distant content.Mip-NeRF 360()Barron et al., 2022

  • •

    For , we use the two outdoor scenes and , featuring large real-world objects, complex backgrounds, and occlusions.Tanks and Temples()Knapitsch et al., 2017traintruck

  • •

    provides laboratory captures of varied objects from 49 or 64 calibrated camera positions per scene, together with structured-light reference scans, enabling geometric evaluation alongside image fidelity.DTU()Jensen et al., 2014

  • •

    contains eight object-centric scenes with detailed geometry and realistic non-Lambertian materials, complementary to real captures.NeRF-Synthetic()Mildenhall et al., 2020

    • We follow the original training pipelines while applying the shared data and evaluation protocols. Images are downsampled according to each method’s requirements. All training and evaluation use a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU with 24 GB memory.Implementation details.

    End-to-end FPS includes CPU processing and GPU rendering. We also report GPU median (P50) and 95th-percentile (P95) frame latency, together with renderer graphics allocations.Timing and resource measurements.

    Before comparing methods, we check our reproductions against published results and public codebases. Across all 27 Mip-NeRF 360 method–scene pairs with published per-scene results, the mean absolute PSNR difference is only 0.075 dB and the maximum relative deviation is below 0.8%. Fig.  shows this close agreement in image quality. Appendix Tab.  provides dataset-level comparisons against paper values and public-code results.Reproducibility.37

    4.2

    Tab.  reports the standardized Source Renderer results across all four datasets. On Mip-NeRF 360 , NeRF-Synthetic , and DTU , 2DTS achieves the highest PSNR (28.16 dB, 33.65 dB, and 29.66 dB), while using the least peak training memory on NeRF-Synthetic and DTU (3172 MiB and 2470 MiB). Triangle-Splatting achieves the lowest LPIPS on Tanks and Temples (0.171) and DTU (0.080). DiffSoup renders and trains fastest on three datasets (up to 371 FPS and 12.2 $\sim$ 16.8 min), but has lower image quality (18.90 dB on Tanks and Temples). MeshSplatting uses shared-vertex connectivity and trains fastest on DTU (10.7 min), with lower PSNR on Mip-NeRF 360 (24.72 dB). Thus, representation dominates fidelity, throughput, memory, and training time simultaneously.3()Barron et al., 2022()Mildenhall et al., 2020()Jensen et al., 2014no

    DTU complements NVS metrics with surface accuracy against reference scans (Tab. ). Results show that image quality and surface accuracy do not always yield the same ranking. While 2DTS leads in both PSNR (29.66 dB) and CD (0.63 mm), Triangle-Splatting achieves the lowest LPIPS (0.080) with a higher CD of 1.27 mm. MeshSplatting has similar PSNR to Triangle-Splatting (27.82 vs. 27.78 dB) but lower surface error (0.80 mm CD), while DiffSoup has the highest CD (3.89 mm). These results motivate evaluating image quality and surface geometry jointly before graphics deployment.2D novel-view fidelity vs. 3D surface geometry.3
