    Tab.  compares quality and throughput across the three settings on Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples; Appendix Fig.  summarizes the PSNR trajectories of the four triangle- and mesh-based methods. Appendix Tab.  retains their per-scene Tanks and Temples results. Under our deployment protocol, 3DGS is unsupported in both engine settings; 2DGS lacks Custom Engine Deployment because TSDF meshing discards appearance variables used by the Source Renderer (though its mesh runs under Standard Mesh Deployment); and DiffSoup lacks a Standard Mesh Deployment opaque path because of its neural feature decoder.4712()Kerbl et al., 2023()Huang et al., 2024

    The evaluated triangle- and mesh-based methods rely on specialized appearance models or compositing operations that limit their direct compatibility with conventional opaque mesh pipelines. Our Standard Mesh Deployment tests this compatibility using static vertex colors and hardware Z-buffering. Methods that depend on rendering operations beyond this pipeline can lose substantial image quality when adapted to it.Deployment quality.

    On Mip-NeRF 360, adapting 2DTS, Triangle-Splatting, and MeshSplatting to Standard Mesh Deployment lowers mean PSNR by 15.64 dB, 12.36 dB, and 4.89 dB, respectively, relative to the Source Renderer (Tab. ). MeshSplatting has the smallest overall deployment gap ( $\Delta Q_{m}^{\mathrm{deploy}}$ ) among these three methods. The rendered examples illustrate the visual losses: 2DTS produces large opaque shards on , and Triangle-Splatting exhibits a similar failure on (Fig. ).4bonsaitreehill4

    We implement method-specific Unity renderers for Custom Engine Deployment to retain each method’s appearance and compositing features. On Mip-NeRF 360, these implementations recover 2.69 $\sim$ 10.76 dB PSNR over Standard Mesh Deployment across 2DTS, Triangle-Splatting, and MeshSplatting, corresponding to their portability gaps ( $\Delta Q_{m}^{\mathrm{port}}$ ). They still fall short of the Source Renderer: the remaining adaptation losses ( $\Delta Q_{m}^{\mathrm{adapt}}$ ) are 4.88 dB for 2DTS, 4.17 dB for Triangle-Splatting, and 2.20 dB for MeshSplatting. Appendix Fig.  shows these changes across the three settings.7

    For DiffSoup, our Custom Engine Deployment retains the color decoder required by its neural texture features, while DiffSoup is unsupported under the Standard Mesh Deployment protocol (marked N/A in Fig. ). Custom Engine Deployment achieves a mean PSNR of 23.15 dB on Mip-NeRF 360, compared with 23.54 dB for the Source Renderer (Tab. ). The example shows visually similar results in the two settings. Thin structures such as brake cables remain poorly resolved in both, so these artifacts cannot be attributed solely to engine deployment. Supplementary videos compare the rendering settings.44bicycle

    As a complementary baseline to the triangle- and mesh-based methods, 2DGS exhibits the inverse deployment trade-off of DiffSoup: while 2DGS achieves high visual fidelity in its Source Renderer (27.02 dB PSNR on Mip-NeRF 360, Tab. ), it is incompatible with Custom Engine Deployment () because TSDF-based mesh reconstruction strips the 2D Gaussian splatting primitives and opacity blending models required by custom engine rendering. Under Standard Mesh Deployment, the extracted TSDF mesh can be natively rasterized at over 4000 FPS, but experiences severe visual degradation (dropping to 12.37 dB PSNR). Appendix Sec.  and Fig.  provide qualitative comparisons on the scene illustrating the loss of specular highlights and geometry oversmoothing under standard rasterization.()Huang et al., 20244N/AE8counter

    The leading method depends on the dataset and deployment setting. Under Custom Engine Deployment, 2DTS has the highest PSNR on Mip-NeRF 360, while Triangle-Splatting leads on Tanks and Temples in all three image metrics (19.54 dB PSNR, 0.719 SSIM, and 0.258 LPIPS). DiffSoup has the highest Custom Engine Deployment throughput on both datasets, reaching 2388 FPS on Tanks and Temples. Among the four triangle- and mesh-based methods, MeshSplatting achieves the best Standard Mesh Deployment quality on both datasets; on Tanks and Temples, it reaches 14.38 dB PSNR, 0.506 SSIM, and 0.490 LPIPS. For the three methods available in both engine settings on Tanks and Temples, Custom Engine Deployment improves all three image metrics but reduces throughput by 5.1 $\sim$ 7.3 $\times$ .Cross-dataset deployment behavior.

On Mip-NeRF 360, Triangle-Splatting gains 8.19 dB PSNR over Standard Mesh Deployment while rendering 32.8 $\times$ slower (70 vs. 2294 FPS). For 2DTS, the gain is 10.76 dB with a 6.9 $\times$ slowdown (545 vs. 3754 FPS). The Source Renderer provides a further 4.17 $\sim$ 4.88 dB PSNR at 70 $\sim$ 94 FPS.     4.4

    We audit MeshSplatting’s exported indexed meshes across all four datasets using the three metric groups defined in Sec. . Tab.  reports the mean of each metric over all scenes in each dataset. We consider the large, unbounded scenes of Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples separately from the smaller, object-centric scenes of DTU and NeRF-Synthetic. Appendix Sec.  provides per-scene results and audit details. We highlight the following results:3.46C

  • •

    Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples exhibit similar vertex sharing, with mean $|\mathbf{V}|/|\mathbf{F}|$ ratios of 0.523 and 0.516 and mean valence of 6.49 on both datasets. The object-centric datasets show greater reuse: DTU and NeRF-Synthetic have lower $|\mathbf{V}|/|\mathbf{F}|$ ratios of 0.428 and 0.339, with higher valence of 7.36 and 8.59, respectively. Vertex sharing is evident in both scene groups, but its extent differs.Local reuse.

  • •

    Vertex sharing does not ensure manifoldness. On Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples, approximately 18% of edges and 65 $\sim$ 66% of vertices are non-manifold. On DTU and NeRF-Synthetic, the non-manifold-edge ratios rise to 22% and 28%, and the non-manifold-vertex ratios to 73% and 87%, respectively. Thus, greater reuse on the object-centric datasets coexists with more non-manifold neighborhoods. Boundary edges account for 37 $\sim$ 46% of edges across the four datasets, indicating open surfaces while such boundaries can be expected in partially observed scenes. Non-manifold edges and vertices, in contrast, violate local manifold connectivity, and lower ratios indicate better local structural integrity.Local structure.

  • •

    On the large-scene datasets, the largest connected component (LCC) contains approximately 70% of faces, with 69% of surface area on Mip-NeRF 360 and 67% on Tanks and Temples. On DTU and NeRF-Synthetic, the LCC contains 77% and 80% of faces and 78% and 80% of area, respectively. Despite these dominant components, approximately 20 $\sim$ 30% of faces and 20 $\sim$ 33% of area remain distributed across other components. Together with mean component counts in the tens to hundreds of thousands, these fractions reveal substantial fragmentation in both scene groups. Absolute component counts depend on mesh size and do not provide a structural-quality ranking across datasets. On the two deployment datasets, MeshSplatting’s leading Standard Mesh Deployment image quality among the four studied methods (Tab. ) coexists with these structural defects, showing that visual fidelity does not ensure structural integrity.Global connectivity.4

    • 5

    We introduced MeshSuite, a unified benchmark for triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering that connects evaluation with official Source Renderers to graphics-engine deployment. MeshSuite combines standardized evaluation protocols, a unified asset interface, and method-specific Unity renderers to compare the Source Renderer, Standard Mesh Deployment, and Custom Engine Deployment. It evaluates visual fidelity and computational cost alongside surface accuracy and mesh structural integrity. Our experiments show that visual quality and method rankings depend on the deployment setting. Custom Engine Deployment better preserves appearance but incurs higher runtime costs than Standard Mesh Deployment. Among the four studied methods, mesh splatting methods achieve the highest image quality under Standard Mesh Deployment on Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples, yet their exported meshes exhibit non-manifold structures and substantial fragmentation across both large, unbounded and object-centric scenes. These findings show that triangle rasterization and shared-vertex connectivity alone do not ensure practical graphics usability. Evaluation must jointly consider appearance preservation, rendering efficiency, and the structural requirements of downstream tasks. Future work can extend the benchmark to additional graphics engines and directly assess exported meshes in tasks such as editing, remeshing, and collision handling.

    • Appendix A

    Fig.  details the modular software architecture of , expanding the conceptual overview in Fig. . The infrastructure is built with decoupling and modularity as first principles, ensuring that model training, format translation, graphics-engine deployment, and multi-dimensional evaluation operate independently through clearly specified interfaces.6MeshSuite1

    MeshSuite is organized into five cohesive subsystems: (1) : Standardizes canonical camera frames, optical axes, field-of-view definitions, and resolution downsampling across datasets. For masked object captures (, DTU), this layer automatically computes object alpha mattes and applies the white-background compositing convention specified in Eq. . (2) : Provides standardized training harnesses wrapping the official implementations of 2DTS , Triangle-Splatting , MeshSplatting , and DiffSoup . It follows each method’s original training pipeline while applying shared data and evaluation protocols under a common single-GPU hardware environment. (3) : The central translation bridge implementing method-specific adapters $\mathcal{E}_{m}$ . It parses trained model parameters and extracts explicit geometry, opacity fields, and appearance representations into standardized intermediate assets $\mathcal{A}_{m}$ . (4) : In-engine renderers implemented in Unity using C# Scriptable Render Pipelines and custom HLSL shaders. This layer provides both Standard Mesh Deployment and Custom Engine Deployment. (5) : Automated evaluation scripts computing standard 2D image fidelity metrics (, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS), hardware timing profiles (GPU P50/P95 latency percentiles and memory allocations), and geometric mesh topology audits.Modular Component Design.Dataset Managemente.g.1Algorithm Pool and Training()Sheng et al., 2025()Held et al., 2026b()Held et al., 2026a()Tojo et al., 2026Universal Translation LayerGraphics Engine DeploymentEvaluation and Audit Suitee.g.

    Under the Universal Translation Layer, trained models are converted into portable asset files prior to engine execution. Independent triangle soup models (2DTS, Triangle-Splatting, DiffSoup) are serialized into flat vertex arrays and attribute textures, whereas indexed meshes (MeshSplatting) are serialized with shared vertex coordinate tables, triangle face indices, and per-vertex SH coefficients. Crucially, the resulting asset bundles are completely self-contained and ingested directly by the graphics engine, decoupling real-time deployment from PyTorch, CUDA extension compilers, and Python runtime overhead. This architectural separation allows new neural rendering representations to be benchmarked by implementing a single translation adapter, and enables future deployment to other graphics engines (, Unreal Engine, Blender) without modifying upstream training pipelines.Asset Serialization and Decoupled Execution.e.g.

    Appendix B

    Tab.  complements the per-scene PSNR reproduction differences illustrated in Fig.  with comprehensive dataset-level evaluations comparing our reproduced metrics against published paper numbers and official public repositories. Sec.  outlines the primary experimental setup.734.1

    For 2DTS, Triangle-Splatting, and MeshSplatting, MeshSuite closely matches published dataset-level PSNR on Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples. On Mip-NeRF 360, the mean absolute PSNR difference across their 27 scene-method pairs is only 0.075 dB, and the maximum relative deviation across these pairs is below 0.8%. Specifically, 2DTS reproduces at 28.16 dB PSNR (vs. 28.18 dB in the paper and 28.51 dB in the public repository), Triangle-Splatting achieves 27.13 dB (vs. 27.17 dB reported and 27.20 dB in public code), and MeshSplatting achieves 24.72 dB (vs. 24.78 dB in both paper and code). For DiffSoup, where per-scene Mip-NeRF 360 results were not reported in the original paper, MeshSuite is closer to the public codebase in dataset-level PSNR (23.54 dB vs. 23.69 dB) than to the paper (24.76 dB); on Tanks and Temples, it achieves 18.90 dB vs. 18.38 dB in public code. LPIPS differences are larger for several methods, so close PSNR agreement does not imply equal agreement across all image metrics.Quantitative Reproduction Fidelity.1 DiffSoup is omitted since it does not report per-scene metrics in its original paper.11

    Differences between published figures, public repositories, and MeshSuite may reflect preprocessing, camera conventions, background compositing, metric implementations, and numerical variation. We do not isolate their individual contributions: (1) : Image interpolation filters can affect reconstructed image values; MeshSuite applies shared data preparation while retaining the downsampling requirements of each method (Sec. ). (2) : Differences in principal point handling and coordinate conventions can affect alignment; MeshSuite enforces standardized projection matrices aligned with graphics conventions. (3) : On masked datasets such as DTU, prior works alternated between evaluating against unmasked black backgrounds and masked white backgrounds; MeshSuite standardizes all evaluations to the alpha matte white-background protocol (Eq. ). (4) : MeshSuite uses a common metric implementation, including VGG-based LPIPS (Sec. ), while parallel floating-point accumulation can also introduce numerical variation. The comparisons document agreement and remaining differences rather than establishing a single cause for them.Sources of Discrepancies and Impact of Standardization.Image Downsampling Kernels4.1Camera Intrinsics and Principal PointsBackground Compositing Conventions1Metric Implementations and Numerical Variation3.1

    Appendix C

    Sec.  defines the structural metrics. For connected-component analysis, we exclude faces with repeated vertex indices from the face-adjacency graph and apply no component-size threshold. Tabs.  and  report per-scene results for all four datasets. Each mean row is the arithmetic average of scene-level metrics. The main-text summary is in Tab. . We highlight the following key findings:3.4896

    Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples exhibit comparable vertex reuse ( $|\mathbf{V}|/|\mathbf{F}|\approx 0.52$ ) and non-manifold ratios (18% NM edges, 65 $\sim$ 66% NM vertices). Within Mip-NeRF 360, achieves the highest LCC face and area fractions (77% and 78%), whereas records the lowest (65% and 63%), showing substantial variation in primary component consolidation. On Tanks and Temples, and allocate approximately 67% of area to the LCC despite divergent NM-vertex ratios (63% vs. 70%).Large, unbounded scenes.kitchenflowerstrucktrain

    Across the fifteen DTU scans, LCC face and area fractions range from 74.3 $\sim$ 79.7% and 74.7 $\sim$ 80.2%, respectively (mean 76.9% and 77.5%), while non-manifold-edge ratios average 22.2% (18.0 $\sim$ 27.8%). For instance, concentrates 79.2% of faces and 79.9% of area into the LCC, yet 27.8% of edges and 79.9% of vertices violate manifold conditions. Concentrated component mass therefore does not preclude local topological defects in the optimized mesh.DTU Results and Local Defects.scan37

    On NeRF-Synthetic, LCC face and area fractions both average 80.4%, while non-manifold-edge ratios average 28.4% (peaking at 33.3% in ), and NM-vertex ratios average 87.3% (91.6% in ). Although vertex reuse is elevated ( $|\mathbf{V}|/|\mathbf{F}|=0.339$ , mean valence 8.59), it coexists with high non-manifold ratios rather than ensuring regular 2-manifold surfaces.NeRF-Synthetic Results and High Vertex Reuse.hotdoglego

    Across all four benchmarks, our geometric audit highlights three critical structural challenges: (1) : The audited MeshSplatting exports exhibit pervasive non-manifold edges and vertices, with dataset mean ratios of 18 $\sim$ 28% and 65 $\sim$ 87%, respectively. (2) : While the LCC encompasses approximately 67 $\sim$ 80% of area, the remaining surface is distributed across many smaller components; mean total component counts range from 43.3k on DTU to 712.9k on Mip-NeRF 360. (3) : These defects motivate additional validation for workflows such as collision handling, UV unwrapping, and simplification. The structural audit does not directly measure performance in these tasks but it reveals that .Structural Audit Analysis and Practical Implications.Non-Manifold StructureSurface FragmentationDownstream Usabilitynovel-view fidelity does not ensure structural usability

    Appendix D

    The following sections, figures, and tables provide the complete deployment-gap visualization, dataset-level runtime summaries, and scene-level measurements supporting Sec. . The primary deployment comparison and four-dataset Source Renderer benchmark are reported in main-text Tabs.  and ; reproduction comparisons are documented in Appendix Sec. .4.343B

    D.1

    Fig.  visualizes the PSNR trajectories of the four studied triangle- and mesh-based NVS representations across the Source Renderer, Standard Mesh Deployment, and Custom Engine Deployment on Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks and Temples. Tab.  summarizes the corresponding GPU latency percentiles (P50 and P95) and active graphics memory allocations, providing an extensive dataset-level view that expands the compact summary in main-text Tab. .7105

    Across both deployment benchmarks, the visual quality trajectories reveal a consistent two-tier pattern: (1) : Unconstrained triangle soup methods (2DTS and Triangle-Splatting) rely heavily on soft blending kernels and continuous opacity to represent fine structures and semi-transparent boundaries. When forced into Standard Mesh Deployment—where triangles are treated as fully opaque surfaces with hardware Z-buffering—these methods suffer dataset-mean PSNR drops of 11.02 $\sim$ 15.64 dB relative to the Source Renderer. In scenes with complex foliage or fine geometric thinness (, or ), overlapping transparent triangles collapse into severe opaque, jagged polygon shards (see Fig. ). (2) : In contrast, MeshSplatting exhibits far greater resilience under Standard Mesh Deployment, dropping by only 4.89 dB on Mip-NeRF 360 (19.83 dB vs. 24.72 dB) and 6.15 dB on Tanks and Temples (14.38 dB vs. 20.53 dB). Because its geometry is constrained to an indexed mesh surface, disabling alpha compositing causes significantly fewer occluding artifacts, allowing it to lead the four triangle- and mesh-based methods under Standard Mesh Deployment despite lower initial Source Renderer fidelity.Cross-Setting Trajectory Analysis.Severe Deployment Degradation for Triangle Soupse.g.treehillbonsai4Surface-Constrained Resilience in MeshSplatting

    As reported in Tab. , Custom Engine Deployment preserves image quality at the expense of substantial computational and memory overhead. On Mip-NeRF 360, Custom Engine Deployment increases GPU P50 latency by approximately 5.8 $\sim$ 7.6 $\times$ compared to Standard Mesh Deployment, based on the displayed dataset means (2.1 $\sim$ 6.4 ms vs. 0.3 $\sim$ 1.1 ms), while mean renderer graphics allocations for these three methods increase from 54 MiB to 927 $\sim$ 1559 MiB. DiffSoup represents a distinct operating point: utilizing neural texture decoding rather than millions of independent Gaussian-like primitives, it achieves sub-millisecond GPU latency (0.4 $\sim$ 0.5 ms) and mean renderer graphics allocations of 276 $\sim$ 288 MiB, though at the cost of lower overall image fidelity (17.02 $\sim$ 23.15 dB).Runtime Resource Trade-Offs.10

    D.2

    Tab.  provides detailed per-scene measurements of GPU frame time percentiles (median P50 and 95th-percentile P95) and active renderer graphics allocations across all nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes under both Custom Engine Deployment and Standard Mesh Deployment settings. Sec.  discusses the primary deployment trade-offs.114.3

    The per-scene breakdown highlights a stark contrast in resource demands between scene categories: (1) : For indoor scenes (, , , ), graphics allocations remain moderately bounded, averaging 571 MiB for 2DTS, 1023 MiB for Triangle-Splatting, and 855 MiB for MeshSplatting. In contrast, outdoor scenes (, , , , ) require dramatic scaling, averaging 1595 MiB for 2DTS (peaking at 1602 MiB on ) and 1988 MiB for Triangle-Splatting (peaking at 2136 MiB on ). This scaling is driven by unbounded background geometry and dense vegetative foliage requiring millions of alpha-blended primitives. DiffSoup, by contrast, maintains an almost invariant footprint of 280 $\sim$ 298 MiB across both indoor and outdoor environments. (2) : Under Standard Mesh Deployment, renderer graphics allocations collapse to an almost identical 51 $\sim$ 57 MiB (mean 54 MiB) across all nine scenes and all three supported methods. This uniformity suggests a substantial fixed overhead in the measured renderer graphics resources at the evaluated viewport resolution; it does not establish the total engine memory footprint.Indoor vs. Outdoor Memory Scaling.Custom Engine Deployment AllocationsbonsaicounterkitchenroombicycleflowersgardenstumptreehillgardenflowersStandard Mesh Deployment Overhead

    GPU latency percentiles show limited spread on the evaluated scenes. Under Custom Engine Deployment, DiffSoup’s displayed P95 exceeds P50 by at most 0.1 ms on every scene, while 2DTS has differences of 0.2 ms on and and at most 0.1 ms elsewhere. Triangle-Splatting and MeshSplatting have maximum differences of 0.5 ms and 0.3 ms, respectively (, Triangle-Splatting on : 3.2 ms P50 vs. 3.7 ms P95). These measurements describe GPU latency variability; they do not establish deterministic end-to-end frame pacing.Latency Stability and Tail Profiling.counterkitchene.g.counter

    The methods differ in geometry and appearance evaluation, but the reported timings do not isolate costs by rendering stage: (1) : 2DTS and Triangle-Splatting use independent triangles, whereas MeshSplatting uses shared vertex indices. These designs imply different geometry-processing requirements; the aggregate GPU latency measurements do not establish which stage dominates. (2) : MeshSplatting combines SH evaluation with alpha compositing. DiffSoup decodes appearance from neural texture features without per-primitive alpha compositing or depth sorting (Tab. ) and achieves sub-millisecond mean GPU latency. The measurements do not isolate the contribution of each feature to this runtime difference.Representation Features and Runtime Differences.Geometry OrganizationAppearance and Compositing2

    D.3

    Tab.  reports per-scene image fidelity, throughput, GPU latency, and resource metrics for and .12traintruck

    Triangle-Splatting achieves the highest Custom Engine Deployment quality on (20.63 dB PSNR, 0.733 SSIM, 0.215 LPIPS), whereas 2DTS leads in PSNR on (18.79 dB), while Triangle-Splatting has the highest SSIM (0.705) and lowest LPIPS (0.301). Under Standard Mesh Deployment, Triangle-Splatting degrades severely on (dropping 9.18 dB from Custom Engine Deployment to 9.26 dB), while MeshSplatting retains 13.88 dB on and 14.88 dB on , leading the four triangle- and mesh-based methods (14.38 dB mean). DiffSoup provides extreme throughput exceeding 2300 FPS (2345 $\sim$ 2431 FPS) at 0.4 ms GPU latency, albeit with lower visual fidelity (17.02 dB mean).Per-Scene Fidelity and Robustness.trucktraintraintraintruck

    Comparing active renderer memory against serialized asset size reveals key trade-offs: (1) Under Standard Mesh Deployment, measured renderer graphics allocations are 48 MiB while serialized assets range from 234 $\sim$ 556 MiB. These allocations do not measure total GPU memory. (2) Custom Engine Deployment reports renderer graphics allocations of 276 MiB for DiffSoup and 518 $\sim$ 1103 MiB for the other three methods (, 1103 MiB for a 469 MiB asset in 2DTS on ). Practical edge deployment must account for renderer allocations, total GPU memory, and storage constraints separately.Serialized Asset Footprint vs. Active Graphics Allocation.e.g.truck

    (1) : MeshSplatting offers higher Standard Mesh Deployment image quality than the two splatting soup methods on the evaluated datasets, with mean renderer graphics allocations of 48 $\sim$ 54 MiB. (2) : DiffSoup reaches 2388 FPS on Tanks and Temples and 1995 FPS on Mip-NeRF 360 without primitive sorting overhead; these benchmark measurements do not directly establish XR performance. (3) : Incorporating geometric priors during training is vital to penalize non-manifold edges and fragmentation for downstream physics.Engine Deployment Recommendations.Standard PipelinesHigh-Framerate XRTopological Regularization

    Appendix E

    Fig.  illustrates the qualitative rendering behavior of 2DGS on the scene across the evaluated deployment protocols, serving as a supplement to the triangle- and mesh-based methods in Fig. .8()Huang et al., 2024counter4

    In Sec. , 2DGS and DiffSoup illustrate opposing extremes of graphics-engine compatibility. DiffSoup couples explicit triangle geometry with neural feature textures: while its neural color decoder prevents native execution under the fixed-function Standard Mesh Deployment protocol, our custom engine shader successfully preserves its appearance under Custom Engine Deployment (reaching 23.15 dB on Mip-NeRF 360 and 18.90 dB on Tanks and Temples). In contrast, 2DGS operates as a collection of 2D oriented planar Gaussian splats rendered with a specialized tile-based splatting rasterizer. To extract polygonal geometry, 2DGS integrates truncated signed distance field (TSDF) fusion across depth maps predicted by the splats, exporting an explicit indexed triangle mesh with per-vertex colors. However, this meshing process completely discards the underlying 2D Gaussian covariances, normal vectors, and view-dependent opacity blending models. Consequently, 2DGS is fundamentally incompatible with our Custom Engine Deployment pipeline (marked in Fig.  and Tab. ), as the exported asset retains no splatting primitives for in-engine custom rasterization.Asymmetry with Neural Feature Decoding.4.3N/A84

    While the reconstructed TSDF mesh can be natively imported and rasterized via standard graphics pipelines at high frame rates (exceeding 4000 FPS on Tanks and Temples and 2700 FPS on Mip-NeRF 360), relying strictly on an opaque triangle surface with static vertex coloring induces drastic perceptual fidelity degradation: (1) : On the metallic mixing bowl shown in Fig. , the official Source Renderer accurately captures sharp, specular reflections and metallic sheen (27.02 dB dataset-mean PSNR). Under Standard Mesh Deployment, the shiny surface collapses into diffuse, cloudy shading, completely erasing the specular highlight in the highlighted red inset. (2) : As shown in the cyan inset (cutting board and background plastic containers), fine object boundaries and high-frequency textural details are blurred out during TSDF voxel discretization and marching cubes extraction. The lack of alpha transparency around thin structures causes occluded background elements to either disappear or merge unnaturally with foreground objects. (3) : Across Mip-NeRF 360, this geometric transition causes a 14.65 dB drop in dataset-mean PSNR (from 26.79 dB to 12.70 dB) and increases LPIPS from 0.252 to 0.594 (Tab. ). These qualitative artifacts confirm that standard triangle mesh conversion cannot faithfully preserve the appearance of 2D Gaussian primitives without specialized real-time engine shaders.Visual Degradation under Standard Mesh Deployment.Loss of View-Dependent Reflection8Geometric Oversmoothing and Boundary ArtifactsQuantitative Contrast4

item.title: 华中师大 CoReFuse-Med：先净化再融合，让低质模态不再拖后腿｜ACM MM 2026
item.description:
一句话：医学影像多模态融合中，低质量模态会把重采样伪影带进网络，作者从浅层污染与深层偏置两头修。

要点：

  • 多模态不是越多越好：模态质量差异会污染融合结果
  • 浅层：清洗重采样伪影；深层：纠正模态偏置
  • ACM MM 2026 论文

为什么值得看：与游戏引擎关联不大，但「低质输入污染融合」的处理思路在做多传感器融合（动捕、眼动与手柄多源输入）时可借鉴。

中文摘要：多模态融合并非总是有效。当 MRI 已空间对齐、但 T1/T2/FLAIR 等模态采样质量差异很大时，低质量模态可能把重采样伪影一并带入融合网络。CoReFuse-Med 从浅层污染与深层模态偏置两方面入手修复：先净化伪影，再做重平衡融合，论文发表于 ACM MM 2026。

来源：雷峰网（中文） 相关度：11.3 正文：2755 字 / 28 图

分类：顶会专区

命中：高斯、遮挡

来源：多模态信息融合 文章链接：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/SVr9DmtPyzORLYad-tNR-g 多模态融合 何时失效？ ACM MM 2026 · CoReFuse-Med 多模态并不是越多越好。当MRI已经空间对齐，但是T1、T2、FLAIR等模态的采样质量差别很大时，低质量模态可能会把高质量模态中产生的重采样伪影一起带入到融合网络中去。CoReFuse-Med从浅层污染和深层模态偏置这两个方面来对症下药地进行修复。 论文标题： When Fusion Fails: Corruption-Aware Rebalanced Fusion for Multi-Modal Medical Image Segmentation 作者： Yuchen Pei, Xiaoyu Hu, Yixiong Zou, Dingwen Hu, Hui Chu, Yutao

来源：多模态信息融合

文章链接：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/SVr9DmtPyzORLYad-tNR-g

多模态融合何时失效？ACM MM 2026 · CoReFuse-Med多模态并不是越多越好。当MRI已经空间对齐，但是T1、T2、FLAIR等模态的采样质量差别很大时，低质量模态可能会把高质量模态中产生的重采样伪影一起带入到融合网络中去。CoReFuse-Med从浅层污染和深层模态偏置这两个方面来对症下药地进行修复。

论文标题：When Fusion Fails: Corruption-Aware Rebalanced Fusion for Multi-Modal Medical Image Segmentation

作者：Yuchen Pei, Xiaoyu Hu, Yixiong Zou, Dingwen Hu, Hui Chu, Yutao Ma, Shijun Qiu, Gang Li

单位：华中师范大学、华中科技大学、广州中医药大学及其第一附属医院、北卡罗来纳大学教堂山分校

论文链接：

https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10261

代码链接：

https://github.com/lrever/CoReFuse

01对齐好了，但是融合为什么还不能成功呢？FUSION FAILURE · FIG. 1论文在IH EPVS数据集中对高分辨率T1单模态DSC进行了观察，并发现了一个出乎意料的结果：高分辨率T1单模态DSC为0.703，融合T1、T2 和 FLAIR 后反而降到大约 0.695。空间对齐并不等同于信息质量的一致性。低分辨率序列经过重采样之后，其图像和T1同大小，但是可能会含有不可靠的信息。三个证据：污染和偏见作者把问题限定在了分辨率不同所引起的质量问题下降上，并没有涉及到未对齐或者模态全部缺失的情况。首先比较浅层特征的F-CNR，然后联合训练梯度和遮挡测试，最后跟踪跳跃连接的噪声传播：由此可以解释为什么“弱训练贡献”也有可能是“强推理干扰”。证据一：低分辨率产生噪声论文中提出的特征对比噪声比F-CNR：用病灶区和背景区的均值之差除以背景区的标准差来衡量可分性。第三页特征可视化显示，T1的F-CNR值是1.0283，T2的F-CNR值是0.4301，FLAIR的F-CNR值只有0.2980；T1 约为 FLAIR 的 3.4 倍。即使从几何上来说是重合的，但是浅层表征的可靠性却不一样。式(1)｜F-CNR：病灶和背景特征可以区分证据二：优化和推理不一致在EPVS的3D U-Net中，T1占据了77.4%的梯度贡献，FLAIR只占到了13.1%；但是遮挡FLAIR会使DSC降低70.2%，和遮挡T1的影响一样大。梯度更新次数少，并不代表在预测的时候就没有影响了。论文把反差看作是优化——推理不一致性的主要证据。证据三｜Skip 连接会传染U 型网络中的 skip connections 本来是用来把空间细节送入解码器的；在各向异性MRI中，它也会把重采样的结构伪影一起带到新的图像中去。网络又倾向于依靠更加“干净”的、容易被优化的高质量模态，因此出现了特征污染和贪婪模态选择的问题。T1、T2、FLAIR等浅层特征F-CNRTable 1 梯度贡献、模态遮挡之后DSC下降02首先进行净化，然后对各个模态的贡献进行平衡COREFUSE-MED·FIG.3CoReFuse-Med 不是简单的再堆一个更强大的cross-attention，而把融合分成两部分：LACE首先给每个MRI序列构建出高效的各向异性编码；IMSH对浅层结构基底和残差之间的可靠传递负责；MBCF 在深层次共享语义空间中重新校准模态贡献。仍然是一套三流、对称U型分割网络。01LACE+IMSH浅层先“去污染”LACE 双分支选择性融合：局部边界和轴向上下文分别提取出来之后，再用自适应权重进行合成。式(2)LACE选择性特征融合IMSH 空间尺度分解：平滑分量承担共享解剖布局，残差包含有效的细节和重采样的噪声。式(3)｜平均池化构建结构基底和残差式(4)｜竞争加权之后回写浅层特征02MBCF｜对深层纠正模态偏见MBCF的作用是针对L3-L4深层跳连特征。首先把T1、T2、FLAIR的全局描述拼接起来，经过共享MLP产生通道权重；再利用空间门控来排除由于位置不稳而产生的不可靠响应；最后得到的是一个不属于任何一个单一模态的公共查询Q，对三模态拼接并下采样K、V执行对称交叉注意力。目的并不是要迫使所有的模态都以相同的权重来发言，而是在融合的时候给可信的信息合理的贡献。全局通道校准并不是通过Softmax强行使三个模态的权重相加等于1，而是在共享MLP和Sigmoid之间产生条件化的通道权重；空间门控和共享查询更加限制了模态的竞争。式(5)为全局通道可靠性的校正式(6)不依赖于一个单一的模态来共享查询式(7)｜三模态拼接和降采样的后K、V式(8)对称跨模态注意力融合实验的结果和边界：怎么去读呢？在EPVS上Ours(Med)DSC=0.7326、HD95=7.35，好于对比中的MedNeXt的0.7085、8.17；在 上DSC=0.80，HD95=6.22，IAVD=0.171，参数量只有2.665M。论文还对BraTS中20%和30%轴向切片的保留情况进行考察，并且分别重新训练了每个模型，在两种不同的设置下取得了最好的DSC/HD95；但这不是同一个权重直接跨退化等级测试。额外的高斯噪声是作为补充来验证的。消融实验：在EPVS中，BaselineDSC为0.7146；组合LACE+IMSH+MBCF之后的Ours(Base)为0.7322，表示这三个模块之间存在互相补充的作用。在EPVS上已经严重退化的地区，模型主要是防止污染破坏T1，并不是“凭空恢复”T2/FLAIR已经丢失的信息。研究边界：主要问题就是空间对齐之后的分辨率下降，并不是所有的模态都缺失了，也没有解决所有的强噪声场景。未来的方向是动态模态缺失以及更多的采集伪影。

一句话：医学影像多模态融合中，低质量模态会把重采样伪影带进网络，作者从浅层污染与深层偏置两头修。

要点：

  • 多模态不是越多越好：模态质量差异会污染融合结果
  • 浅层：清洗重采样伪影；深层：纠正模态偏置
  • ACM MM 2026 论文

为什么值得看：与游戏引擎关联不大，但「低质输入污染融合」的处理思路在做多传感器融合（动捕、眼动与手柄多源输入）时可借鉴。

中文摘要：多模态融合并非总是有效。当 MRI 已空间对齐、但 T1/T2/FLAIR 等模态采样质量差异很大时，低质量模态可能把重采样伪影一并带入融合网络。CoReFuse-Med 从浅层污染与深层模态偏置两方面入手修复：先净化伪影，再做重平衡融合，论文发表于 ACM MM 2026。

分类：顶会专区

item.title: GLoD-LVSM：为大幅面视图合成模型学习基于几何的连续 LoD 表示 ｜ GLoD-LVSM: Learning Geometry-Grounded Continuous-LoD Scene Representations for Large View Synthesis Models
item.description:
一句话：大视图合成模型的 token 冗余导致存储与渲染成本高，用连续 LoD 的紧凑几何表示来压缩。

要点：

  • LVSMs 从稀疏视角重建并快速渲染，但 token 冗余严重
  • 不学习固定锚点集，而是学一个连续场来初始化表示
  • 支持连续 Level-of-Detail，按需分配容量

为什么值得看：和引擎里的 LOD 体系是同一类问题，只是对象换成了神经表示，对做场景流式加载有直接参考。

中文摘要：大视图合成模型（LVSM）能从稀疏视角重建场景并快速渲染新视角，但由于 token 冗余会带来不必要的存储与渲染开销。作者提出 GLoD-LVSM：一种紧凑的、基于几何的场景表示，具备连续 Level-of-Detail 能力。它不学习一组固定的场景锚点初始化，而是学习一个连续场来初始化表示，从而按需分配容量、减少冗余。

来源：arXiv·cs.GR 最新（English） 相关度：10.3 正文：51098 字 / 23 图

作者：Weikai Lin、Nicholas Milef、Carl S Marshall 等 6 人

分类：cs.CV / cs.GR

接收/备注：38 pages, including supplementary material

PDF：https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20254v1

命中：lod、rendering、lighting、texture

Large view synthesis models (LVSMs) reconstruct scenes from sparse views and render novel views quickly, but they incur unnecessary storage and rendering costs due to token redundancy. We present GLoD-LVSM, a compact, geometry-grounded scene representation for LVSMs with continuous levels of detail. First, instead of learning a fixed set of scene anchor initializations, GLoD-LVSM learns a continuo

GLoD-LVSM

Weikai LinNicholas MilefCarl S MarshallGrant Kaijuin YangTodd KeelerYuhao ZhuUniversity of Rochester Reality Labs, Meta

Abstract

Large view synthesis models (LVSMs) reconstruct scenes from sparse views and render novel views quickly, but they incur unnecessary storage and rendering costs due to token redundancy. We present , a compact, geometry-grounded scene representation for LVSMs with continuous levels of detail. First, instead of learning a fixed set of scene anchor initializations, learns a continuous field that initializes a flexible number of anchors to match the desired budget. A condenser then aggregates scene information into these anchors, with both the field and condenser trained end-to-end. Second, the condenser infers reference-token and anchor geometry to guide compression through geometry-grounded attention, improving rendering quality and enabling frustum culling during decoding. Compared with existing LVSM scene-compression baselines, achieves the best trade-off between rendering quality and scene token count. Compared with the uncompressed base model, reduces the scene-token count by 33.4% and accelerates rendering by $1.23\times$ with no quality loss. Under a relaxed quality-loss budget, the reduction increases to 85.5%, with $3.00\times$ rendering speedup. Further analysis reveals that view-synthesis supervision yields emergent scene depth and self-organized anchors that align with surfaces and adapt their density to local texture complexity. Beyond rendering, we further show that our scene representation also supports scene-semantic understanding, highlighting its potential for broader downstream tasks.GLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSM

1

Large view synthesis models (LVSMs) learn a reconstruction prior for novel view synthesis (NVS) , reducing scene reconstruction to a single feed-forward pass and enabling high-quality rendering from sparse reference views. Recent high-quality LVSMs commonly adopt a highway representation, where each reference-image patch is directly mapped to a scene token . While this design preserves detailed appearance information, the resulting scene-token count grows with the number of reference views, increasing both storage and decoding costs. This tight coupling between image and scene-representation sizes becomes a bottleneck with more reference views.(; ; )Jin et al., 2025Kim et al., 2026Szymanowicz et al., 2026(; )Szymanowicz et al., 2026Kim et al., 2026

In addition to scaling poorly with reference view count, highway representations allocate scene capacity inefficiently in two ways. First, overlapping 3D regions observed from different views are stored as separate tokens rather than consolidated. Second, every image patch receives the same one-token capacity regardless of texture complexity. An ideal LVSM representation should therefore (1) support flexible scene-token count independent of the input-view count, (2) consolidate multi-view observations into a unified, 3D representation, and (3) allocate capacity adaptively to scene complexity. Thus, we propose , which provides two key features: (1) a geometry-grounded scene representation that supports (2) continuous level-of-detail. We refer to scene tokens in as to emphasize their scene-centric 3D nature.scene-centricGLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSManchors

Different storage and rendering budgets require different scene-token numbers, which correspond to different levels of scene detail. To support arbitrary scene-token counts and thus continuous levels of detail (CLoD), we first design an anchor initialization scheme that can generate a flexible number of tokens. Specifically, we introduce a CLoD scene-anchor initialization that parameterizes anchor initialization as a continuous field (Sec. ). Sampling this field at different densities generates different numbers of anchors. This decouples the scene-token count from the reference-view count and allows our model to operate under different storage and rendering budgets.3.2

A compact scene representation should consolidate multi-view observations and allocate capacity where it is most useful. To achieve this, we (1) use unified, scene-centric 3D anchors to consolidate redundant multi-view tokens, and (2) learn the spatial allocation of these anchors end-to-end. Specifically, we use an end-to-end learned, geometry-grounded condenser that aggregates reference-view tokens into 3D anchors (Sec. ). The condenser predicts geometry for both views and anchors and uses their geometric relationships to guide cross-attention. The resulting anchors have 3D positions, which further enable target-view frustum culling to reduce decoding cost (Sec. ). Both the geometry and scene-complexity-aware anchor allocation emerge from the NVS objective (Sec. ).3.33.44.6

We evaluate across datasets, reference-view counts and scene-token budgets. Quantitatively, consistently achieves the best quality–token-count trade-off among the baselines. Qualitatively, the learned anchors emerge near scene surfaces and allocate higher density to regions with richer texture, suggesting that NVS supervision and compression alone can induce a geometry- and complexity-aware efficient scene representation. Beyond rendering, we further evaluate the learned representation on scene-semantic understanding, demonstrating its potential as a 3D scene representation for broader downstream tasks. Our contributions are threefold:GLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSM

  • •

    We introduce a scene-conditioned continuous query field that enables flexible scene anchor budgets independent of the reference-view count.Continuous-LoD scene representation.

  • •

    We learn scene-centric 3D anchors end-to-end, enabling efficient multi-view consolidation and scene-adaptive capacity allocation.Geometry-grounded scene condensation.

  • •

    achieves the best quality–scene-token trade-off for rendering and supports scene semantic understanding.Efficient and generalizable scene anchors.GLoD-LVSM

    • 2

    2.1

    Novel view synthesis (NVS) is a widely studied problem and can be broadly categorized into per-scene optimization methods and feed-forward generalizable methods. NeRF  and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)  achieve photorealistic novel-view synthesis by optimizing a radiance field or a set of Gaussian primitives for each scene. However, they typically require time-consuming per-scene optimization and dense image capture to achieve high rendering quality. In contrast, generalizable NVS methods , including recent Transformer-based approaches such as LVSMs , learn reconstruction priors from large datasets and can reconstruct unseen scenes from sparse input views in a single feed-forward pass, avoiding costly dense image capture and per-scene optimization. Our work builds on Transformer-based generalizable NVS and focuses on learning a compact, geometry-grounded scene representation that reduces redundancy among scene tokens, thereby lowering storage and rendering costs.()Mildenhall et al., 2020()Kerbl et al., 2023(; ; )Sajjadi et al., 2022Chen et al., 2024Xu et al., 2025(; ; ; )Jin et al., 2025Kim et al., 2026Sun et al., 2026Szymanowicz et al., 2026

    2.2

    Compact scene representations have been widely studied for efficient NVS. For example, 3DGS methods prune or compress Gaussian primitives to reduce representation size while preserving visual quality . Some methods further support multiple or continuous levels of detail (CLoD), allowing representation complexity to adapt to runtime rendering budgets . Compact scene-token representations have also been explored for LVSMs. LVSM-ED  uses a fixed latent bottleneck and cannot support flexible compression rates. CLiFT  uses K-means to select representative reference-view tokens, relying on handcrafted clustering that may be suboptimal. Our work also targets compact scene representations for LVSMs. Unlike prior methods, we support CLoD and learn scene anchors end-to-end, enabling flexible compression with less handcrafted design.(; ; )Fan et al., 2024Fang and Wang, 2024Lin et al., 2025(; )Milef et al., 2025Cheng et al., 2026()Jin et al., 2025()Wang et al., 2025

    3 GLoD-LVSM

    Fig.  illustrates . Given $V$ reference images and their camera parameters, constructs a compact scene representation with a chosen budget of $K$ anchors. A highway scene encoder first extracts reference-view tokens (Sec. ). Our anchor initializer then generates $K$ anchors from a continuous field (Sec. ). These anchors are passed to our condenser, which produces scene-centric 3D anchors (Sec. ). The anchors will be used to render the RGB images given the target views (Sec. ). We train end-to-end using the NVS loss (Sec. ).2GLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSM3.13.23.33.4GLoD-LVSM3.5

    3.1

    We use the encoder from LagerNVS . The inputs are $\mathcal{X}=\{(\mathbf{I}_{v},\mathcal{P}_{v})\}_{v=1}^{V}$ , where $\mathbf{I}_{v}$ is the $v$ -th reference image and $\mathcal{P}_{v}$ is its camera parameters. The encoder patchifies each reference image, embeds each patch as a token, embeds $\mathcal{P}_{v}$ into a camera token $\mathbf{t}^{\mathrm{cam}}_{v}$ , and appends four register tokens $\mathbf{t}^{\mathrm{reg}}_{1:4}$ to each view . For each view, input token sequence $\mathbf{T}_{v}^{\mathrm{in}}=[\mathbf{t}^{\mathrm{cam}}_{v},\mathbf{t}^{\mathrm{reg}}_{1:4},\operatorname{PatchEmbed}(\mathbf{I}_{v})]$ . The resulting tokens are jointly encoded across all $V$ views:()Szymanowicz et al., 2026()Darcet et al., 2024

    $\mathbf{H}=\operatorname{Encoder}(\{\mathbf{T}_{v}^{\mathrm{in}}\}_{v=1}^{V}),\qquad{\bm{Z}}=\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{patch}}\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}.$ (1)

    Here, $\mathbf{W}$ linearly maps the encoded patch tokens to a defined $D$ -dimensional space, and $N$ is the total number of input patches across all views. We refer to the output ${\bm{Z}}$ as and retain the encoded register and camera tokens for anchor initialization (Sec. ). This one-patch-one-token highway design causes storage and decoding costs to grow with reference-view count.reference-view tokens3.2

    3.2

    Given reference-view tokens ${\bm{Z}}$ , our condenser compresses them into scene anchors. The first challenge is anchor initialization. Fixed learned vectors  support only a predefined anchor count. Clustering-based initialization  supports variable counts, but relies on handcrafted clustering that may be suboptimal and remains image-centric rather than scene-centric. We instead learn a scene-conditioned continuous initialization field end-to-end with minimal handcrafted design (Fig. (a)). Sampling the field at different densities yields different anchor budgets, enabling continuous levels of detail under varying storage and rendering constraints.()Jin et al., 2025()Wang et al., 20252

    Continuous field parameterization.

    Given a total anchor budget $K$ , we distribute $K$ evenly across the $V$ reference views, assigning $K_{v}$ anchors to view $v$ . For each view, our goal is to learn a $D$ -dimensional continuous field that maps query indices $i\in\{0,\ldots,K_{v}-1\}$ to $K_{v}$ vectors in the $D$ -dimensional anchor space, with $D$ set to the highway model’s scene-token dimension. We parameterize this continuous field as an MLP conditioned jointly on the anchor indices and the current scene/view context. Specifically, each anchor index $i$ is mapped to a continuous coordinate $u_{v,i}$ and encoded with our anti-aliased positional encoding $\bar{\gamma}(u_{v,i})$ (Eqn. ). To condition the field on the current input, we mean-pool the encoded registers and camera tokens (Sec. ) of view $v$ and map them through $\operatorname{MLP}_{\mathrm{context}}$ to obtain a view- and scene-specific context vector $\mathbf{c}_{v}$ . $\bar{\gamma}(u_{v,i})$ and $\mathbf{c}_{v}$ are then concatenated and passed to $\operatorname{MLP}_{\mathrm{field}}$ to produce the $D$ -dimensional anchor initialization ${\bm{a}}_{v,i}$ :33.1

    ${\bm{a}}_{v,i}=\operatorname{MLP}_{\mathrm{field}}\left(\left[\bar{\gamma}(u_{v,i}),\mathbf{c}_{v}\right]\right),\qquad\mathbf{c}_{v}=\operatorname{MLP}_{\mathrm{context}}\left(\operatorname{MeanPool}([\mathbf{H}^{\mathrm{reg}}_{v,1:4},\mathbf{H}^{\mathrm{cam}}_{v}])\right).$ (2)

    Finally, we concatenate the initializations from all views to obtain $K=\sum_{v}K_{v}$ anchor initializations and feed them to the condenser. The field is optimized end-to-end through the NVS objective.

    Anti-Aliased Positional Encoding Across Anchor Budgets.

    To sample the same continuous field at different anchor budgets, we map each discrete query index $i$ to a continuous coordinate $u_{v,i}$ in a fixed canonical domain $[0,K_{\mathrm{canonical}}]$ , where $K_{\mathrm{canonical}}=2000$ . For each view with budget $K_{v}$ , we divide the domain into $K_{v}$ intervals. Changing $K_{v}$ therefore changes the sampling density while preserving coverage of the domain. To help the field capture high-frequency variation, we follow NeRF-style positional encoding (PE)  and encode each coordinate as $\gamma(u)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{F}}[\cos(2\pi\mathbf{f}u),\sin(2\pi\mathbf{f}u)]\in\mathbb{R}^{2F}$ . Here, $\mathbf{f}=(f_{0},\ldots,f_{F-1})$ is logarithmically spaced between $f_{\min}=1/20000$ and $f_{\max}=0.5$ . We set $F=D/2$ , where $D$ is the dimension of anchor space. At small budgets, sparse sampling can alias the high-frequency components of PE. We therefore integrate PE over the sampling interval, analogous to box filtering :()Mildenhall et al., 2020()Barron et al., 2021

    $\bar{\gamma}_{v,i}=\frac{1}{\Delta_{v}}\int_{I_{v,i}}\gamma(u)\,du,\quad I_{v,i}=[u_{v,i},u_{v,i}+\Delta_{v}],\quad u_{v,i}=i\Delta_{v},\quad\Delta_{v}=\frac{K_{\mathrm{canonical}}}{K_{v}}.$ (3)

    As the anchor budget decreases, the intervals become wider and more strongly attenuate high-frequency components. The sine and cosine integrals have closed-form solutions, given in Supplementary . The resulting $\bar{\gamma}(u_{v,i})\in\mathbb{R}^{D}$ provides a $D$ -dimensional encoding of each anchor index whose frequency content reflects the anchor budget, with lower budgets inducing stronger attenuation.A.1

    3.3

    As illustrated in Fig. (b), our condenser maps $K$ initialized anchors and $N$ reference-view tokens ${\bm{Z}}$ to $K$ compact scene anchors. It uses $L=8$ bidirectional Transformer blocks , where the two streams attend to each other. Content-only attention can mix spatially unrelated information because it lacks 3D awareness. We therefore predict geometry for both streams (Sec. ) and use it to modulate the bidirectional cross-attention (Sec. ). In the condenser, we retain the reference-view register and camera tokens and add four anchor registers. These tokens also participate in attention, but with no geometry modulation.2()Szymanowicz et al., 20263.3.13.3.2

    3.3.1

    View Geometry.

    We predict geometry for each reference-view token directly from its feature. Following RayRoPE , a linear depth head maps token ${\bm{z}}_{j}$ to a log-depth center $\mu_{j}$ and an uncertainty scale $\sigma_{j}$ . Using the known camera parameters, we back-project the four corners of the corresponding image patch at depth $d_{j}=e^{\mu_{j}}$ to obtain its spatial span in 3D space $\mathbf{p}_{j,1:4}$ . We also use the unit center-ray direction $\mathbf{v}_{j}$ to encode its viewing direction. Together, $\{\mathbf{p}_{j,1:4},\mathbf{v}_{j},\sigma_{j}\}$ describes the spatial support and viewing direction of reference-view token $j$ . The geometry is recomputed from the updated reference-view features at every condenser layer.()Wu et al., 2026

    Anchor Geometry.

    Rather than directly regressing unconstrained 3D coordinates for each anchor, we derive its geometry by aggregating the geometry of the reference-view tokens. This introduces a useful prior: it constrains anchors to the convex hull of the observed geometry rather than allowing unconstrained 3D positions. Specifically, we use a lightweight single-head cross-attention to compute aggregation weights $\beta_{ij}$ between anchor $i$ and reference-view token $j$ :

    $\beta_{ij}=\operatorname{softmax}_{j}\left(\frac{\hat{\mathbf{q}}_{i}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{k}}_{j}}{\sqrt{64}}\right),\qquad\mathbf{p}_{i}^{A}=\sum_{j}\beta_{ij}\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{j},\qquad\mathbf{v}_{i}^{A}=\sum_{j}\beta_{ij}\mathbf{v}_{j},$ (4)

    where $\hat{\mathbf{q}}_{i}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{k}}_{j}$ are 64-dimensional query and key projections, and $\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{j}=\tfrac{1}{4}\sum_{c=1}^{4}\mathbf{p}_{j,c}$ is the center of the back-projected view-token patch. The same weights aggregate both position and viewing direction, giving each anchor a 3D position $\mathbf{p}_{i}^{A}$ and a viewing-direction descriptor $\mathbf{v}_{i}^{A}$ . $\beta_{ij}$ is normalized over the reference-view tokens. Importantly, we use the anchor geometry predicted at the final condenser block as the anchor’s final geometry for subsequent rendering.

    3.3.2

    After geometry prediction, each condenser block first applies self-attention to the anchor stream, followed by bidirectional cross-attention between anchors and reference-view tokens and MLPs. We inject the inferred geometry into this cross-attention using geometry-dependent RoPE.

    We define the geometric descriptors for the two token streams as follows. A reference-view token $j$ corresponds to an image patch and is represented by its four back-projected patch corners $\mathbf{p}_{j,1:4}$ , viewing direction $\mathbf{v}_{j}$ , and depth uncertainty $\sigma_{j}$ . An anchor $i$ , in contrast, has a single 3D position $\mathbf{p}_{i}^{A}$ and viewing-direction descriptor $\mathbf{v}_{i}^{A}$ . To match the geometric layout of the reference-view tokens, we repeat $\mathbf{p}_{i}^{A}$ four times for each anchor. Following RayRoPE , we represent a 3D point using $\pi(\mathbf{p})$ , which first transforms the point into the reference camera frame to obtain $(X,Y,Z)$ , then computes $\pi(\mathbf{p})=(X/r,Y/r,1/|Z|)$ with $r=\sqrt{X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}}$ . The four points therefore provide 12 coordinates. Appending the 3D viewing-direction descriptor gives a 15-dimensional geometric descriptor for both reference-view tokens and anchors:()Wu et al., 2026

    $\mathbf{g}^{R}_{j}=[\pi(\mathbf{p}_{j,1}),\ldots,\pi(\mathbf{p}_{j,4}),\mathbf{v}_{j}],\qquad\mathbf{g}^{A}_{i}=[\pi(\mathbf{p}^{A}_{i}),\ldots,\pi(\mathbf{p}^{A}_{i}),\mathbf{v}^{A}_{i}]\in\mathbb{R}^{15}.$ (5)

    For reference-view token geometry $\mathbf{g}^{R}_{j}$ , we use RayRoPE’s expected RoPE as encoding to account for the predicted depth uncertainty $\sigma_{j}$ (Sec. ). For anchor geometry $\mathbf{g}^{A}_{i}$ , we use standard RoPE encoding . The encodings are then used to rotate the query, key, value, and output features in the bidirectional cross-attention, following the rotation mechanism in RayRoPE.3.3.1()Su et al., 2024

    A key challenge is choosing the RoPE coordinate frame. When an anchor interacts with tokens from a reference view, we express RoPE in that view’s frame for both cross-attention directions. This avoids dependence on the arbitrary world coordinate system, similar to conventional graphics pipelines that transform scene geometry into camera space before rasterization .()Akenine-Möller et al., 2016

    3.4

    Culling.

    After scene reconstruction, the same set of anchors can be reused across different target views. We use the anchor geometry from the final condenser layer as the geometry of each anchor. Given a target camera $\mathcal{P}_{t}$ , we project each anchor position $\mathbf{p}_{i}^{A}$ into the target camera frame and obtain its normalized image coordinate $(u_{i}^{t},v_{i}^{t})$ and camera-space depth $z_{i}^{t}$ . We retain anchors that lie in front of the camera and inside a slightly padded image region, $\mathcal{K}_{t}=\{i:z_{i}^{t}>0,\;(u_{i}^{t},v_{i}^{t})\in[-\delta,1+\delta]^{2}\}$ , with $\delta=0.1$ . The padding retains anchors close to the image boundary. Only anchors in $\mathcal{K}_{t}$ are passed to the decoder, reducing the number of scene tokens processed for each target view.

    Novel-View Rendering.

    We use the bidirectional decoder of LagerNVS , modified with our geometry-grounded RoPE for anchor–target-token cross-attention (Sec. ). The target camera is converted into a ray map and patch-embedded into target tokens, which predict their view geometry with a linear head (as for reference-view tokens) and interact with anchors through bidirectional cross-attention. Anchors use the fixed geometry from the final condenser layer. The target camera frame is used as the RoPE coordinate frame. Finally, a linear projection maps target tokens to RGB patches, which form the rendered image $\hat{\mathbf{I}}_{t}$ .()Szymanowicz et al., 20263.3.2

    3.5

    We freeze the pretrained scene encoder and jointly optimize the continuous query field, condenser, and decoder. The decoder is supervised by the LagerNVS rendering loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{render}}$  . We additionally regularize the predicted depth uncertainty $\sigma_{j}^{\ell}$ of reference-view token $j$ at condenser layer $\ell$ (Sec. ) to encourage sharp, localized geometry:()Szymanowicz et al., 20263.3.1

    $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{render}}+\lambda_{\sigma}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{decay}},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{decay}}=\frac{1}{LN}\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N}|\sigma_{j}^{\ell}|,\qquad\lambda_{\sigma}=10^{-3}.$ (6)

    We first train without culling, then enable culling and perform culling-aware fine-tuning. During training, we sample 1–10 reference views and uniformly sample the anchor budget from 256 to the corresponding highway-token count $N$ . No explicit depth or anchor-position supervision is used.

    We further examine whether the learned anchors capture scene semantics beyond rendering. We use VLM-generated annotations for RealEstate10K  to categorize scenes into eight semantic classes.     5

    We propose , a compact, geometry-grounded LVSM representation with continuous levels of detail. achieves a strong quality–token trade-off through two key designs: (1) an end-to-end learned continuous field with minimal handcrafted design, and (2) a condenser that consolidates multi-view observations into scene-centric, geometry-grounded anchors. Trained with the NVS objective, learns geometry- and texture-aware anchor allocation. We further show its utility on scene semantic understanding, highlighting the potential beyond rendering.GLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSM

    For query $i$ in view $v$ , let $a=u_{v,i}$ , $b=u_{v,i}+\Delta_{v}$ , and $\Delta_{v}=b-a$ . A normalized box filter averages each sinusoidal component over this interval. Using the antiderivatives of cosine and sine, we obtain

    $\displaystyle\bar{C}_{j}$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Delta_{v}}\int_{a}^{b}\cos(2\pi f_{j}u)\,du=\left[\frac{\sin(2\pi f_{j}u)}{2\pi f_{j}\Delta_{v}}\right]_{a}^{b}$ (S1) $\displaystyle=\frac{\sin(2\pi f_{j}b)-\sin(2\pi f_{j}a)}{2\pi f_{j}\Delta_{v}},$ $\displaystyle\bar{S}_{j}$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Delta_{v}}\int_{a}^{b}\sin(2\pi f_{j}u)\,du=\left[-\frac{\cos(2\pi f_{j}u)}{2\pi f_{j}\Delta_{v}}\right]_{a}^{b}$ $\displaystyle=\frac{\cos(2\pi f_{j}a)-\cos(2\pi f_{j}b)}{2\pi f_{j}\Delta_{v}}.$

    Concatenating these coefficients and dividing by $\sqrt{F}$ gives $\bar{\gamma}_{v,i}$ .

    RealEstate10K.

    When we require more reference views beyond the official dataset settings, we retain the official reference views and incrementally add frames using farthest-point sampling in the temporal domain, which reduces redundancy among selected views. Let $\mathcal{R}$ denote the current set of selected reference-frame indices and $\mathcal{C}$ the candidate frames from the source video, which exclude the target views and the selected reference views. At each step, we select

    $f^{*}=\arg\max_{f\in\mathcal{C}\setminus\mathcal{R}}\min_{r\in\mathcal{R}}|f-r|,$

    This process is repeated until the desired number of reference views is reached.

    DL3DV.

    We use the frame indices provided by LagerNVS  to define each 50-frame window. Within each 50-frame window, we first use temporal farthest-point sampling to meet the desired number of reference views beyond the official setting. We then use the remaining frames in the window as target views, so $V$ reference views leave $50-V$ target views.()Szymanowicz et al., 2026

    Fig.  instead uses a fixed target set across all reference-view counts for DL3DV. Under the original DL3DV protocol, the target set is defined as the complement of the reference views and therefore changes with view count. To enable direct quality comparison when scaling views, we use the same 40 targets per scene from the 10-view setting for all DL3DV results in this figure. This set is a subset of the original targets at every reference-view count.S9

    A.3

    We follow the 1–10-view training recipe of the LagerNVS general model , with a few modifications.()Szymanowicz et al., 2026

    LagerNVS fine-tuning.

    We fine-tune LagerNVS for 100K iterations with a 1.2K-step warmup, using learning rates of $10^{-4}$ on RealEstate10K and $10^{-5}$ on DL3DV. We follow its dynamic batching strategy with a base batch size of 128, which decreases the batch size for larger reference-view counts.

    GLoD-LVSM

    We train for 50K iterations with a 1K-step warmup, using a learning rate of $10^{-4}$ and a base batch size of 64. For the culling-aware model, we further fine-tune for 25K iterations with a 1K-step warmup, using a learning rate of $10^{-5}$ and the same base batch size.GLoD-LVSM

    A.4

    To visualize the noisy predicted reference-view depth as a point cloud, we apply a $3\times 3$ median filter to the patch-level depth and upsample it to image resolution using joint bilateral upsampling  guided by the corresponding RGB image. We then back-project the filtered depth using the camera intrinsics, transform the points into a shared scene coordinate system using the camera poses, and color them with RGB values. This post-processing is used only for point-cloud visualization; the displayed depth maps are raw predictions, and the model geometry, anchors, and rendering remain unchanged.()Kopf et al., 2007

    A.5

    We report results for both with and without culling in Fig. . We evaluate rendering speed on an NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU using BF16 with a batch size of 1 and 1 target view. For the baseline and our no-culling model, we directly benchmark rendering latency at fixed scene-token counts. For the culling-enabled model, the effective decoder-token count varies across scenes and target poses. We therefore estimate its speed by measuring rendering speed at the average post-culling decoder-token count over the test set. The estimated rendering latency includes the measured culling overhead.GLoD-LVSMS1

    A.6

    We first test scene-semantic understanding using VLM-generated annotations for RealEstate10K  to categorize scenes into eight semantic classes: living room, bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, dining room, hallway, staircase, and outdoor. Each scene receives one class derived from its caption. We filter out scenes that belong to multiple classes or do not belong to any of the predefined classes. This results in 40,857 training scenes and 4,606 validation scenes. We train for 500 epochs with a learning rate of $3\times 10^{-2}$ , batch size 256, and weight decay $10^{-4}$ . We use cosine annealing to decay the learning rate to zero over training.(; )He et al., 2025Li et al., 2023
