一句话：大视图合成模型的 token 冗余导致存储与渲染成本高，用连续 LoD 的紧凑几何表示来压缩。

要点：

  • LVSMs 从稀疏视角重建并快速渲染，但 token 冗余严重
  • 不学习固定锚点集，而是学一个连续场来初始化表示
  • 支持连续 Level-of-Detail，按需分配容量

为什么值得看：和引擎里的 LOD 体系是同一类问题，只是对象换成了神经表示，对做场景流式加载有直接参考。

中文摘要：大视图合成模型（LVSM）能从稀疏视角重建场景并快速渲染新视角，但由于 token 冗余会带来不必要的存储与渲染开销。作者提出 GLoD-LVSM：一种紧凑的、基于几何的场景表示，具备连续 Level-of-Detail 能力。它不学习一组固定的场景锚点初始化，而是学习一个连续场来初始化表示，从而按需分配容量、减少冗余。

来源：arXiv·cs.GR 最新（English） 相关度：10.3 正文：51098 字 / 23 图

作者：Weikai Lin、Nicholas Milef、Carl S Marshall 等 6 人

分类：cs.CV / cs.GR

接收/备注：38 pages, including supplementary material

PDF：https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20254v1

命中：lod、rendering、lighting、texture

Large view synthesis models (LVSMs) reconstruct scenes from sparse views and render novel views quickly, but they incur unnecessary storage and rendering costs due to token redundancy. We present GLoD-LVSM, a compact, geometry-grounded scene representation for LVSMs with continuous levels of detail. First, instead of learning a fixed set of scene anchor initializations, GLoD-LVSM learns a continuo

GLoD-LVSM

Weikai LinNicholas MilefCarl S MarshallGrant Kaijuin YangTodd KeelerYuhao ZhuUniversity of Rochester Reality Labs, Meta

Abstract

Large view synthesis models (LVSMs) reconstruct scenes from sparse views and render novel views quickly, but they incur unnecessary storage and rendering costs due to token redundancy. We present , a compact, geometry-grounded scene representation for LVSMs with continuous levels of detail. First, instead of learning a fixed set of scene anchor initializations, learns a continuous field that initializes a flexible number of anchors to match the desired budget. A condenser then aggregates scene information into these anchors, with both the field and condenser trained end-to-end. Second, the condenser infers reference-token and anchor geometry to guide compression through geometry-grounded attention, improving rendering quality and enabling frustum culling during decoding. Compared with existing LVSM scene-compression baselines, achieves the best trade-off between rendering quality and scene token count. Compared with the uncompressed base model, reduces the scene-token count by 33.4% and accelerates rendering by $1.23\times$ with no quality loss. Under a relaxed quality-loss budget, the reduction increases to 85.5%, with $3.00\times$ rendering speedup. Further analysis reveals that view-synthesis supervision yields emergent scene depth and self-organized anchors that align with surfaces and adapt their density to local texture complexity. Beyond rendering, we further show that our scene representation also supports scene-semantic understanding, highlighting its potential for broader downstream tasks.GLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSM

1

Large view synthesis models (LVSMs) learn a reconstruction prior for novel view synthesis (NVS) , reducing scene reconstruction to a single feed-forward pass and enabling high-quality rendering from sparse reference views. Recent high-quality LVSMs commonly adopt a highway representation, where each reference-image patch is directly mapped to a scene token . While this design preserves detailed appearance information, the resulting scene-token count grows with the number of reference views, increasing both storage and decoding costs. This tight coupling between image and scene-representation sizes becomes a bottleneck with more reference views.(; ; )Jin et al., 2025Kim et al., 2026Szymanowicz et al., 2026(; )Szymanowicz et al., 2026Kim et al., 2026

In addition to scaling poorly with reference view count, highway representations allocate scene capacity inefficiently in two ways. First, overlapping 3D regions observed from different views are stored as separate tokens rather than consolidated. Second, every image patch receives the same one-token capacity regardless of texture complexity. An ideal LVSM representation should therefore (1) support flexible scene-token count independent of the input-view count, (2) consolidate multi-view observations into a unified, 3D representation, and (3) allocate capacity adaptively to scene complexity. Thus, we propose , which provides two key features: (1) a geometry-grounded scene representation that supports (2) continuous level-of-detail. We refer to scene tokens in as to emphasize their scene-centric 3D nature.scene-centricGLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSManchors

Different storage and rendering budgets require different scene-token numbers, which correspond to different levels of scene detail. To support arbitrary scene-token counts and thus continuous levels of detail (CLoD), we first design an anchor initialization scheme that can generate a flexible number of tokens. Specifically, we introduce a CLoD scene-anchor initialization that parameterizes anchor initialization as a continuous field (Sec. ). Sampling this field at different densities generates different numbers of anchors. This decouples the scene-token count from the reference-view count and allows our model to operate under different storage and rendering budgets.3.2

A compact scene representation should consolidate multi-view observations and allocate capacity where it is most useful. To achieve this, we (1) use unified, scene-centric 3D anchors to consolidate redundant multi-view tokens, and (2) learn the spatial allocation of these anchors end-to-end. Specifically, we use an end-to-end learned, geometry-grounded condenser that aggregates reference-view tokens into 3D anchors (Sec. ). The condenser predicts geometry for both views and anchors and uses their geometric relationships to guide cross-attention. The resulting anchors have 3D positions, which further enable target-view frustum culling to reduce decoding cost (Sec. ). Both the geometry and scene-complexity-aware anchor allocation emerge from the NVS objective (Sec. ).3.33.44.6

We evaluate across datasets, reference-view counts and scene-token budgets. Quantitatively, consistently achieves the best quality–token-count trade-off among the baselines. Qualitatively, the learned anchors emerge near scene surfaces and allocate higher density to regions with richer texture, suggesting that NVS supervision and compression alone can induce a geometry- and complexity-aware efficient scene representation. Beyond rendering, we further evaluate the learned representation on scene-semantic understanding, demonstrating its potential as a 3D scene representation for broader downstream tasks. Our contributions are threefold:GLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSM

  • •

    We introduce a scene-conditioned continuous query field that enables flexible scene anchor budgets independent of the reference-view count.Continuous-LoD scene representation.

  • •

    We learn scene-centric 3D anchors end-to-end, enabling efficient multi-view consolidation and scene-adaptive capacity allocation.Geometry-grounded scene condensation.

  • •

    achieves the best quality–scene-token trade-off for rendering and supports scene semantic understanding.Efficient and generalizable scene anchors.GLoD-LVSM

    • 2

    2.1

    Novel view synthesis (NVS) is a widely studied problem and can be broadly categorized into per-scene optimization methods and feed-forward generalizable methods. NeRF  and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)  achieve photorealistic novel-view synthesis by optimizing a radiance field or a set of Gaussian primitives for each scene. However, they typically require time-consuming per-scene optimization and dense image capture to achieve high rendering quality. In contrast, generalizable NVS methods , including recent Transformer-based approaches such as LVSMs , learn reconstruction priors from large datasets and can reconstruct unseen scenes from sparse input views in a single feed-forward pass, avoiding costly dense image capture and per-scene optimization. Our work builds on Transformer-based generalizable NVS and focuses on learning a compact, geometry-grounded scene representation that reduces redundancy among scene tokens, thereby lowering storage and rendering costs.()Mildenhall et al., 2020()Kerbl et al., 2023(; ; )Sajjadi et al., 2022Chen et al., 2024Xu et al., 2025(; ; ; )Jin et al., 2025Kim et al., 2026Sun et al., 2026Szymanowicz et al., 2026

    2.2

    Compact scene representations have been widely studied for efficient NVS. For example, 3DGS methods prune or compress Gaussian primitives to reduce representation size while preserving visual quality . Some methods further support multiple or continuous levels of detail (CLoD), allowing representation complexity to adapt to runtime rendering budgets . Compact scene-token representations have also been explored for LVSMs. LVSM-ED  uses a fixed latent bottleneck and cannot support flexible compression rates. CLiFT  uses K-means to select representative reference-view tokens, relying on handcrafted clustering that may be suboptimal. Our work also targets compact scene representations for LVSMs. Unlike prior methods, we support CLoD and learn scene anchors end-to-end, enabling flexible compression with less handcrafted design.(; ; )Fan et al., 2024Fang and Wang, 2024Lin et al., 2025(; )Milef et al., 2025Cheng et al., 2026()Jin et al., 2025()Wang et al., 2025

    3 GLoD-LVSM

    Fig.  illustrates . Given $V$ reference images and their camera parameters, constructs a compact scene representation with a chosen budget of $K$ anchors. A highway scene encoder first extracts reference-view tokens (Sec. ). Our anchor initializer then generates $K$ anchors from a continuous field (Sec. ). These anchors are passed to our condenser, which produces scene-centric 3D anchors (Sec. ). The anchors will be used to render the RGB images given the target views (Sec. ). We train end-to-end using the NVS loss (Sec. ).2GLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSM3.13.23.33.4GLoD-LVSM3.5

    3.1

    We use the encoder from LagerNVS . The inputs are $\mathcal{X}=\{(\mathbf{I}_{v},\mathcal{P}_{v})\}_{v=1}^{V}$ , where $\mathbf{I}_{v}$ is the $v$ -th reference image and $\mathcal{P}_{v}$ is its camera parameters. The encoder patchifies each reference image, embeds each patch as a token, embeds $\mathcal{P}_{v}$ into a camera token $\mathbf{t}^{\mathrm{cam}}_{v}$ , and appends four register tokens $\mathbf{t}^{\mathrm{reg}}_{1:4}$ to each view . For each view, input token sequence $\mathbf{T}_{v}^{\mathrm{in}}=[\mathbf{t}^{\mathrm{cam}}_{v},\mathbf{t}^{\mathrm{reg}}_{1:4},\operatorname{PatchEmbed}(\mathbf{I}_{v})]$ . The resulting tokens are jointly encoded across all $V$ views:()Szymanowicz et al., 2026()Darcet et al., 2024

    $\mathbf{H}=\operatorname{Encoder}(\{\mathbf{T}_{v}^{\mathrm{in}}\}_{v=1}^{V}),\qquad{\bm{Z}}=\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{patch}}\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}.$ (1)

    Here, $\mathbf{W}$ linearly maps the encoded patch tokens to a defined $D$ -dimensional space, and $N$ is the total number of input patches across all views. We refer to the output ${\bm{Z}}$ as and retain the encoded register and camera tokens for anchor initialization (Sec. ). This one-patch-one-token highway design causes storage and decoding costs to grow with reference-view count.reference-view tokens3.2

    3.2

    Given reference-view tokens ${\bm{Z}}$ , our condenser compresses them into scene anchors. The first challenge is anchor initialization. Fixed learned vectors  support only a predefined anchor count. Clustering-based initialization  supports variable counts, but relies on handcrafted clustering that may be suboptimal and remains image-centric rather than scene-centric. We instead learn a scene-conditioned continuous initialization field end-to-end with minimal handcrafted design (Fig. (a)). Sampling the field at different densities yields different anchor budgets, enabling continuous levels of detail under varying storage and rendering constraints.()Jin et al., 2025()Wang et al., 20252

    Continuous field parameterization.

    Given a total anchor budget $K$ , we distribute $K$ evenly across the $V$ reference views, assigning $K_{v}$ anchors to view $v$ . For each view, our goal is to learn a $D$ -dimensional continuous field that maps query indices $i\in\{0,\ldots,K_{v}-1\}$ to $K_{v}$ vectors in the $D$ -dimensional anchor space, with $D$ set to the highway model’s scene-token dimension. We parameterize this continuous field as an MLP conditioned jointly on the anchor indices and the current scene/view context. Specifically, each anchor index $i$ is mapped to a continuous coordinate $u_{v,i}$ and encoded with our anti-aliased positional encoding $\bar{\gamma}(u_{v,i})$ (Eqn. ). To condition the field on the current input, we mean-pool the encoded registers and camera tokens (Sec. ) of view $v$ and map them through $\operatorname{MLP}_{\mathrm{context}}$ to obtain a view- and scene-specific context vector $\mathbf{c}_{v}$ . $\bar{\gamma}(u_{v,i})$ and $\mathbf{c}_{v}$ are then concatenated and passed to $\operatorname{MLP}_{\mathrm{field}}$ to produce the $D$ -dimensional anchor initialization ${\bm{a}}_{v,i}$ :33.1

    ${\bm{a}}_{v,i}=\operatorname{MLP}_{\mathrm{field}}\left(\left[\bar{\gamma}(u_{v,i}),\mathbf{c}_{v}\right]\right),\qquad\mathbf{c}_{v}=\operatorname{MLP}_{\mathrm{context}}\left(\operatorname{MeanPool}([\mathbf{H}^{\mathrm{reg}}_{v,1:4},\mathbf{H}^{\mathrm{cam}}_{v}])\right).$ (2)

    Finally, we concatenate the initializations from all views to obtain $K=\sum_{v}K_{v}$ anchor initializations and feed them to the condenser. The field is optimized end-to-end through the NVS objective.

    Anti-Aliased Positional Encoding Across Anchor Budgets.

    To sample the same continuous field at different anchor budgets, we map each discrete query index $i$ to a continuous coordinate $u_{v,i}$ in a fixed canonical domain $[0,K_{\mathrm{canonical}}]$ , where $K_{\mathrm{canonical}}=2000$ . For each view with budget $K_{v}$ , we divide the domain into $K_{v}$ intervals. Changing $K_{v}$ therefore changes the sampling density while preserving coverage of the domain. To help the field capture high-frequency variation, we follow NeRF-style positional encoding (PE)  and encode each coordinate as $\gamma(u)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{F}}[\cos(2\pi\mathbf{f}u),\sin(2\pi\mathbf{f}u)]\in\mathbb{R}^{2F}$ . Here, $\mathbf{f}=(f_{0},\ldots,f_{F-1})$ is logarithmically spaced between $f_{\min}=1/20000$ and $f_{\max}=0.5$ . We set $F=D/2$ , where $D$ is the dimension of anchor space. At small budgets, sparse sampling can alias the high-frequency components of PE. We therefore integrate PE over the sampling interval, analogous to box filtering :()Mildenhall et al., 2020()Barron et al., 2021

    $\bar{\gamma}_{v,i}=\frac{1}{\Delta_{v}}\int_{I_{v,i}}\gamma(u)\,du,\quad I_{v,i}=[u_{v,i},u_{v,i}+\Delta_{v}],\quad u_{v,i}=i\Delta_{v},\quad\Delta_{v}=\frac{K_{\mathrm{canonical}}}{K_{v}}.$ (3)

    As the anchor budget decreases, the intervals become wider and more strongly attenuate high-frequency components. The sine and cosine integrals have closed-form solutions, given in Supplementary . The resulting $\bar{\gamma}(u_{v,i})\in\mathbb{R}^{D}$ provides a $D$ -dimensional encoding of each anchor index whose frequency content reflects the anchor budget, with lower budgets inducing stronger attenuation.A.1

    3.3

    As illustrated in Fig. (b), our condenser maps $K$ initialized anchors and $N$ reference-view tokens ${\bm{Z}}$ to $K$ compact scene anchors. It uses $L=8$ bidirectional Transformer blocks , where the two streams attend to each other. Content-only attention can mix spatially unrelated information because it lacks 3D awareness. We therefore predict geometry for both streams (Sec. ) and use it to modulate the bidirectional cross-attention (Sec. ). In the condenser, we retain the reference-view register and camera tokens and add four anchor registers. These tokens also participate in attention, but with no geometry modulation.2()Szymanowicz et al., 20263.3.13.3.2

    3.3.1

    View Geometry.

    We predict geometry for each reference-view token directly from its feature. Following RayRoPE , a linear depth head maps token ${\bm{z}}_{j}$ to a log-depth center $\mu_{j}$ and an uncertainty scale $\sigma_{j}$ . Using the known camera parameters, we back-project the four corners of the corresponding image patch at depth $d_{j}=e^{\mu_{j}}$ to obtain its spatial span in 3D space $\mathbf{p}_{j,1:4}$ . We also use the unit center-ray direction $\mathbf{v}_{j}$ to encode its viewing direction. Together, $\{\mathbf{p}_{j,1:4},\mathbf{v}_{j},\sigma_{j}\}$ describes the spatial support and viewing direction of reference-view token $j$ . The geometry is recomputed from the updated reference-view features at every condenser layer.()Wu et al., 2026

    Anchor Geometry.

    Rather than directly regressing unconstrained 3D coordinates for each anchor, we derive its geometry by aggregating the geometry of the reference-view tokens. This introduces a useful prior: it constrains anchors to the convex hull of the observed geometry rather than allowing unconstrained 3D positions. Specifically, we use a lightweight single-head cross-attention to compute aggregation weights $\beta_{ij}$ between anchor $i$ and reference-view token $j$ :

    $\beta_{ij}=\operatorname{softmax}_{j}\left(\frac{\hat{\mathbf{q}}_{i}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{k}}_{j}}{\sqrt{64}}\right),\qquad\mathbf{p}_{i}^{A}=\sum_{j}\beta_{ij}\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{j},\qquad\mathbf{v}_{i}^{A}=\sum_{j}\beta_{ij}\mathbf{v}_{j},$ (4)

    where $\hat{\mathbf{q}}_{i}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{k}}_{j}$ are 64-dimensional query and key projections, and $\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{j}=\tfrac{1}{4}\sum_{c=1}^{4}\mathbf{p}_{j,c}$ is the center of the back-projected view-token patch. The same weights aggregate both position and viewing direction, giving each anchor a 3D position $\mathbf{p}_{i}^{A}$ and a viewing-direction descriptor $\mathbf{v}_{i}^{A}$ . $\beta_{ij}$ is normalized over the reference-view tokens. Importantly, we use the anchor geometry predicted at the final condenser block as the anchor’s final geometry for subsequent rendering.

    3.3.2

    After geometry prediction, each condenser block first applies self-attention to the anchor stream, followed by bidirectional cross-attention between anchors and reference-view tokens and MLPs. We inject the inferred geometry into this cross-attention using geometry-dependent RoPE.

    We define the geometric descriptors for the two token streams as follows. A reference-view token $j$ corresponds to an image patch and is represented by its four back-projected patch corners $\mathbf{p}_{j,1:4}$ , viewing direction $\mathbf{v}_{j}$ , and depth uncertainty $\sigma_{j}$ . An anchor $i$ , in contrast, has a single 3D position $\mathbf{p}_{i}^{A}$ and viewing-direction descriptor $\mathbf{v}_{i}^{A}$ . To match the geometric layout of the reference-view tokens, we repeat $\mathbf{p}_{i}^{A}$ four times for each anchor. Following RayRoPE , we represent a 3D point using $\pi(\mathbf{p})$ , which first transforms the point into the reference camera frame to obtain $(X,Y,Z)$ , then computes $\pi(\mathbf{p})=(X/r,Y/r,1/|Z|)$ with $r=\sqrt{X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}}$ . The four points therefore provide 12 coordinates. Appending the 3D viewing-direction descriptor gives a 15-dimensional geometric descriptor for both reference-view tokens and anchors:()Wu et al., 2026

    $\mathbf{g}^{R}_{j}=[\pi(\mathbf{p}_{j,1}),\ldots,\pi(\mathbf{p}_{j,4}),\mathbf{v}_{j}],\qquad\mathbf{g}^{A}_{i}=[\pi(\mathbf{p}^{A}_{i}),\ldots,\pi(\mathbf{p}^{A}_{i}),\mathbf{v}^{A}_{i}]\in\mathbb{R}^{15}.$ (5)

    For reference-view token geometry $\mathbf{g}^{R}_{j}$ , we use RayRoPE’s expected RoPE as encoding to account for the predicted depth uncertainty $\sigma_{j}$ (Sec. ). For anchor geometry $\mathbf{g}^{A}_{i}$ , we use standard RoPE encoding . The encodings are then used to rotate the query, key, value, and output features in the bidirectional cross-attention, following the rotation mechanism in RayRoPE.3.3.1()Su et al., 2024

    A key challenge is choosing the RoPE coordinate frame. When an anchor interacts with tokens from a reference view, we express RoPE in that view’s frame for both cross-attention directions. This avoids dependence on the arbitrary world coordinate system, similar to conventional graphics pipelines that transform scene geometry into camera space before rasterization .()Akenine-Möller et al., 2016

    3.4

    Culling.

    After scene reconstruction, the same set of anchors can be reused across different target views. We use the anchor geometry from the final condenser layer as the geometry of each anchor. Given a target camera $\mathcal{P}_{t}$ , we project each anchor position $\mathbf{p}_{i}^{A}$ into the target camera frame and obtain its normalized image coordinate $(u_{i}^{t},v_{i}^{t})$ and camera-space depth $z_{i}^{t}$ . We retain anchors that lie in front of the camera and inside a slightly padded image region, $\mathcal{K}_{t}=\{i:z_{i}^{t}>0,\;(u_{i}^{t},v_{i}^{t})\in[-\delta,1+\delta]^{2}\}$ , with $\delta=0.1$ . The padding retains anchors close to the image boundary. Only anchors in $\mathcal{K}_{t}$ are passed to the decoder, reducing the number of scene tokens processed for each target view.

    Novel-View Rendering.

    We use the bidirectional decoder of LagerNVS , modified with our geometry-grounded RoPE for anchor–target-token cross-attention (Sec. ). The target camera is converted into a ray map and patch-embedded into target tokens, which predict their view geometry with a linear head (as for reference-view tokens) and interact with anchors through bidirectional cross-attention. Anchors use the fixed geometry from the final condenser layer. The target camera frame is used as the RoPE coordinate frame. Finally, a linear projection maps target tokens to RGB patches, which form the rendered image $\hat{\mathbf{I}}_{t}$ .()Szymanowicz et al., 20263.3.2

    3.5

    We freeze the pretrained scene encoder and jointly optimize the continuous query field, condenser, and decoder. The decoder is supervised by the LagerNVS rendering loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{render}}$  . We additionally regularize the predicted depth uncertainty $\sigma_{j}^{\ell}$ of reference-view token $j$ at condenser layer $\ell$ (Sec. ) to encourage sharp, localized geometry:()Szymanowicz et al., 20263.3.1

    $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{render}}+\lambda_{\sigma}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{decay}},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{decay}}=\frac{1}{LN}\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N}|\sigma_{j}^{\ell}|,\qquad\lambda_{\sigma}=10^{-3}.$ (6)

    We first train without culling, then enable culling and perform culling-aware fine-tuning. During training, we sample 1–10 reference views and uniformly sample the anchor budget from 256 to the corresponding highway-token count $N$ . No explicit depth or anchor-position supervision is used.

    4

    4.1

    Datasets.

    We evaluate on RealEstate10K  and DL3DV  at resolutions of $256\times 256$ and $256\times 448$ , respectively. We study varying-reference-view settings from $2$ to $10$ views. Since the official protocols cover only 2 views for RealEstate10K and 2/4/6 views for DL3DV, we construct the higher-view settings using the method described in Supplementary .()Zhou et al., 2018()Ling et al., 2024A.2

    Training.

    We fine-tune the pretrained general LagerNVS checkpoint  on each dataset using its $1$ – $10$ -view training protocol, obtaining , which is our base model. We initialize our decoder from and train the condenser and decoder, followed by culling-aware fine-tuning. See Supplementary  for training details.()Szymanowicz et al., 2026LagerNVS-FTLagerNVS-FTA.3

    Baselines.

    We compare against two groups of baselines:

  • •

    We compare against , , , and .System-level baselines.GLoD-LVSMCLiFT()Wang et al., 2025LVSM()Jin et al., 2025MVSplat()Chen et al., 2024DepthSplat()Xu et al., 2025

  • •

    Alternative condensers using the same base model and training schedule:Condenser baselines.

  • –

    : randomly selects scene tokens to match the desired budget.Random pruning

  • –

    : sets the number of clusters to the desired token budget, clusters the reference-view token features, and retains only the token closest to each cluster centroid.K-means pruning

  • –

    : uses a trained token pruner to select 90% of the token budget, then fills the remaining 10% through feature-diversity-based sampling .Learned Pruning()Takezoe et al., 2026

  • –

    : uses a K-means-based Transformer condenser adapted from , with the number of blocks increased to eight to match our condenser.CLiFT-styleCLiFT()Wang et al., 2025

    • Metrics.

    We report novel-view PSNR, SSIM , and LPIPS  under different reference view counts and scene token budgets. For all quality metrics, we report the mean and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) from 2,000 scene-level resamples with replacement.()Wang et al., 2004()Zhang et al., 2018

    4.2

    Our base model is strong.

    To show that we build on a strong highway backbone, we first compare our base model, , against other systems. Fig.  shows the results, where filled markers denote view counts seen during training and hollow markers denote unseen counts. consistently achieves substantially higher PSNR than all compared systems; SSIM and LPIPS show similar trends (Supplementary Fig. ). It also improves as more reference views are provided. LagerNVS-FT4LagerNVS-FT1 LVSM is evaluated only on RealEstate10K because no official DL3DV checkpoint is available.11S42 DL3DV results in Fig.  are not directly comparable across reference-view counts because the official target set is defined as the complement of the reference views and therefore changes slightly with view count.224

    GLoD-LVSM

    We compare the quality–scene-token trade-off with because all other systems do not support flexible scene-token counts. Fig.  shows the results for different reference views. achieves a better PSNR–token-count trade-off than . The advantage comes from both our strong base model and our better condenser design. SSIM and LPIPS show similar trends (see Supplementary Fig. ).CLiFT4GLoD-LVSMCLiFTS3

    4.3

    To isolate the effect of the strong base model, we conduct controlled experiments using the same base model and training schedule across different condenser designs. Because the baseline condensers do not produce geometry-grounded tokens, applying frustum-culling is not straightforward. For a fair comparison, we disable culling for all methods and report the compressed scene-token count. Fig.  compares quality–token trade-offs with 2 and 6 reference views on both datasets; 4- and 10-view results are shown in Fig. . Our condenser achieves a better PSNR–token-count trade-off across datasets and reference-view counts. SSIM and LPIPS show similar trends (see Supplementary Figs. –). We also visualize novel-view predictions from all condensers in Fig. , which visually confirms our method’s quality advantage. More visualizations across scenes, reference-view counts, and compression rates are provided in Supplementary Figs. –.51S5S86S13S25

    4.4

    We now evaluate the token reduction and rendering speedup against the base model. Efficiency gains must be considered in the context of rendering quality. Using as the quality reference, we measure scene-token reduction under PSNR losses of $X\in\{2,1,0.5,0\}$  dB. Fig.  shows the results. On 10-view RealEstate10K, reduces the scene-token count by 85.5% at a 2 dB quality loss. Even with no quality loss (0 dB), it still reduces the token count by 33.4%, which we attribute to the more effective geometry-grounded representation. The corresponding rendering speedups are $3.00\times$ and $1.23\times$ over , respectively. With culling, the estimated speedups further increase to $3.20\times$ and $1.55\times$ . More speed results and evaluation details are provided in Supplementary Fig.  and Supplementary .LagerNVS-FT10GLoD-LVSMLagerNVS-FTS1A.5

    4.5

    We now highlight two properties of . First, unlike highway designs whose scene tokens grow with reference-view count, can exploit more views at a . Fig.  shows that, at a fixed token budget, generally improves with more views. For example, on RealEstate10K with a 2048-token budget, 10 views outperform 2 views by 2.8 dB. In contrast, a 10-view highway model requires over 13K tokens. At small capacity, such as 512 tokens, gains saturate/degrade beyond 6 views. See Supplementary Fig.  for more results.GLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSMfixed scene-token budget10GLoD-LVSMS9

    Second, because learns a continuous anchor-initialization field (Sec. ), it can sample more anchors ( $K$ ) than the original highway representation tokens ( $N$ ), which baseline condensers cannot support. Fig.  reports the PSNR gain relative to at the uncompressed budget. Although exceeds the base-model quality at the same token budget, its quality continues to improve for $K>N$ . See Supplementary Fig.  for more results.GLoD-LVSM3.210GLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSMS10

    4.6

    To understand , we visualize its representation using four reference views with 2048 scene anchors (Fig. ). Without explicit geometry supervision, consistent scene depth emerges across reference views, while the learned anchors concentrate near scene surfaces. Projecting the anchors back onto the reference images further reveals scene-adaptive allocation: anchors are denser in texture-rich regions and sparser in textureless regions. These results show that the NVS loss can induce an efficient geometry- and texture-aware scene representation. More visualizations are in Supplementary Figs. –. We process raw depth before point-cloud visualization; see Supplementary .GLoD-LVSM1S26S31A.4

    4.7

    Fig.  compares quality–decoder-token trade-offs for our ablations on 6-view DL3DV. denotes without culling. enables our frustum-culling (Sec. ). removes geometry-dependent RoPE (Sec. ) from both the condenser and decoder. removes anti-aliasing from the positional encoding (Eqn. ). removes positional encoding and instead feeds normalized anchor indices to the field MLP. removes scene- and view-specific conditioning from the anchor initialization field (Eqn. ). replaces our end-to-end learned anchor initialization field (Sec. ) with K-means centroids of the reference-view tokens . The results show that each component contributes to the quality–token trade-off of . Results with other reference-view counts show similar trends and are provided in Supplementary Figs. –.10OursGLoD-LVSMOurs + Culling3.4w/o Geo.3.3.2w/o Box.3w/o PE.w/o Context.3 Removing the context vector makes the per-view initialization identical across views. We therefore replace the per-view fields with a single global initialization field and set $K_{\mathrm{canonical}}=20{,}000$ .332w. K-means Init.3.2()Wang et al., 2025GLoD-LVSMS11S12

    4.8 GLoD-LVSM

    We further examine whether the learned anchors capture scene semantics beyond rendering. We use VLM-generated annotations for RealEstate10K  to categorize scenes into eight semantic classes. For each scene, compresses 10 reference views into 1,024 anchors, which are mean-pooled into a single 768-dimensional . We train only a linear probe on this vector for scene classification and achieve 80.40%/91.73% top-1/top-2 accuracy. This result shows that learned anchors already contain scene semantics. See Supplementary  for evaluation protocol and Supplementary Fig.  for the confusion matrix.(; )He et al., 2025Li et al., 2023GLoD-LVSMscene vectorA.6S2

    5

    We propose , a compact, geometry-grounded LVSM representation with continuous levels of detail. achieves a strong quality–token trade-off through two key designs: (1) an end-to-end learned continuous field with minimal handcrafted design, and (2) a condenser that consolidates multi-view observations into scene-centric, geometry-grounded anchors. Trained with the NVS objective, learns geometry- and texture-aware anchor allocation. We further show its utility on scene semantic understanding, highlighting the potential beyond rendering.GLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSMGLoD-LVSM

    Appendix A

    A.1

    For query $i$ in view $v$ , let $a=u_{v,i}$ , $b=u_{v,i}+\Delta_{v}$ , and $\Delta_{v}=b-a$ . A normalized box filter averages each sinusoidal component over this interval. Using the antiderivatives of cosine and sine, we obtain

    $\displaystyle\bar{C}_{j}$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Delta_{v}}\int_{a}^{b}\cos(2\pi f_{j}u)\,du=\left[\frac{\sin(2\pi f_{j}u)}{2\pi f_{j}\Delta_{v}}\right]_{a}^{b}$ (S1) $\displaystyle=\frac{\sin(2\pi f_{j}b)-\sin(2\pi f_{j}a)}{2\pi f_{j}\Delta_{v}},$ $\displaystyle\bar{S}_{j}$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Delta_{v}}\int_{a}^{b}\sin(2\pi f_{j}u)\,du=\left[-\frac{\cos(2\pi f_{j}u)}{2\pi f_{j}\Delta_{v}}\right]_{a}^{b}$ $\displaystyle=\frac{\cos(2\pi f_{j}a)-\cos(2\pi f_{j}b)}{2\pi f_{j}\Delta_{v}}.$

    Concatenating these coefficients and dividing by $\sqrt{F}$ gives $\bar{\gamma}_{v,i}$ .

    A.2

    RealEstate10K.

    When we require more reference views beyond the official dataset settings, we retain the official reference views and incrementally add frames using farthest-point sampling in the temporal domain, which reduces redundancy among selected views. Let $\mathcal{R}$ denote the current set of selected reference-frame indices and $\mathcal{C}$ the candidate frames from the source video, which exclude the target views and the selected reference views. At each step, we select

    $f^{*}=\arg\max_{f\in\mathcal{C}\setminus\mathcal{R}}\min_{r\in\mathcal{R}}|f-r|,$

    This process is repeated until the desired number of reference views is reached.

    DL3DV.

    We use the frame indices provided by LagerNVS  to define each 50-frame window. Within each 50-frame window, we first use temporal farthest-point sampling to meet the desired number of reference views beyond the official setting. We then use the remaining frames in the window as target views, so $V$ reference views leave $50-V$ target views.()Szymanowicz et al., 2026

    Fig.  instead uses a fixed target set across all reference-view counts for DL3DV. Under the original DL3DV protocol, the target set is defined as the complement of the reference views and therefore changes with view count. To enable direct quality comparison when scaling views, we use the same 40 targets per scene from the 10-view setting for all DL3DV results in this figure. This set is a subset of the original targets at every reference-view count.S9

    A.3

    We follow the 1–10-view training recipe of the LagerNVS general model , with a few modifications.()Szymanowicz et al., 2026

    LagerNVS fine-tuning.

    We fine-tune LagerNVS for 100K iterations with a 1.2K-step warmup, using learning rates of $10^{-4}$ on RealEstate10K and $10^{-5}$ on DL3DV. We follow its dynamic batching strategy with a base batch size of 128, which decreases the batch size for larger reference-view counts.

    GLoD-LVSM

    We train for 50K iterations with a 1K-step warmup, using a learning rate of $10^{-4}$ and a base batch size of 64. For the culling-aware model, we further fine-tune for 25K iterations with a 1K-step warmup, using a learning rate of $10^{-5}$ and the same base batch size.GLoD-LVSM

    A.4

    To visualize the noisy predicted reference-view depth as a point cloud, we apply a $3\times 3$ median filter to the patch-level depth and upsample it to image resolution using joint bilateral upsampling  guided by the corresponding RGB image. We then back-project the filtered depth using the camera intrinsics, transform the points into a shared scene coordinate system using the camera poses, and color them with RGB values. This post-processing is used only for point-cloud visualization; the displayed depth maps are raw predictions, and the model geometry, anchors, and rendering remain unchanged.()Kopf et al., 2007

    A.5

    We report results for both with and without culling in Fig. . We evaluate rendering speed on an NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU using BF16 with a batch size of 1 and 1 target view. For the baseline and our no-culling model, we directly benchmark rendering latency at fixed scene-token counts. For the culling-enabled model, the effective decoder-token count varies across scenes and target poses. We therefore estimate its speed by measuring rendering speed at the average post-culling decoder-token count over the test set. The estimated rendering latency includes the measured culling overhead.GLoD-LVSMS1

    A.6

    We first test scene-semantic understanding using VLM-generated annotations for RealEstate10K  to categorize scenes into eight semantic classes: living room, bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, dining room, hallway, staircase, and outdoor. Each scene receives one class derived from its caption. We filter out scenes that belong to multiple classes or do not belong to any of the predefined classes. This results in 40,857 training scenes and 4,606 validation scenes. We train for 500 epochs with a learning rate of $3\times 10^{-2}$ , batch size 256, and weight decay $10^{-4}$ . We use cosine annealing to decay the learning rate to zero over training.(; )He et al., 2025Li et al., 2023

    Appendix B

    Our Base Model is Strong

    We provide more results for Sec. , including PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS comparisons with 2–16 reference views on both datasets (Fig. ).4.2S4

    GLoD-LVSM

    We provide more results for Sec. , including PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS versus scene-token counts for and with 2, 4, 6, and 10 reference views on both datasets (Fig. ).4.2GLoD-LVSMCLiFTS3

    We provide more results for Sec. , including PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS comparisons across condenser designs with 2, 4, 6, and 10 reference views on both datasets (Figs. –). All methods use the same base model with culling disabled.4.3S5S8

    We provide more results for Sec. , including rendering FPS and speedups at 0, 0.5, 1, and 2 dB quality-loss budgets on both datasets with 10 reference views (Fig. ). The evaluation protocol is described in .4.4S1A.5

    Scaling Quality with Reference Views and Token Budget

    We provide more results for Sec. , including PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS on both datasets for increasing reference-view counts at fixed budgets of 512, 1,024, and 2,048 tokens (Fig. ) and increasing anchor budgets from 100% to 150% of the input token count (Fig. ). Culling is disabled in both experiments. For DL3DV with two reference views, the 2,048-anchor setting exceeds the corresponding highway token count of 1554. This is enabled by our continuous anchor field (Sec. ), which can sample an arbitrary number of anchors beyond the input token count.4.5S9S103.2

    Ablation Studies

    We provide more results for Sec. , including PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS for the same component ablations with 2, 4, 6, and 10 reference views on DL3DV (Figs. –).4.7S11S12

    GLoD-LVSM

    We provide scene-classification confusion matrix (Fig. ) for Sec. . The downstream evaluation protocols are given in .S24.8A.6

    Visual Comparison across Different Condensers.

    We provide more results for Sec. , including 34 selected novel-view examples with 2 and 10 reference views at 0%, 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80% token reduction on both datasets (Figs. –). For compact figure files, we JPEG-compress the full images at quality 88 without chroma subsampling (4:4:4), while keeping the zoom-in crops losslessly encoded.4.3S13S25

    We provide more results for Sec. , including emergent depth, point-cloud, 3D anchors, and projected-anchor visualizations for 12 RealEstate10K scenes and 15 DL3DV scenes using four reference views and 2,048 anchors (Figs. –).4.6S26S31

item.title: Stable Signer V3：4D 可变形基元泼溅做手语虚拟人 ｜ Stable Signer V3: 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting Is All You Need for Sign Language Production
item.description:
一句话：用 4D 可变形基元泼溅构建高分辨率手语数字人，补齐表情、身份形变与细节三个短板。

要点：

  • 共享面部基元泼溅用于更丰富的表情控制
  • 测试时身体基元修正与身份相关的形变
  • 保留细粒度外观细节

为什么值得看：做高保真角色与面部动画时，这套「共享基元加测试时个体化」的路子可迁移到虚拟角色系统。

中文摘要：Stable Signer V3 是一个基于 4D 可变形基元泼溅的交互式高分辨率手语虚拟人系统，针对现有方案的三点不足：面部表情受限、身份相关的身体形变不准、细节丢失。作者引入共享面部基元泼溅，以可迁移的超二次曲面基元实现更丰富的表情控制，并用测试时身体基元修正身份形变，同时保留细节。

来源：arXiv·cs.GR 最新（English） 相关度：10.2 正文：58055 字 / 15 图

作者：Sen Fang、Liwei Che、Dimitris N. Metaxas

分类：cs.CV / cs.AI cs.CL cs.GR

接收/备注：12 figures, 10 tables. Project Page at: https://signerx.github.io/Stable-Signer-V3

PDF：https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24926v1

命中：splatting

We present Stable Signer V3, an interactive high-resolution sign language avatar system built on 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting. It addresses three limitations of existing avatars: restricted facial expression, inaccurate identity-specific body deformation, and loss of fine appearance details. Shared Face Primitive Splatting adds transferable superquadric primitives for richer expression contro

Stable Signer V3: 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting Is All You Need for Sign Language Production

Sen Fang Liwei Che Dimitris N. Metaxas Rutgers University Affiliation: Affiliation: https://signerx.github.io/Stable-Signer-V3

Abstract

We present , an interactive high-resolution sign language avatar system built on . It addresses three limitations of existing avatars: restricted facial expression, inaccurate identity-specific body deformation, and loss of fine appearance details. adds transferable superquadric primitives for richer expression control; learns an identity-specific virtual muscle layer for more faithful motion; and uses TunnelingNet to recover identity-specific high-resolution details. Both test-time modules are optimized once per signer identity; inference then runs entirely from the stored identity parameters. Together, they reduce facial geometry error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2% on held-out evaluations, while retaining interactive streaming.Stable Signer V34D Deformable Primitive SplattingShared Face Primitive SplattingTest-Time Body Primitive SplattingTest-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution

1

Sign language production aims to translate text or lexical sequences into intelligible, natural, and expressive signing videos . Sign language conveys information through coordinated manual gestures, facial expressions, head poses, and body movements . A practical production system must therefore go beyond predicting skeletons or parametric poses: it must consistently express these motions through avatars with diverse identities and appearances, preserve subtle expressions and visual details, and meet the latency requirements of interactive applications .[, , ]57497[, , , ]4325178[, , ]261661

Existing approaches broadly follow two routes. synthesizes signing videos from intermediate poses with pose-conditioned image or video generation models . predicts language-conditioned 3D signing motion and uses it to animate explicit characters . Pose-guided human-video models provide additional tools for this pipeline . Dictionary-based production also exploits reusable signing segments and their transitions . Pose generation models provide structured representations of signing motion . Within these pipelines, 3D Gaussian splatting  enables efficient rendering, with recent extensions supporting signing avatars  and real-time upper-body animation . Fine-grained signing remains a central rendering challenge even with accurate 3D pose prediction and fast rendering. The resulting motion is jointly constrained by the local expressiveness of the parametric human model, the compatibility between template deformation and individual geometry, and the image decoder’s ability to reconstruct fine details. We investigate how compact adaptation mechanisms can improve signing expression by building on existing motion and avatar priors.Text2Pose2Video[, , , , , , ]5758485054638Text2Avatar[, , , , , ]18634132077[, , , ]935845[, ]6362[, , , , ]495170737[]25[, ]1320[]77

Three challenges motivate this work. First, the compact expression spaces of parametric face models such as FLAME  suppress subtle local motion and impose a geometric ceiling on facial detail. Second, shared skinning and deformation rules cannot consistently accommodate identity-specific body shape and local surface motion . An avatar that appears plausible in its reference pose can therefore develop local shape errors as the pose changes. Third, general-purpose decoders can discard identity-specific high-frequency details when reconstructing images from compact Gaussian features . These challenges concern facial control, identity-specific body deformation, and high-resolution appearance, respectively. Together, they limit the quality of existing sign language production systems.[]30[, , , ]28851538[, , ]712477

To address these challenges, we introduce , a sign language production system based on . Our key idea is to introduce a learnable local deformation layer between the parametric human model and the avatar, separating shared facial motion capabilities from identity-specific body and appearance adaptation. We instantiate the deformable primitives as superquadrics, allowing local residual deformations to vary with pose and expression while preserving the existing human control interface and avatar bindings. Given text or gloss input, the system uses SignSparK  for motion completion and GUAVA  for avatar initialization and feature rendering. A shared facial layer learns local residual deformations driven by FLAME expression, jaw, and eye controls and transfers them to the avatar through surface bindings. For the body, a pose-conditioned virtual muscle layer is fitted to each identity from reference videos; it corrects geometry before skinning so that bound Gaussians follow the adjusted surface, with displacement and smoothness constraints discouraging implausible deformations. For appearance, an independently normalized Softmax tunneling path uses terminal decoder semantics to learn identity-specific high-resolution detail while preserving the early Gaussian feature pathway. Test-time adaptation forms a one-time per-identity character-preparation stage. The resulting body and detail parameters serve every subsequent sequence, cleanly separating identity adaptation from online generation.Stable Signer V34D Deformable Primitive Splatting[]34[]77

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    A shared deformable primitive layer enables more complex and controllable facial expressions.Shared Face Primitive Splatting.

  • •

    An identity-specific virtual muscle layer adapts body deformation from reference videos while keeping the avatar generation backbone frozen.Test-Time Body Primitive Splatting.

  • •

    A late tunneling path learns identity-specific high-resolution detail from reference videos and stores it in the deployed decoder.Test-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution.

    • 2

    Resources such as WLASL , How2Sign , JWSign , and YouTube-SL-25  support research across lexical signs, continuous signing, and multiple languages. Pose-conditioned video synthesis has been explored through Text2Sign , SignSynth , and Everybody Sign Now , with subsequent work on appearance control, large-scale co-articulation, and diffusion-based synthesis . Broader human-video synthesis develops pose-guided generation through DreaMoving , Follow Your Pose , and MimicMotion , with ControlVideo  and Wan-Animate  further exploring controllable video generation and character animation. The 3D route combines signing-motion generation  with controllable avatar rendering . For motion generation, some methods retrieve and concatenate signing clips from existing dictionaries , while others learn to predict continuous motion from language inputs using progressive prediction or motion primitives . Motion modeling has also explored adversarial training, skeletal graph structure, and non-autoregressive generation . Related text-to-human-motion research studies diffusion-based synthesis and language-like motion modeling , providing a broader context for language-conditioned animation. Recent motion generators explore discrete diffusion for gloss-to-pose synthesis , autoregressive motion tokens , and multilingual generation from text and prompts . SignSparK  combines sparse keyframe control with conditional flow matching to generate dense 3D signing motion. Appearance transfer in skeletal pose sequences further studies how signer-specific characteristics can be changed while retaining signing motion . Together, these directions address motion accuracy, co-articulation, appearance control, and efficient generation . We build on this motion completion capability and focus on facial, body, and appearance adaptation for personalized avatar rendering.Sign Language Production.[]29[]6[]10[]59[]57[]58[]48[, , ]50548[]9[]35[]84[]83[]5[, , ]18634[, , ]132077[, , , ]76546362[, , ]495152[, , ]475317[, , ]806021[]70[]73[]7[]34[]37[, ]1661

    SMPL-X  provides joint body, hand, and facial controls for animatable humans, while FLAME  models facial shape, expression, and articulation. These parametric representations support pose-driven signing avatars . Whole-body reconstruction methods, including SMPLer-X and component-aware mesh recovery , and dedicated hand reconstruction  support detailed avatar controls; DWPose provides complementary whole-body keypoint estimates . Complementary work improves 3D pose estimation for sign language  and resolves hand-to-hand intersections , supporting more reliable motion inputs. Accurate facial and body motion is particularly relevant to signing, where non-manual cues contribute to meaning . Building on 3D Gaussian splatting , SplattingAvatar  embeds Gaussians on a deformable mesh surface, while GART  learns forward skinning and latent bones to capture articulated and non-rigid motion. Articulated Gaussian models further explore cage-based deformation in D3GA , monocular human reconstruction in GauHuman , and efficient human rendering in ASH and HiFi4G . Related efforts address monocular Gaussian avatar reconstruction in GVA , image-based body estimation in GST , and generalizable sparse-view synthesis in GHG . Expressive avatar reconstruction is also studied by X-Avatar  and EVA , with EVA learning Gaussian human avatars from monocular RGB video. SignSplat  adapts Gaussian avatars to signing through sequence-level mesh fitting and Gaussian regularization, emphasizing accurate hands and facial expressions. We retain structured human controls and surface bindings while adding a shared facial residual layer and identity-specific body deformation.3D Humans and Gaussian Avatars for Sign Language.[]40[]30[, ]186[, ]332[]41[]72[]18[]19[, ]2678[]25[]55[]28[]85[]15[, ]3824[]33[]44[]27[]56[]13[]20

    Video-based character reconstruction has developed through HumanNeRF  and NeuMan , with Vid2Avatar exploring self-supervised scene decomposition for videos in the wild . Efficient character preparation is explored by InstantAvatar , which learns avatars from monocular video. Subject-specific optimization can recover detailed avatar appearance: Gaussian Head Avatar  jointly learns neutral Gaussians and an expression-driven deformation field for high-fidelity 2K head rendering. Reference-conditioned image and video synthesis transfers appearance from exemplar images . High-resolution conditional synthesis and latent diffusion provide complementary image-generation frameworks , with ControlNet  and ControlNeXt  exploring additional conditioning for image and video generation. For 3D avatars, GUAVA  predicts an animatable upper-body Gaussian avatar from a single image and refines rendered features with a neural decoder. Lightweight adaptation offers a way to reuse pretrained representations: LoRA  learns low-rank weight updates, and LLaMA-Adapter  introduces new conditioning through zero-initialized attention. Adapters also connect pretrained visual representations to dense prediction tasks . These adaptation mechanisms motivate compact trainable paths around a frozen backbone. We combine generalizable avatar initialization with identity-specific adaptation of body geometry and high-resolution appearance. Character reference videos supervise a body deformation layer and a detail module at the decoder’s terminal stage, with the pretrained backbone held fixed. Both modules are optimized once per signer, and online signing directly reuses the stored parameters.Personalized Avatars and Test-Time Training.[]69[]23[]11[]22[]71[, ]7564[, ]6546[]79[]42[]77[]12[]81[]4

    3

    3.1

    Given text or gloss input, SignSparK  completes dictionary-retrieved sparse poses into body, hand, and facial controls $\{\mathbf{q}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ . GUAVA  initializes a surface-bound Gaussian avatar from a reference image. We augment this pipeline with shared facial deformation and identity-specific body and appearance adaptation.[]34[]77

    For signer $s$ , aligned reference images, controls, and cameras $\mathcal{V}_{s}=\{I_{t},\mathbf{q}_{t},\pi_{t}\}$ supervise image formation:

    $\widehat{I}_{t}=\mathcal{D}_{\psi_{s}}\!\left(\mathcal{R}_{\pi_{t}}\!\left[\mathcal{G}_{s}(\mathbf{q}_{t};\phi,\theta_{s})\right]\right),$ (1)

    where $\phi$ is the shared facial controller, $\theta_{s}$ is the body adaptation, and $\mathcal{G}_{s}$ transports Gaussians with the deformed surface. The rasterizer $\mathcal{R}$ projects Gaussian features, and $\mathcal{D}_{\psi_{s}}$ decodes them into high-resolution RGB. Adaptation occurs once per identity; inference runs from stored parameters.

    3.2

    Here denotes pose- and time-conditioned primitive transformations across motion sequences. A sparse field blends control-dependent affine residuals over superquadric supports. Primitive $k$ has center $\mathbf{c}_{k}$ , orthonormal frame $\mathbf{R}_{k}$ , positive axis lengths $\mathbf{a}_{k}$ , and normalized distance4D

    $d_{k}(\mathbf{x})=\left\|\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{a}_{k})^{-1}\mathbf{R}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}_{k})\right\|_{4}.$ (2)

    The level set $d_{k}(\mathbf{x})=1$ defines a superellipsoid with fixed shape exponents. Centers are initialized in bilateral pairs, and local surface covariance determines orientations and scales. The supports remain fixed during controller learning. Each surface sample receives a sparse neighborhood $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x})$ with weights

    $w_{k}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\exp[-2d_{k}(\mathbf{x})^{2}]}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x})}\exp[-2d_{j}(\mathbf{x})^{2}]}.$ (3)

    Fixed reference-surface bindings blend controller-predicted affine residuals $(\mathbf{A}_{k,t},\mathbf{b}_{k,t})$ :

    $\Delta\mathbf{x}_{t}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x})}w_{k}(\mathbf{x})\left[\mathbf{A}_{k,t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{c}_{k})+\mathbf{b}_{k,t}\right],$ (4)

    Here $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ uses local coordinates. Zero-initialized controller outputs preserve geometry. The field deforms the surface, while bound Gaussians supply appearance.

    3.3

    The shared facial field is conditioned on

    $\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{face}}_{t}=[\mathbf{e}_{t},\mathbf{j}_{t},\mathbf{o}_{t},\boldsymbol{\ell}_{t}],$ (5)

    comprising 50 expression coefficients, three jaw parameters, six eye-pose parameters, and two eyelid controls. Global head orientation is handled by the body rig. A multilayer perceptron maps normalized facial controls to the affine residuals in Eq. . Common facial surface correspondences provide the interface for transferring the shared controller across identities.4

    Paired geometry from a tracked FLAME sequence uses ten expression coefficients for the base and fifty for the target, with other controls identical. For corresponding surface samples $\mathbf{x}_{ti}$ and $\mathbf{y}_{ti}$ , we minimize

    $\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{face}}={}&\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{(t,i)\in\Omega}\omega_{i}\rho(\mathbf{x}_{ti}+\Delta\mathbf{x}_{ti}-\mathbf{y}_{ti})\\ &+\lambda_{f}\mathbb{E}_{t}\|\mathbf{T}_{t}\|_{F}^{2},\end{split}$ (6)

    where $\rho$ is a smooth $L_{1}$ penalty, $\Omega$ indexes training samples, and $\mathbf{T}_{t}$ collects affine coefficients. Weights $\omega_{i}$ emphasize lips and eyes. Appearance, opacity, and the decoder remain frozen; compatible facial bindings transfer the controller across identities.

    3.4

    An identity-specific virtual muscle layer covers the torso, shoulders, arms, and wrists. Static and pose-dependent affine corrections capture individual surface motion:

    $\mathbf{T}_{s,t}=\tanh\!\left(\mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{static}}_{s}+f_{\theta_{s}}(\overline{\mathbf{p}}_{t})\right),$ (7)

    where $\overline{\mathbf{p}}_{t}$ is the normalized 63-dimensional body pose. Static and dynamic components capture shape and articulation effects, with bounded coefficients limiting distortion.

    The blended field modifies the canonical carrier before skinning:

    $\widetilde{\mathbf{V}}_{s,t}=\operatorname{LBS}\!\left(\mathbf{V}^{\mathrm{can}}_{s}+\mathcal{S}(\Delta\mathbf{V}_{s,t}),\mathbf{q}_{t}\right).$ (8)

    Here $\mathcal{S}$ smooths offsets along body mesh edges, preserving the head, hands, and motion controls. Template and UV Gaussians follow corrected vertices and parent triangles, respectively.

    Differentiable rendering supervises a dilated visibility region of body-bound Gaussians. Raw and decoded RGB, gradients, SSIM , silhouette, and boundary losses enforce video alignment:[]67

    $\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{body}}={}&\lambda_{r}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{raw}}+\lambda_{c}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rgb}}+\lambda_{g}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grad}}+\lambda_{s}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ssim}}\\ &+\lambda_{m}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mask}}+\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{boundary}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}.\end{split}$ (9)

    Regularization penalizes affine magnitude, neighboring translations, and mean vertex displacement. The avatar generator, appearance, and renderer remain frozen. Held-out reconstruction guides selection.

    3.5

    A late Softmax tunnel adapts terminal decoder features into identity-specific detail before RGB prediction.

    Let $\mathbf{h}_{t}(\mathbf{p})$ be the terminal feature at location $\mathbf{p}$ . Learnable spatial keys and values $\{\mathbf{k}_{s,n},\mathbf{v}_{s,n}\}_{n=1}^{N}$ are initialized from reference frames and optimized by video reconstruction. Interpolation to the feature resolution gives

    $\displaystyle\alpha_{t,n}(\mathbf{p})$ $\displaystyle=\frac{\exp[\mathbf{z}_{t}(\mathbf{p})^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{k}_{s,n}(\mathbf{p})/\sqrt{r}]}{\sum_{m=1}^{N}\exp[\mathbf{z}_{t}(\mathbf{p})^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{k}_{s,m}(\mathbf{p})/\sqrt{r}]},$ (10) $\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}(\mathbf{p})$ $\displaystyle=\mathbf{h}_{t}(\mathbf{p})+W_{o}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\alpha_{t,n}(\mathbf{p})\mathbf{v}_{s,n}(\mathbf{p}),$ (11)

    Here $N$ is the number of memory slots, $\mathbf{z}_{t}(\mathbf{p})=W_{q}\mathbf{h}_{t}(\mathbf{p})$ , and $r$ is the query/key dimension. Projections $W_{q}$ and $W_{o}$ map into and out of the tunnel, while $\alpha_{t,n}$ weights slot $n$ . Softmax normalizes slots per location; zero-initialized $W_{o}$ preserves the original feature path.

    Low-rank updates $\Delta W=BA$ , with trainable factors $A$ and $B$ , complement the tunnel with pretrained weights frozen. Training and inference use one StyleUNet  pass; stored identity memory supplies the deployed inference path.[]66

    High-resolution reconstruction.

    Let $J_{t}$ be the decoded RGB image and $\mathcal{U}_{q}$ denote spatial upsampling by factor $q$ . The intermediate reconstruction is

    $\widehat{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{mid}}=\mathcal{U}_{q}(J_{t})+\mathcal{H}_{s}(\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t},J_{t}),$ (12)

    where $\mathcal{H}_{s}$ is an identity-adapted PixelShuffle residual head. A shared fully convolutional head refines aligned native-resolution crops for 4K output. High-resolution target patches preserve supervision detail.

    Appearance objective.

    We learn appearance parameters from aligned video frames with fixed geometry and Gaussian features. Intermediate-resolution supervision combines RGB, image-gradient, multiscale high-pass, detail-band, local-contrast, perceptual, and low-frequency penalties. The native-resolution head receives RGB, gradient, high-pass, and local-detail supervision:

    $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{detail}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{mid}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mid}}+\mathbb{E}_{t,\mathcal{P}}\sum_{a}\lambda_{a}\mathcal{L}_{a}(\widehat{I}_{t}^{\mathcal{P}},I_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}),$ (13)

    Here $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mid}}$ is the intermediate loss above; $\lambda_{\mathrm{mid}}$ and $\lambda_{a}$ are nonnegative weights. The crop $\mathcal{P}$ is shared by prediction and target, and $a$ indexes the native-resolution loss terms. Patch sampling preserves target-frequency information while bounding training memory. Body and detail adaptation are optimized with their respective frozen components, yielding a geometric controller and an appearance decoder for each identity. Online signing combines these modules with the shared facial field and newly generated motion.

    4

    4.1

    The evaluation covers facial expression reconstruction, identity-specific body adaptation, and high-resolution detail recovery.

    Controlled face and body studies use chronological 80%/20% training–evaluation splits and fixed optimization budgets; checkpoint selection uses the training segment exclusively. Detail adaptation is evaluated on held-out frames, and cross-method rendering uses identical poses, cameras, backgrounds, and target-defined crops for every method. Scores are first aggregated per identity and then macro-averaged.Data and protocol.

    Facial geometry is measured by Euclidean point error in the native shared tracked coordinates. Body adaptation reports refined RGB L1, boundary L1, and SSIM . Rendering comparisons use foreground PSNR  together with SSIM and LPIPS  inside a shared ground-truth person crop. Runtime measurements distinguish independently warmed stage throughput from measured resident-pipeline wall time. Semantic preservation is evaluated through fixed back-translation using BLEU-4  and ROUGE-L F1  on poses re-extracted from the rendered RGB videos.Metrics.[]67[]68[]82[]39[]31

    4.2

    We train the shared face layer on the tracked FLAME sequence provided with GUAVA , using a chronological 80%/20% training–evaluation split and a fixed optimization budget. The restricted FLAME carrier and the full-expression target share identical articulation, isolating the expression geometry that our layer must recover.[]77

    Table  reports Euclidean error over all retained head samples, including template- and UV-bound samples: mean head error falls from 1.267 to 0.362 mm (71.4%), and facial error falls from 1.492 to 0.518 mm. Figure  shows the held-out midpoint with a shared error scale and $5\times$ deviation magnification. The shared primitive controller reduces head error by 71.4% and recovers fine expression geometry across the face; region-wise results are provided in the supplement.14

    4.3

    Figure  compares frozen GUAVA, an Adapter, and our tunneling decoder through synchronized facial crops. The 512-resolution baseline is enlarged for display. Both adapted outputs are generated at 1024 resolution, and the visualization presents the combined effect of adaptation and native-resolution decoding. All trainable variants use the same frames, Gaussian features, targets, optimizer, and update budget. On held-out frames, Adapter reduces mean RGB L1 by 13.5%, while tunneling reduces it by 24.2% relative to the frozen baseline.6

    4.4

    Under a fixed 249-step adaptation budget and chronological 80%/20% training–evaluation split, Table  shows that increasing $K$ from 512 to 1,024 reduces refined RGB L1 from 0.0599 to 0.0575 and boundary L1 from 0.0282 to 0.0270.2

    Figure  compares frozen GUAVA with identity-specific Body SQ under the same frame, pose, and camera; the learned layer locally adapts the carrier around the torso and upper arms.5

    Reference overlays locate the learned patches, carrier views expose their geometric support, and RGB errors use the same $[0,0.08]$ range with darker colors indicating larger error, separating surface alignment from its effect on rendering. Figure  highlights the resulting geometric fit, and Table  confirms simultaneous gains in RGB fidelity, boundary alignment, and structural similarity.52

    4.5

    Table  reports warmed batch-one component throughput on a single Quadro RTX 8000. Motion synthesis and primitive deformation run at 198.7 and 320.9 FPS, while HD avatar rendering and 4K detail refinement reach 52.0 and 47.6 FPS. In the resident pipeline, stages overlap across streaming chunks. A warmed 784-frame, three-chunk text-to-HD-avatar run completes in 31.0 seconds wall time (25.3 generated FPS), including composition, motion synthesis, streamed rendering, encoding, and chunk concatenation. Body and detail adaptation are performed once for each new avatar and baked into the deployed model; subsequent sequences run directly from the baked parameters.Online efficiency.3

    Table  tests whether the proposed visual enhancement components alter the linguistic content of the output. Both configurations render the same motion sequence; the full configuration additionally activates shared face primitives, test-time body primitives, and detail tunneling. We re-extract signing poses from each rendered video and translate them with the same frozen back-translation model. Activating all three components raises BLEU-4 from 25.6450 to 26.8897 (4.9%) and ROUGE-L from 59.4771 to 61.7298 (3.8%). The complete enhancement stack therefore improves geometric and rendering fidelity while fully preserving the underlying signs.Back-translation evaluation.4

    Table  first compares our system with four reproducible open-source avatar methods at one shared held-out pose for each of four input reference videos. We compute PSNR inside the shared ground-truth foreground mask and SSIM/LPIPS within the same ground-truth person bounding box, then macro-average identities. The second block evaluates our identity-adapted renderer against frozen GUAVA using matched cached features and crops sampled directly from held-out 4K targets.Rendering fidelity.5

    The second block measures identity adaptation by comparing frozen GUAVA and our complete renderer on the same held-out subset from each of ten reference videos. Both methods receive identical cached Gaussian features, crop coordinates, and $768{\times}768$ crops sampled directly from the held-out 4K frames. Macro-averaged over identities, Stable Signer V3 raises PSNR from 19.418 to 21.790 dB and SSIM from 0.833 to 0.860, while reducing LPIPS from 0.245 to 0.226. This corresponds to a 2.372 dB PSNR gain and an 8.0% relative LPIPS reduction over the frozen renderer.

    4.6

    Figure  compares methods column by column on the same sign-language sequence. The four published baselines are followed by our method and Ground Truth. The shared framing makes facial detail, finger articulation, and garment boundaries directly comparable across columns. Across identities and poses, our method preserves facial character, articulated fingers, silhouettes, and garment boundaries more consistently than the reproduced baselines.7

    5

    We presented Stable Signer V3, a sign language production framework combining shared facial primitives, test-time identity-specific body primitives, and a tunneling decoder for high-resolution appearance. Together, they unify expressive control and personalized rendering through a reusable deformable representation. Reference-video adaptation is performed once, after which the stored identity parameters drive subsequent signing sequences. On held-out evaluations, the three modules reduce head reconstruction error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2%, while retaining interactive inference. Future work will broaden signer and motion coverage and include evaluation by proficient sign-language users.
